items.title: Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma, Version 4.2026, NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines In Oncology.
items.abstract: The NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology (NCCN Guidelines) for Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma provide multidisciplinary diagnostic workup, staging, and treatment recommendations for resectable, borderline resectable, unresectable, locally advanced, and metastatic disease. This article summarizes the studies and Panel discussion that serve as the rationale for comprehensive care recommendations included in the NCCN Guidelines for Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma.

items.title: Strategies to develop therapeutic cancer vaccines for pancreatic cancer.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest malignancies. Conventional immunotherapies have shown little clinical benefit, largely due to the low neoantigenicity and profoundly immunosuppressive microenvironment of this cancer. Therapeutic cancer vaccines have emerged as a rational strategy to prime or amplify antitumour immunity, supported by advances in antigen discovery, genomic profiling, and vaccine engineering. Here, we report a review of clinical trials evaluating therapeutic cancer vaccines in PDAC. Eligible studies were identified through searches of ClinicalTrials.gov from database inception to Aug 31, 2025, with manual screening of trial-linked publications up to Jan 31, 2026. 135 records were identified, of which 120 met the eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis. Across vaccine platforms-cell-based, nucleic acid-based, protein and peptide-based, microorganism-based, and multiplatform strategies-early-phase clinical studies consistently show feasibility, favourable safety profiles, and the induction of tumour-specific immune responses. However, immune activation has rarely translated into durable clinical benefit. To date, the most compelling biological signals derive from personalised neoantigen vaccines, particularly mRNA-based approaches, which can elicit high-magnitude CD8+ T-cell responses and long-lived clonal persistence in postoperative PDAC. Emerging evidence also supports the potential of shared neoantigens, such as KRASmut, as biologically relevant and scalable targets. Collectively, our findings highlight a shift towards rational vaccine combination strategies aimed at overcoming stromal and myeloid-mediated immunosuppression. Future progress will depend on integrating therapeutic vaccination into multimodal regimens and evaluating these approaches in adequately powered, biomarker-selected clinical trials.

items.title: Prognostic and Clinicopathological Significance of CD74 Expression in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal solid malignancies, and reliable prognostic biomarkers are urgently needed to guide risk stratification and treatment. CD74 has been implicated in tumor progression, invasion, and pro-inflammatory signaling in various cancers. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the association between CD74 expression and key clinicopathological features and survival outcomes in patients with PDAC. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus to identify eligible studies reporting on CD74 expression in PDAC tissues (PROSPERO: CRD420261402709). Studies were selected following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the QUIPS tool. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for the associations between CD74 expression and perineural invasion (PNI), lymphatic invasion, lymph node metastasis (pN), vascular permeation, pTNM stage, and overall survival. Statistical analyses were performed using Review Manager v5.4. DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models were applied as sensitivity analysis for every outcome, with Mantel-Haenszel fixed-effects models as the primary analysis according to the level of heterogeneity, which was quantified using the I2 statistic. A total of 83 records were initially identified, of which five studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the quantitative synthesis. CD74-positive expression was significantly associated with an increased risk of perineural invasion (four cohorts, 351 patients; OR = 3.69; 95% CI: 2.27-5.99; p < 0.00001; I2 = 0%), lymphatic invasion (four cohorts, 351 patients; OR = 2.05; 95% CI: 1.21-3.46; p = 0.007; I2 = 0%), and lymph node metastasis (four cohorts, 462 patients; OR = 1.94; 95% CI: 1.27-2.96; p = 0.002; I2 = 0%). A non-significant trend toward increased vascular permeation (three cohorts, 181 patients; OR = 1.99; 95% CI: 0.84-4.68; p = 0.12; I2 = 0%) and advanced pTNM stage (three cohorts, 284 patients; OR = 1.62; 95% CI: 0.93-2.82; p = 0.09; I2 = 0%) was also observed. Importantly, CD74 positivity was significantly associated with worse overall survival (three cohorts, 293 patients; HR = 2.04, 95% CI: 1.45-2.88; p < 0.00001; I2 = 0%). This analysis was structured into two subgroups: HR = 2.21 (95% CI: 1.50-3.25) in the two cohorts contributing multivariable-adjusted, immunohistochemistry-based estimates, and HR = 1.52 (95% CI: 0.72-3.21) in the single cohort contributing a univariable estimate reconstructed from transcript-level data, with no significant difference between the subgroups (p = 0.38). Because the estimated between-study variance was zero for every outcome, random-effects estimates were almost identical to the fixed-effects estimates throughout. As the pooled survival estimate combines adjusted with unadjusted estimates, it describes a prognostic association rather than established independent prognostic value. This meta-analysis demonstrates that elevated CD74 expression in PDAC is significantly associated with perineural invasion, lymphatic invasion, lymph node metastasis, and poorer overall survival, supporting an association with an adverse prognostic. Because the evidence base comprises few retrospective cohorts that used different, non-standardized thresholds to define CD74 positivity and different definitions of several outcomes, these findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating: they identify CD74 as a candidate for prospective validation and mechanistic investigation rather than as an established biomarker for risk stratification or therapeutic decision-making. Further large-scale prospective studies are warranted to validate these results and explore the clinical utility of CD74-targeted strategies.

items.title: Efficacy and Safety of Daraxonrasib (RMC-6236) in Previously Treated Metastatic RAS-Mutated Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Introduction: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is associated with a poor prognosis, and RAS gene mutations are present in more than 90% of cases. For this reason, direct RAS inhibition is a promising, but thus far difficult to achieve, therapeutic strategy. Daraxonrasib (RMC-6236) is a first-in-class, oral, non-covalent, multiselective inhibitor of the active form of RAS. It forms an intracellular trimeric complex with cyclophilin A, blocking both mutant and wild-type variants of the KRAS, NRAS, and HRAS genes. The aim of this systematic review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of daraxonrasib in previously treated patients with RAS-mutated PDAC. Methods: This review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov for studies published between January 2020 and July 2026. Two studies met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed: the Phase 1-2 RMC-6236-001 (n = 168) and the Phase 3 RASolute 302 trial (n = 500), involving a total of 668 patients. The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool for the randomized trial and the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies (MINORS) tool. Results: In the RASolute 302 trial, daraxonrasib out performed investigator-selected chemotherapy in a population of patients with the RAS G12 mutation, improving median overall survival (13.2 vs. 6.6 months; HR 0.40), progression-free survival (7.3 vs. 3.5 months; HR 0.45), and objective response rate (33.2% vs. 11.8%; all p < 0.001), and also delayed the onset of pain and deterioration in quality of life. These results were consistent with the earlier RMC-6236-001 study (objective response rate [ORR] 35%, median overall survival [OS] 13.1 months in patients with RAS G12 mutation treated in the second-line setting). Daraxonrasib exhibited a predictable toxicity profile, consisting mainly of Grade 1-2 dermatologic and gastrointestinal symptoms, with lower rates of hematologic toxicity and treatment discontinuation than with chemotherapy. Conclusions: Daraxonrasib demonstrates clinically relevant and statistically significant efficacy with an acceptable safety profile in previously treated patients with metastatic RAS G12-mutated PDAC, the population for which the strongest randomized evidence is currently available. These findings support its potential as a promising new treatment option in this setting. Further studies are needed regarding rare RAS gene variants and forms of the disease with wild-type RAS.

items.title: Histotripsy x Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest malignancies, with 5-year survival around 12% despite advances in surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy. Existing ablative therapies (RFA, microwave, irreversible electroporation) are limited by thermal injury risk, proximity to vessels/ducts. Novel local therapies that can be integrated with systemic regimens are urgently needed. Histotripsy is a non-thermal focused ultrasound modality that uses controlled cavitation to mechanically liquefy tissue without thermal coagulation or ionizing radiation, with precision under real-time ultrasound guidance. Preclinical and early translational work in pancreatic models shows that histotripsy can safely ablate pancreatic tissue while sparing major vessels and ducts in large-animal models, and can alter the tumour microenvironment (TME) with increased release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), enhanced dendritic cell and macrophage activation, and increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration in murine pancreatic tumours.

This proposal aims to evaluate the safety, local tumour control, and immunologic effects of histotripsy in pancreatic cancer especially PDAC, positioning it as a platform to enhance responsiveness to contemporary systemic therapies.

The HistoSonics Histotripsy System is now registered in the Medical Device Administration Control System from Department of Health in Hong Kong (HKMD no: 252842).

items.title: Radiotherapy combined with serplulimab, and chemotherapy as first-line treatment for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma: a multicenter, single-arm, phase II trial.
items.abstract:
PURPOSE: The prognosis for metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (mPDAC) remains dismal. In this multicenter, single-arm, phase II study, we evaluated the combination of serplulimab, gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel, and radiotherapy (ICSBR regimen) as first-line treatment for mPDAC patients (ChiCTR2300073237).
METHODS: Patients with mPDAC were enrolled in the first-line setting. The treatment regimen consisted of serplulimab and gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel administered in 21-day cycles, combined with stereotactic body radiotherapy directed at the primary or metastatic sites during cycle 2. Additionally, comprehensive biomarker analysis was conducted. The primary endpoint was the 6-month progression-free survival (PFS) rate, with a predefined target of 60%.
RESULT: Forty-six patients received at least one dose of treatment. The 6-month PFS rate was 78.3% (95% CI, 67.2%-91.1%). The median PFS and overall survival (OS) were 8.5 months (95% CI, 7.3-12.0 months) and 14.0 months (95% CI, 12.0 months-not reached), respectively. The objective response rate was 73.9% (95% CI, 58.9%-85.7%). The combination treatment was well tolerated, and no treatment-related deaths or unexpected safety signals were observed. Notably, patients with baseline ctDNA negativity achieved a better survival. Moreover, tumor microenvironment (TME) analysis revealed that baseline fibroblast activation protein-positive cancer-associated fibroblast and T-cell proportions in tumor tissue correlated with clinical outcomes, with distinct spatial distribution and interaction tendencies observed among patients with different responses.
CONCLUSION: Overall, the ICSBR regimen demonstrated a promising survival benefit as first-line treatment for mPDAC. Furthermore, ctDNA status and TME analysis highlighted potential markers for guiding precision treatment.

items.title: Prognostic Value and Longitudinal Dynamics of Multigene Circulating Tumor DNA in Advanced Pancreatic Cancer Treated with 5-Fluorouracil-Based Chemotherapy.
items.abstract: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is a minimally invasive biomarker in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), but the prognostic information added by multigene ctDNA metrics beyond KRAS and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) is uncertain. In this prospective observational pilot study, 51 patients with advanced PDAC receiving 5-fluorouracil-based chemotherapy underwent 118-gene ctDNA profiling at baseline and 4 and 8 weeks after treatment initiation. ctDNA burden was summarized with variant allele frequency (VAF) metrics: Sum VAF and Top4 VAF (KRAS, TP53, CDKN2A, SMAD4). Twelve-month progression-free survival (PFS) areas under the curve were 0.816 for Top4 VAF, 0.812 for Sum VAF, 0.788 for KRAS VAF, and 0.687 for CA19-9; the Top4-KRAS difference was not statistically significant (95% confidence interval, -0.120 to 0.131). Baseline ctDNA detection and high Top4 VAF remained associated with shorter PFS and overall survival after adjustment for clinical covariates. Detectable Top4 VAF at 4 weeks was associated with shorter PFS (hazard ratio, 5.739; p < 0.001). Top4 VAF changes differed across radiologic response categories at 8 but not 4 weeks; CA19-9 showed no significant paired change. These exploratory findings suggest that baseline and early on-treatment multigene ctDNA carries prognostic information in advanced PDAC, although superiority over KRAS or CA19-9 was not established.

items.title: Repurposing Mefloquine for Pancreatic Cancer Treatment
items.abstract:
Pancreatic cancer (specifically pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, PDAC) is a very aggressive disease that is often diagnosed too late for surgery, and the medicines currently available, mainly two chemotherapy combinations called modified FOLFIRINOX (mFFX) and gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel (GnP), can extend life but rarely cure patients.

This study examines mefloquine, a well-studied antimalarial drug, as a new way to attack pancreatic cancer. Laboratory work has shown that mefloquine can block an enzyme (TYMS) that cancer cells need to make DNA, and unlike many existing drugs it does not cause the cancer cells to produce more of that enzyme and become resistant. In several mouse models, as well as tumors grown from human patients, oral mefloquine at doses that were well tolerated (up to 300 mg/kg) slowed tumor growth and helped the animals live longer.

This trial aims to find a safe dose of mefloquine for PDAC patients. A classic "3 + 3" design will be used in three separate arms: one taking mFFX, one taking GnP, and one taking mefloquine as monotherapy after exhausting standard of care treatment options. The main goals are to determine the recommended Phase 2 dose and to collect early signals that the drug might help shrink tumors when combined with existing chemotherapy. If the trial shows that mefloquine can be given safely and hints at improved tumor control, it would pave the way for larger studies that could eventually add an established and already-approved drug to the existing treatment options for advanced pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Driver mutation profiling by next-generation sequencing predicts survival and recurrence after curative-intent resection for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: a genomic cohort study.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is standard practice in metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), yet its prognostic utility in patients undergoing curative-intent resection remains poorly defined. Characterizing whether driver mutations independently influence post-surgical outcomes [overall survival (OS), time-to-recurrence (TTR), and pathological response (PR)] may inform perioperative risk stratification and patient selection for emerging targeted therapies.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults undergoing pancreatectomy for PDAC at a single high-volume academic center (2016-2025), with concurrent NGS profiling. Clinicopathologic and genomic data (KRAS, TP53, CDKN2A, SMAD4, and BRCA2 mutations) were obtained from an integrated institutional data commons. OS and TTR were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression. PR (College of American Pathologists grade 0-1) was assessed using logistic regression.
RESULTS: Of 188 eligible patients (median age: 66; 42.5% female), 83.5% received neoadjuvant chemotherapy and 12.8% achieved major pathological response. KRAS was the most prevalent mutation (84.6%), followed by TP53 (61.7%), CDKN2A (33.0%), SMAD4 (18.1%), and BRCA2 (3.2%). Median TTR and OS were 10.8 and 27.1 months, respectively. In multivariable analysis, TP53 mutation was associated with shorter OS (HR, 1.65 95% CI 1.02-2.66), and CDKN2A mutation with shorter TTR (HR 1.69, 95% CI 1.19-2.39). KRAS was associated with poorer PR compared to wild type (OR 4.45, 95% CI 1.26-15.65).
CONCLUSION: In this exploratory analysis, TP53 and CDKN2A mutations were independently associated with poorer outcomes post-PDAC resection, supporting the potential of upfront NGS for perioperative risk stratification. Prospective, multicenter validation is needed to establish clinical utility.

items.title: Toward Clinically Actionable Prediction of Recurrence and Metastatic Progression in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract:
PURPOSE: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has high rates of early recurrence (ER), occult metastasis, and poor survival despite curative-intent therapy. Predictive factors and models span clinical, biomarker, imaging, radiomics, pathologic, and molecular domains, but clinical readiness remains uncertain.
METHODS: We performed a systematic review in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses. Five databases were searched for studies evaluating predictors or models of PDAC recurrence, metastasis, lymph node metastasis (LNM), occult metastatic disease, disease-free survival (DFS) or recurrence-free survival, or recurrence patterns. Studies were screened and coded for end point, modality, model type, validation, discrimination, calibration, clinical utility, and predictor timing.
RESULTS: Of 234 full-text records, 208 studies were included, comprising 144 prediction models and 64 predictor/prognostic factor studies. Computed tomography/radiomics (141/208), clinical/electronic health record variables (104/208), and serum/urine biomarkers (46/208) were the most common modalities. External validation, calibration, and decision-curve analyses were reported in 52, 36, and 38 model studies, respectively. AUCs ranged from 0.70 to 0.92 for ER, 0.75-0.95 for LNM, and 0.71-0.88 for liver or occult metastasis; DFS/relapse-free survival models had C-indices of 0.62-0.82. One externally validated occult-metastasis model had a C-statistic of 0.56. Model maturity was limited by retrospective design, heterogeneous end points, incomplete calibration reporting, and postoperative variables in preoperative models.
CONCLUSION: Prediction models for PDAC recurrence and metastatic progression are rapidly expanding, particularly through radiomics, machine learning, and multimodal modeling. Clinical translation requires decision-aligned design, transparent reporting, external validation, calibration, interpretability, and prospective evaluation of clinical utility.

items.title: Efficacy and toxicities of modified FOLFIRINOX versus gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel as first-line chemotherapy for unresectable pancreatic cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Modified FOLFIRINOX (mFFX) and gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (GnP) are both recommended as standard first-line regimens for unresectable pancreatic cancer (PC). However, direct head-to-head comparative evidence remains scarce, and prior studies have largely failed to distinguish mFFX from standard FOLFIRINOX (sFFX). We systematically compared mFFX with GnP to evaluate their efficacy and toxicities.
METHODS: We searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies comparing mFFX with GnP as first-line therapy for unresectable PC published between January 2013 and May 2026. Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were assessed using hazard ratios (HRs). Objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) were evaluated using risk ratios (RRs). Events of toxicities were assessed using odds ratios (ORs).
RESULTS: Five studies (three RCTs and two retrospective studies) involving 1204 patients (578 in the mFFX arm and 626 in the GnP arm) were included. Compared with GnP, mFFX was associated with a shorter OS (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.09-1.45; P = 0.002) and PFS (HR 1.21, 95% CI 1.04-1.40; P = 0.01), along with a borderline lower DCR (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.81-1.00; P = 0.05; I2 = 62%), which was consistent across RCTs (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.81-0.94; I2 = 0%) but not observed in retrospective studies (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.71-1.29; I2 = 87%), and ORR did not differ significantly between the two regimens. As for toxicity profiles, mFFX showed an elevated incidence of grade ≥3 diarrhea (OR 5.63) and anorexia (OR 4.44). By contrast, grade ≥3 neutropenia (OR 0.66) and white blood cell decrease (OR 0.49) occurred more frequently under GnP.
CONCLUSIONS: GnP was associated with more favorable OS and PFS than mFFX, a borderline DCR advantage, and distinct toxicity profiles. Given the modest effect size and the limitations of this study, clinical decision-making should integrate patient age, performance status, and anticipated second-line therapy.

items.title: Utilizing Standard of Care Induction Chemotherapy Followed by MR-LINAC Radiotherapy and Surgical Exploration to Improve Resectability Rates in Potentially Resectable Locally Advanced Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract: Locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC) is a high-mortality condition. This single-institution, Phase II, single-arm investigator-initiated trial at Allegheny Health Network investigates the optimal timing and integration of established standard-of-care interventions for biopsy-proven LAPC. Eligible participants will receive standard 4 months of induction chemotherapy, followed by standard MR-LINAC-guided radiotherapy, and subsequent surgical exploration with curative intent where feasible. The research question specifically pertains to the efficacy and safety of this predefined treatment sequence, aiming to increase the proportion of LAPC patients who achieve R0 resection and to translate local control gains into better survival and quality of life. The study plans to accrue approximately 18-20 patients.

items.title: Tobacco Carcinogen Induces Persistent DNA Damage and Homologous Recombination Dysregulation in Pancreatic Ductal Carcinogenesis.
items.abstract: Cigarette smoking is a well-established risk factor for the development of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), yet the mechanisms by which tobacco carcinogens, such as Nicotine-Derived Nitrosamine Ketone (NNK), drive pancreatic carcinogenesis remain incompletely understood. We investigated the impact of NNK on pancreatic epithelium by treating human pancreatic ductal epithelial cells (HPDE6-E6E7; H6c7) with NNK for 5 or 50 days followed by genome-wide RNA sequencing, qRT-PCR, immunofluorescence, comet assay, and γH2AX ELISA. We assessed γH2AX by immunohistochemistry in human PDAC tissue microarrays and in TCGA-PAAD datasets to identify clinical correlates. Acute NNK exposure (5 days) induced DNA double-strand breaks and activated ATM-γH2AX signaling, accompanied by increased RAD51 and BRCA2 recruitment, consistent with activation of homologous recombination (HR)-mediated DNA repair. In contrast, chronic NNK exposure (50 days) resulted in persistent DNA damage signaling and transcriptional upregulation of HR-associated genes, including RAD51, BRCA1, BRCA2, FANCD2, and PLK1. Despite sustained accumulation of RAD51- and BRCA2-positive repair foci, chronic NNK exposure was associated with altered RAD51 localization, persistent DNA damage, and chromosomal instability, suggesting dysregulation of HR repair fidelity during prolonged genotoxic stress. γH2AX expression was significantly elevated in NNK-treated cells, KRAS-driven premalignant pancreatic lesions, and pancreatic tissues from smokers. Increased γH2AX expression correlated with tumor progression and poor overall survival, while elevated RAD51 expression was associated with adverse outcomes in patients with PDAC. Collectively, these findings reveal a biphasic DNA damage response to NNK characterized by early activation of ATM-γH2AX-dependent DNA repair followed by persistent DNA damage signaling, dysregulated HR repair, and genomic instability during chronic exposure. Tobacco-induced disruption of DNA repair homeostasis may represent a key mechanism driving pancreatic carcinogenesis and supports γH2AX as a clinically relevant prognostic biomarker in tobacco-associated PDAC.

items.title: Allele-Stratified Activity of RAS Inhibitors in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Systematic Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract: Background: PDAC is a highly aggressive malignancy driven predominantly by activating KRAS mutations, and allele-specific and pan-RAS inhibitors have emerged as candidate targeted therapies. Evidence supporting them is dominated by experimental studies of which the models differ widely in how faithfully they reproduce human disease, and clinical maturity is uneven across alleles. Objectives: The objective of this study was to evaluate allele-stratified RAS-inhibitor activity across KRAS subtypes in PDAC, synthesizing experimental and clinical evidence separately, and determine whether the principal conclusions of the review survive when the experimental evidence is stratified by the level of model validation achieved. Methods: PubMed, Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched from inception to 26 June 2026, with a pre-specified updated search in June 2026. Experimental studies were appraised with a modified JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Quasi-Experimental Studies supplemented by preclinical-specific reporting domains, and were independently classified by the highest level of model validation achieved, from conventional two-dimensional cell lines through to multi-model validation spanning patient-derived and immunocompetent in vivo systems; clinical studies were appraised with ROBINS-I. Experimental and clinical evidence was synthesized separately. Single-arm proportions from KRAS G12C trials were pooled on the logit scale using inverse-variance random-effects meta-analysis with Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals, and certainty was rated using GRADE. Results: Twenty-four studies were included (twenty experimental and four early-phase, single-arm clinical trials). Four of the twenty experimental studies (20%) rested on conventional two-dimensional cell lines alone, nine (45%) incorporated patient-derived material, seven (35%) used immunocompetent models, and fourteen (70%) reproduced their principal finding in at least two independent model classes. The allele-dependent pattern of single-agent activity persisted when cell-line-only studies were set aside, whereas 6 of the 17 studies reporting combination strategies provided no confirmation in any higher-order system. Across three single-arm KRAS G12C trials, the pooled objective response rate was 36.9% (95% CI, 9.8-75.7%; I2 = 66.2%; individual trials 21.1%, 45.5%, and 46.9%), the pooled disease control rate was 85.9% (95% CI, 62.1-95.8%; I2 = 0%; individual datasets 81.8%, 84.2%, and 93.8%), and the grade ≥ 3 treatment-related adverse event rate was 23.8% (95% CI, 11.2-43.5%; I2 = 0%). GRADE certainty was very low for all three outcomes. Conclusions: The available evidence is consistent with allele-dependent activity of RAS-targeted therapy in PDAC and supports biomarker-guided treatment selection, but the clinical evidence base is confined to small, single-arm, early-phase trials of KRAS G12C inhibitors. The pooled estimates are exploratory descriptions of observed activity in selected early-phase populations, not comparative estimates of treatment efficacy. KRAS G12D-directed therapy remains at a substantially earlier stage of clinical validation than KRAS G12C-directed therapy despite a much larger preclinical literature.

items.title: The PancreaSure Multianalyte Blood Test Performs Well at Distinguishing Early-Stage Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma from High-Risk Controls: A Retrospective Secondary Analysis.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Biomarkers that can facilitate early detection of pancreatic cancer and extend patient survival are a significant unmet need. PancreaSure is a serum biomarker signature that performed well at distinguishing Stage I and II pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) from both high-risk and non-high-risk controls in two previous validations. The goal of this study was to perform a secondary analysis of test performance exclusively in individuals at high risk of PDAC due to a pathogenic variant in a susceptibility gene or strong family history of the disease. To this end, we extracted and analyzed raw data from appropriate samples used in the prior validations. Methods: Data from the two prior validations were pooled at the participant level, and sensitivity and specificity were estimated as pooled proportions with exact binomial 95% confidence intervals. One-sided exact binomial tests were used to compare the performance of the PancreaSure test to the performance goals of 65% sensitivity and 90% specificity. Results: PancreaSure detected early-stage PDAC with 77.5% sensitivity (95% CI, 66.0-86.5) and 93.6% specificity (95% CI, 91.8-95.1), significantly outperforming predefined success criteria. Test performance was consistent between Stage I (80.0% sensitivity) and Stage II (75.6% sensitivity) PDAC cases. PancreaSure also demonstrated favorable performance in individuals with only genetic susceptibility to PDAC (84.8% sensitivity, 94.5% specificity), with only a family history of the disease (79.2% sensitivity, 93.7% specificity), and with high-penetrance variants. Conclusions: The performance demonstrated by PancreaSure in genetic/familial high-risk individuals further suggests that it has the potential to facilitate early detection of PDAC in surveillance populations and warrants prospective evaluation as an adjunct to imaging.

items.title: Revisiting chronic pancreatitis as a risk factor for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: toward precision risk stratification.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is an established risk factor for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). However, individual risk varies substantially, and the association between CP and PDAC is more complex than a uniform inflammation-driven pathway. Reverse causation, shared etiological factors, and biological heterogeneity may contribute to the observed association.
AREAS COVERED: We critically review epidemiological, mechanistic, and causal evidence linking CP with PDAC, focusing on heterogeneity across CP subtypes and disease trajectories. We examine five domains potentially relevant to individual PDAC risk: genetic susceptibility, cumulative pancreatic injury, metabolic trajectories including new-onset diabetes, longitudinal imaging phenotypes, and emerging molecular alterations. We propose a multidomain framework for individualized and dynamic risk stratification and risk-adapted surveillance.
EXPERT OPINION: CP should not be regarded as a uniformly high-risk condition for PDAC. Individual risk is shaped by the interaction of genetic, inflammatory, metabolic, structural, and molecular factors. The key question should therefore shift from whether CP increases PDAC risk to which patients are most likely to develop clinically consequential PDAC. Although multidomain and longitudinal assessment may enable targeted surveillance, most biomarkers and prediction strategies remain insufficiently validated. Prospective studies are required to determine whether this approach improves early detection and patient outcomes.

items.title: Pancreatic cancer cell and stellate cell-derived exosome crosstalk mediates pancreatic cancer-related diabetes.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetes is a known risk factor, and a distinct form termed pancreatic cancer-related diabetes (PCRD) often precedes the diagnosis of cancer by 3-5 years, offering a potential window for intervention. We hypothesised that interactions between stromal pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs) and cancer cells trigger secretion of exosomal factors that impair islet function and insulin signalling, contributing to PCRD pathogenesis.
METHODS: KC (KrasLSL-G12D/+; Pdx1-Cre) mice were fed a high-fructose diet (HFrD) or control diet for 16 weeks. Exosomes were isolated from monocultures and co-cultures of cancer/PanIN cells with PSCs, characterised by nanoparticle tracking analysis and transmission electron microscopy, and incubated with mouse β-cells (MIN6) and peripheral cells (hepatocytes, adipocytes, skeletal myocytes). Effects on insulin secretion and insulin-signalling factors were examined. Exosomal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) expression was modulated by siRNA to assess functional impact.
RESULTS: HFrD induced marked glucose intolerance in KC mice and was accompanied by enhanced PSC activation, macrophage infiltration, inflammation, and accelerated PanIN progression. Exosomes from PSCs, cancer cells, and co-cultures displayed typical morphology and marker expression and were efficiently internalised by β-cells and hepatocytes. Functionally, exosomes significantly impaired glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in mouse and human β-cells without altering insulin content. In hepatocytes, PSC-, cancer-, and co-culture-derived exosomes reduced key insulin-signalling components, including IR, IRS, AKT, FOXO1 and GLUT2, and inhibited glucose uptake. Silencing exosomal G6PD partially restored hepatocyte insulin signalling.
CONCLUSION: This study identifies a potential contributor to PCRD and suggests a possible mechanistic role for exosomal G6PD in impaired insulin signalling associated with PCRD.

items.title: Research trends and knowledge structure of pancreatic cancer and type 2 diabetes mellitus research: a two-decade CiteSpace analysis.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic cancer and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are closely linked through complex epidemiological and biological interactions. However, the development, knowledge structure, and research trends of this field have not been systematically characterized. This study aimed to investigate the research landscape and knowledge structure of pancreatic cancer and T2DM research from 2006 to 2025.
METHODS: We conducted the primary bibliometric analysis using WOSCC records, and separately analyzed PubMed-indexed clinical trials as a supplementary dataset. A total of 1,989 WOSCC publications were included in the bibliometric analysis, while 54 PubMed-indexed Clinical Trial records were included in the supplementary clinical trial assessment. CiteSpace was used to perform collaboration, co-citation, keyword, timeline, and burst analyses of the WOSCC dataset.
RESULTS: The number of publications increased steadily over the study period, particularly after 2015. The United States and China were the leading contributors, while the University of California System and Harvard University were among the most productive institutions. Major research themes included cancer risk, insulin resistance, metabolic inflammation, incretin-based therapies, and new-onset diabetes. Keyword evolution and burst analyses indicated increasing attention to mechanistic investigation, biomarker discovery, risk stratification, and precision medicine approaches.
CONCLUSION: This study characterizes the development and knowledge structure of research on the relationship between pancreatic cancer and T2DM and highlights major research themes, emerging hotspots, and future directions for mechanistic investigation and clinical translation.

items.title: Diagnostic Utility of Protein Biomarkers in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
items.abstract:
The goal of this prospective multicenter observational study is to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of blood-based protein biomarkers for detecting pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) in adults aged 18 years and older. The study will investigate whether these biomarkers can help distinguish pancreatic cancer from chronic pancreatitis and mucinous pancreatic lesions, including intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs) and mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs).

The main questions it aims to answer are:

Can blood-based protein biomarkers accurately identify patients with PDAC and distinguish them from patients with chronic pancreatitis or mucinous pancreatic lesions?

Does combining protein biomarkers with CA 19-9 improve diagnostic accuracy compared with using individual biomarkers alone?

Are protein biomarker levels associated with tumor stage, tumor size, or the presence of metastases in patients with PDAC?

Researchers will compare blood levels of protein biomarkers across four groups of patients: those with PDAC, chronic pancreatitis, IPMNs, and MCNs. The biomarkers will include GDF-15, ICAM-1, osteopontin, CXCL10, HGF, Nectin-4, periostin, and VEGF-A.

Participants will:

Provide informed consent before enrollment.

Provide an additional blood sample for protein biomarker measurement, collected alongside routine blood tests and before any oncological or interventional treatment.

Have relevant clinical information, medical history, laboratory results, and imaging findings collected for analysis.

items.title: Association of Social Determinants of Health with Delays in Diagnosis and Treatment of Resected Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Delayed diagnosis and treatment worsen survival in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Despite many potential causes, the influence of social determinants of health (SDoH) is understudied. We evaluated whether SDoH impact delays in diagnosis and treatment among patients who underwent resection for PDAC.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Adults resected at a high-volume center were included (January 2016-November 2024). SDoH included insurance status, census-level income and education, rural-urban residence, and Area Deprivation Index. Primary endpoints were time from first imaging to histological diagnosis and time from first imaging to treatment initiation. Delay thresholds were derived using receiver operating characteristic analysis against overall survival. Uni- and multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with delays, adjusting for demographic and clinical covariates, stratified by outpatient (OUP) versus emergency room (ER) presentation.
RESULTS: Among 317 patients, the median age was 67 years, and 42.3% were female; 50.1% presented through ER. The median imaging-to-diagnosis interval was 11 days (interquartile [IQR] 3-27 days), and the median imaging-to-treatment interval was 40 days (IQR 27-59 days). In the OUP cohort, Medicare insurance was associated with delayed diagnosis compared with private insurance (OR 3.34 [95% CI 1.09-11.70]), whereas higher income was associated with up to 84% lower odds of delayed treatment. In the ER cohort, higher education was associated with reduced odds of delayed diagnosis (OR 0.27 [95% CI 0.07-0.88]) and delayed treatment (OR 0.33 [95% CI 0.11-0.91]). Post-endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) hospitalization predicted delays in the ER setting, whereas alarm symptoms reduced delays in both settings.
CONCLUSIONS: SDoH are associated with diagnostic and treatment delays in resected PDAC. Targeted interventions may accelerate care and improve equity in outcomes.

items.title: Evolving Molecular Drug Targets in Pancreatic Cancer: An Updated Review.
items.abstract: Pancreatic Cancer (PC) remains one of the most aggressive and lethal malignancies with an extremely low survival rate. Existing conventional therapies such as surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy have demonstrated limited effectiveness in significantly improving overall survival outcomes, largely due to the unique and hostile Tumour Microenvironment (TME) of PC. The TME is characterised by a desmoplastic stroma, an immunosuppressive, hypovascular, and hypoxic microenvironment, which collectively contribute to therapeutic failure. These features not only limit effective drug delivery but also promote tumour progression and treatment resistance. In recent years, the emergence of molecular targeted therapies has enabled the targeting of aberrantly activated kinases or other highly expressed targets in PC, such as KRAS, CDKN2A, TP53, SMAD4, epigenetic regulators, and signalling pathways. However, the clinical efficacy of many targeted agents remains limited, highlighting the complexity of tumour heterogeneity and adaptive resistance mechanisms. These limitations underscore the need to develop more effective therapeutic strategies for PC. Advances in precision oncology, immunotherapy, and patient derived models offer promising opportunities to improve the understanding of tumour biology, elucidate mechanisms underlying therapeutic response and resistance, and identify novel treatment strategies tailored to individual patients. Herein, this review aims to provide an updated overview of the current state of molecular therapies and the underlying molecular mechanisms and oncogenic pathways that contribute to PC initiation, development, progression and metastasis.

items.title: Molecular landscape of anaplastic transformation in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) with anaplastic features is a rare and highly aggressive subtype with an extremely poor prognosis. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying anaplastic transformation remain poorly understood. To characterize the anaplastic transformation molecular landscape, we analyzed genomic alterations in 5,997 conventional PDAC and 41 anaplastic carcinoma cases from the Memorial Sloan Kettering-Integrated Mutation Profiling of Actionable Cancer Targets (MSK-IMPACT) cohort. Additionally, four PDAC samples from the Kyorin cohort with both tubular and anaplastic components were subjected to spatial transcriptomics using the Visium platform. Differential gene expression and pathway enrichment analyses were performed to identify key molecular drivers. Genomic analysis revealed higher KRAS (90 versus 75%), TP53 (85 versus 60%), and CDKN2A (50 versus 30%) mutation frequencies, but notably fewer SMAD4 mutations (5 versus 20%; p = 0.022), in anaplastic carcinoma than in conventional PDAC. Spatial transcriptomics identified distinct molecular signatures, with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathways significantly enriched in anaplastic regions. Levels of ELF3, an epithelial transcription factor, were consistently downregulated in all anaplastic components. Importantly, we detected a strong inverse correlation between SMAD4 and ELF3 expression in both the bulk RNA sequencing cohort and spatial transcriptomic data. Functional validation using the KC-shSmad4 mouse model demonstrated that increased Smad4 suppressed Elf3 expression and promoted mesenchymal reprogramming. Our findings suggest a novel SMAD4-ELF3 regulatory axis that may contribute to anaplastic transformation in PDAC. The retention of SMAD4 functions coupled with ELF3 downregulation may promote EMT and contribute to tumor dedifferentiation. This SMAD4-ELF3 regulatory axis may provide a framework for identifying therapeutic vulnerabilities in this aggressive PDAC variant and further highlight the utility of spatial transcriptomics for understanding tumor heterogeneity. © 2026 The Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland.

items.title: Hitting KRAS G12D without the gut punch: Can immunotherapy make it last?
items.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Shi et al. report encouraging early-phase results combining HRS-4642, an allele-specific KRAS G12D inhibitor, with the PD-L1 inhibitor adebrelimab in previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer. The intravenous combination was safe and well tolerated, notably sparing patients the gastrointestinal toxicity common to oral KRAS inhibitors, and achieved a promising 43% response rate at the recommended dose.

items.title: Vascular Resection in Robotic Pancreaticoduodenectomy for Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract: Data for this propensity score-matched (PSM) comparative study were obtained from a prospectively maintained database comprising 679 cases of robotic pancreaticoduodenectomy (RPD). This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and justification of vascular resection (VR) in RPD for pancreatic cancer. The primary study endpoint was to compare the surgical outcomes between patients undergoing VR (+) and VR (-) in RPD using PSM to minimize selection bias and allow for balanced comparisons. The secondary study endpoint was to assess the impact of VR on oncological outcomes and overall survival in patients with pancreatic cancer undergoing RPD.

items.title: A Study Looking at Whether a Nutritional Composition Can Help People With Pancreatic Cancer Stay Stronger and Better Tolerate Chemotherapy
items.abstract: The HEXCARE-PDAC study is a Phase III, randomized, double-blind, controlled, multicenter trial evaluating the effectiveness of a cancer-specific oral nutritional supplement in preserving skeletal muscle mass and improving chemotherapy tolerance in adults with non-metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) receiving neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX-based chemotherapy. The study aims to determine whether targeted nutritional intervention can mitigate cancer-associated muscle loss and improve treatment delivery and clinical outcomes in patients with PDAC

interventions: A novel cancer-specific high energy high protein medical nutrition solution
A commercially available isocaloric isonitrogenous medical nutritional solution.

items.title: Multiple R1 margins are associated with shorter overall survival: national register-based study on pancreatic cancer.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Resection status is associated with overall survival among patients operated on for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). This study investigated whether the number of R1 margins is associated with shorter survival.
METHODS: Adult patients who underwent pancreatoduodenectomy for primary resectable PDAC between 2017 and 2024 recorded in the Swedish National Pancreatic Registry were included. Overall survival was analysed according to overall R status and the number of R1 margins. Overall survival was analysed using Kaplan-Meier estimates, Cox regression analysis for estimated adjusted survival time, and Laplace regression for analysis of percentile distribution.
RESULTS: Overall, 1043 patients were included, 398 patients (38.2%) with R0 and 645 patients (61.8%) with R1 margins. The adjusted median survival was 8.2 (95% confidence interval (c.i.) -12.0 to -4.3) months shorter for patients with R1 versus R0 margins, with a progressively shorter survival with a higher number of R1 margins. Specifically, compared with R0 margins, the adjusted median survival for one, two and three or more R1 margins was 4.6 (95% c.i. -10.2 to 1.0), 6.7 (95% c.i. -11.9 to -1.5), and 12.4 (95% c.i. -16.5 to -8.3) months shorter, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: Patients with R1 margins had an adjusted median survival that was 8 months shorter than patients with R0 margins. An increased number of R1 margins was associated with shorter survival. These results suggest that the current practice of reporting binary R status is insufficient, and future guidelines should consider revising this routine and adopt a standardized, detailed margin assessment protocol.

items.title: Implementation of Risk Prediction Models Using Electronic Health Data for Early Detection of Pancreatic Cancer: A Prospective Pilot Feasibility Study.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: We previously developed multiple machine-learning and regression-based risk prediction models using retrospective electronic health records (EHR) to estimate near-term risk of pancreatic cancer (PC). This pilot study aimed to assess the feasibility of an early detection strategy combining initial EHR-based risk prediction with downstream imaging and blood-based testing.
METHODS: This prospective study included adults aged 50-84 years with an estimated ≥ 1% 18-month risk of PC, identified between January 2021 and March 2023 using four previously validated models. Patients with a history or active suspicion of PC were excluded. Participants completed cross-sectional imaging and CA19-9 Labs at baseline and again at 18 months. Outcomes included enrollment rates, test completion rate, and burden of incidental findings.
RESULTS: Of 1251 eligible patients, 102 (8.2%) enrolled (median age 69 years [IQR 62-75]; 58% women; 48% Hispanic, 34% White, 11% Black, and 7% Asian). At baseline, 89 (87%) completed imaging and 98 (96%) completed CA19-9. At 18 months, 79% completed both imaging and CA19-9. Ten (10%) participants underwent additional clinical evaluations triggered by imaging findings. Evaluations included an endoscopic ultrasound, renal imaging, and FibroScan. CA19-9 results were normal in most participants, though 18% had elevated levels at baseline.
CONCLUSIONS: Real-time EHR-based ML algorithms can be combined with blood- and imaging-based surveillance for early detection of PC with acceptable burden of incidental findings. However, improved patient engagement is a key aspect that will need to be addressed in order to successfully scale an AI-guided strategy for early detection.

items.title: Skeletal Muscle Index, Tumor and Systemic Immunity, and Survival in Advanced Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study investigated relationships between the skeletal muscle index (SMI) and the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), peripheral immune phenotypes, and serum biomarkers in advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and evaluated the prognostic significance of these parameters.
METHODS: A retrospective analysis of 119 advanced PDAC patients was performed. Sarcopenia was diagnosed using sex-specific SMI cut-offs from baseline L3-level computed tomography (CT) images. The TIME was characterized by multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF; n = 31), peripheral immunity by flow cytometry, and serum biomarkers by routine testing. Associations with SMI were examined using Spearman correlation; prognostic relevance was assessed using Cox proportional hazards models.
RESULTS: Sarcopenia (56/119, 47.1%) was associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS) (8.83 vs. 12.03 months, p = 0.016) and overall survival (OS) (10.20 vs. 17.33 months, p = 0.014). SMI correlated most strongly with stromal CD8+ T cells (ρ = 0.52), stromal total T cells (ρ = 0.52), and stromal M2 macrophages (ρ = 0.50) in the TIME; with circulating Th2-like cells (ρ = -0.58) and CD4+ memory T cells (ρ = 0.45) peripherally; and with hemoglobin (ρ = 0.32) among serum markers. In multivariable Cox regression, stromal CD4+ Treg percentage independently predicted OS (hazard ratio [HR] = 7.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.60-36.22, p = 0.011), stromal CD56dim natural killer (NK)-cell density predicted PFS (HR = 1.015, 95% CI 1.001-1.028, p = 0.031), and the lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR) predicted both PFS (HR = 0.86, p = 0.023) and OS (HR = 0.83, p = 0.009). No peripheral lymphocyte subset reached prognostic significance.
CONCLUSION: SMI is broadly associated with local and systemic immune phenotypes in advanced PDAC. Stromal CD4+ regulatory T cells (Tregs), CD56dim NK cells, and LMR carry independent prognostic information and may complement body-composition assessment.

items.title: Understanding Genomic Instability Score in Platinum-Treated Advanced Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: First-line treatment selection for advanced (locally advanced or metastatic) pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is currently based on clinical characteristics rather than predictive biomarkers. While homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) is associated with increased sensitivity to platinum-based chemotherapy, established predictive biomarkers, such as pathogenic alterations in BRCA1, BRCA2, and PALB2, identify only a small subset of patients who are likely to benefit from platinum-based first-line treatment. The Genomic Instability Score (GIS) may capture broader HRD-associated genomic scarring beyond single-gene testing and support biomarker-guided platinum selection. However, the clinical utility of the GIS in PDAC remains uncertain, and no PDAC-specific GIS cutoff has yet been established. Methods: In this retrospective multicenter cohort, 127 patients with advanced PDAC underwent TruSight Oncology 500 HRD testing between 2022 and 2025. GIS was evaluable in 99 patients; 80 received first-line therapy. The primary endpoint was time to failure of the first-line strategy (TFS). An exploratory candidate GIS cutoff for platinum sensitivity was identified using maximally selected log-rank statistics, and survival was analyzed using Kaplan-Meier estimates and Cox regression. Results: In the first-line platinum cohort, an exploratory GIS threshold of 39 showed the greatest discrimination for treatment failure-free survival (TFS) within this cohort. Patients with GIS ≥ 39 had significantly longer TFS than those with GIS < 39 (9.9 vs. 5.9 months; HR 0.33, 95% CI 0.13-0.80; p = 0.015), and this association remained significant after multivariable adjustment. Among individual genes, BRCA2-mutated tumors exhibited significantly higher GIS than BRCA2-wild-type tumors (median 54 vs. 19; FDR-adjusted p = 0.002), although 30% of GIS-high tumors lacked BRCA1/2 mutations. Combined stratification by GIS and first-line treatment demonstrated a stepwise improvement in overall survival, with median OS of 8.2 months in non-platinum/GIS < 39 patients, 15.1 months in platinum/GIS < 39 patients, and 30.7 months in platinum/GIS ≥ 39 patients (p = 0.002). Conclusions: GIS may identify patients with advanced PDAC who experience favorable outcomes during first-line platinum-based chemotherapy. The observed association between higher GIS and improved treatment outcomes supports further investigation of GIS as a biomarker for treatment stratification in advanced PDAC and warrants prospective validation.

items.title: NeoBridge: Biophysics-informed neoantigen prioritization and clonal architecture profiling in pancreatic cancer.
items.abstract: Accurate identification of immunogenic neoantigens remains a bottleneck in personalized cancer vaccine development, particularly in low-mutation-burden tumors such as pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). We developed NeoBridge, a hybrid ensemble integrating gradient boosting and a deep neural network across four biologically grounded feature dimensions: HLA binding and processing, differential agretopicity, tumor neoantigen abundance, and TCR recognition potential. Trained on 11,188 experimentally validated neoantigens, NeoBridge achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.904 on held-out data, with cross-cancer generalization (AUC: 0.73-0.82), including 0.82 in pancreatic cancer, and outperformed established tools. Differential agretopicity emerged as the dominant predictive feature. In 118 PDAC patients with resolved phylogenies and complete follow up, subclonal neoantigen load was associated with worse progression-free survival (p < 0.001) and overall survival (p = 0.038). These findings are hypothesis generating and require prospective immunopeptidomic and functional validation.

items.title: Strategy for early diagnosis of pancreatic cancer.
items.abstract: Exocrine pancreatic cancer, particularly Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma, is regarded as one of the most aggressive cancers with a poor prognosis. Its bleak outlook mainly results from its silent progression, late diagnosis, and unreliable early detection methods. Globally, PC ranks among the leading causes of cancer-related deaths, and its incidence continues to increase. Because the pancreas is situated deep within the abdomen, early symptoms such as mild abdominal pain, fatigue, or weight loss are often vague. Most patients are only diagnosed after the disease has spread beyond the point where curative treatment is possible. Although surgery provides the best chance for long-term survival, only a small number of patients qualify for it at the time of initial diagnosis. Several factors increase the risk of developing PC, including chronic pancreatitis, smoking, obesity, inherited genetic mutations (like BRCA1/2), and new-onset diabetes (NOD), which has recently gained attention as a possible early warning sign. However, widespread screening for PC isn't yet practical because the disease is relatively uncommon and there are no highly accurate, non-invasive biomarkers. The most widely used blood test, CA 19-9, often gives unreliable results, while newer molecular approaches-like circulating tumor DNA, exosomal markers, microRNAs, and metabolomic profiles-are still being refined. Recent advances in imaging technology, artificial intelligence, and targeted screening for high-risk individuals hold promise for catching pancreatic cancer earlier. As we advance, combining multi-omics biomarkers with precision imaging may finally make earlier diagnosis-and improved survival-a reality for this devastating disease.

items.title: Intestinal Low-Dose Radiotherapy Combined With Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in Solid Tumors With Liver Metastases
items.abstract:
This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of combining low-dose radiotherapy to the intestines with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in patients with liver metastases from solid tumors.

Liver metastases often create an "immune desert" that makes immunotherapy less effective. Recent research has shown that low-dose irradiation of the gut (1 Gy) can reshape the gut microbiome and activate the immune system, potentially reversing resistance to immunotherapy.

This is a prospective, single-arm, single-center cohort study. We plan to enroll 120 patients with liver metastases from non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), colorectal cancer, or pancreatic cancer. All participants will receive a single low dose of radiotherapy to the intestine (1 Gy), followed by standard immune checkpoint inhibitors and chemotherapy.

The main goal of this study is to see how well the liver metastases respond to this combined treatment. We will also monitor survival, side effects, and changes in the gut bacteria and blood immune markers to understand how this treatment works. This strategy may provide a low-cost, low-toxicity new option for patients whose liver metastases have stopped responding to standard immunotherapy.

items.title: Routine H&E Histology Encodes Postoperative Risk Heterogeneity in Resected Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Multicohort Evaluation of TIGERS.
items.abstract: Patients with resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) can have different outcomes despite similar TNM stage. We developed TIGERS (Tumor Intelligence Grading and Evaluation Risk Score), a nine-feature prognostic biomarker derived from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole-slide images. TIGERS quantifies tumor burden, glandular and nuclear morphology, chromatin texture, and tumor-stroma topology. The score was trained in 644 treatment-naive cases and evaluated in an internal validation cohort (n = 385), a separate post-neoadjuvant cohort (n = 275), two external cohorts (n = 260 and n = 235), the TCGA-PAAD cohort (n = 133), and a prospectively accrued external cohort (n = 155) with subsequent offline inference. Overall survival was the primary endpoint; the same formula and locked cutoff were applied throughout. The cutoff stratified survival in the internal validation cohort and three of four retrospective test cohorts. In the remaining external cohort, 226 of 235 patients (96.2%) were classified as high risk, showing limited transportability of the fixed threshold. Adding TIGERS to the clinicopathologic model increased Harrell's C-index in all six retrospective cohorts (range 0.015-0.047). In the prospectively accrued cohort, mortality was 47.5% in the high-risk group and 22.7% in the low-risk group; high risk remained associated with worse survival after adjustment (hazard ratio, 4.45; 95% confidence interval, 2.28-8.70; P < .001). Automated quality control passed 92.3% of screened cases, and scoring was completed in all included cases with a median turnaround time of 13.5 minutes. TIGERS assigned 43.2% of patients to a different risk category than the prespecified stage-based definition. Higher TIGERS correlated with a more basal-like proteomic profile in both the training and internal validation cohorts, supporting a molecular basis for its prognostic value. Routine H&E histology may therefore provide prognostic information complementary to conventional clinicopathologic assessment. Prospective interventional studies are needed before TIGERS can guide treatment or surveillance.

items.title: Association of Irreversible Electroporation Treatment with Overall Survival in Stage III Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: DIRECT Registry Results.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Irreversible electroporation (IRE) is used in selected patients with Stage III pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), but its association with survival relative to standard-of-care (SOC) therapy remains uncertain.
METHODS: This multicenter observational study included 137 patients from the DIRECT registry: 99 treated within an IRE-based strategy and 38 receiving SOC without IRE. Overall survival (OS) from diagnosis was evaluated using propensity-score overlap weighting as the principal adjusted analysis. Conventional inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), propensity-score matching, 3- and 6-month landmark analyses, and a time-dependent Cox model treating IRE as a time-varying exposure were sensitivity analyses. Restricted mean survival time (RMST) at 24 months was estimated.
RESULTS: Median time from diagnosis to enrollment was 8 months (IQR, 6-10) with IRE and 4 months (IQR, 3-6) with SOC (P < 0.0001). Unadjusted median OS was 28 months (95% CI, 23-33) and 15 months (95% CI, 12-21), respectively. Overlap weighting was associated with lower mortality with IRE (HR, 0.28; 95% bootstrap CI, 0.12-0.48). Twenty-four-month RMST was 21.22 versus 16.24 months, an absolute difference of 4.99 months (95% bootstrap CI, 1.15-8.12). The time-dependent analysis attenuated but retained the association (HR, 0.59; 95% bootstrap CI, 0.37-0.94). Other sensitivity analyses were directionally consistent.
CONCLUSIONS: An IRE-based treatment strategy was associated with longer OS than SOC without IRE. Attenuation in the time-dependent analysis indicates that treatment timing and selection contributed to the observed difference. Given the nonrandomized design and potential residual confounding, these findings demonstrate association rather than an independent causal effect of IRE.

items.title: Targeted inhibition of OTUD7B enhances therapeutic sensitivity in KRAS- mutant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma by promoting ubiquitination of DHODH
items.abstract: Background Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is frequently driven by oncogenic KRAS and remains highly refractory to therapy. Ferroptosis represents a therapeutically exploitable vulnerability in KRAS-mutant PDAC, yet the molecular mechanisms that sustain ferroptosis resistance remain incompletely understood. Methods An in vivo CRISPR/Cas9 screen was performed in KRAS-mutant and KRAS-wild-type PDAC models under erastin treatment to identify genotype-selective ferroptosis regulators. The function and mechanism of OTUD7B were investigated using PDAC cell lines, patient tissues, biochemical and ubiquitination assays, and spontaneous PDAC mouse models. An OTUD7B-targeting antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) was further evaluated alone or in combination with erastin or anti-PD-1 therapy. Results OTUD7B was identified as a selective determinant of erastin resistance in KRAS-mutant PDAC. OTUD7B was preferentially upregulated in KRAS-mutant PDAC, and oncogenic KRAS enhanced OTUD7B transcription through STAT3 activation. Mechanistically, OTUD7B directly interacted with dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) and stabilized DHODH by removing K48-linked ubiquitin chains at K169 and K254, thereby reinforcing ferroptosis defense. OTUD7B depletion increased reactive oxygen species, iron accumulation and lipid peroxidation, reduced glutathione levels, and markedly potentiated erastin-induced ferroptosis in vitro and in spontaneous PDAC models. Therapeutic OTUD7B-ASO recapitulated these effects and enhanced the antitumor efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy, accompanied by increased intratumoral CD8 + T-cell infiltration. Conclusions These findings establish the KRAS–STAT3–OTUD7B–DHODH axis as a key ferroptosis-protective pathway in KRAS-mutant PDAC and identify OTUD7B as a potential therapeutic target for sensitizing tumors to ferroptosis induction and immunotherapy.

items.title: 10-Year Survivorship, Metastatic Risk, and Clinicopathologic Characteristics of Early- Onset Pancreatic Cancer: A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression
items.abstract: Purpose Pancreatic cancer (PC) remains a global burden with low overall survival yet a distinct group referred to as early-onset (EOPC) remains poorly observed. This review aims to investigate survival outcomes, metastatic risk, and clinicopathologic features of EOPC compared with non-early-onset PC using meta analysis, meta regression, and individual patient data (IPD) reconstruction. Methods Literature search was conducted on January 9, 2026, in PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect. Random-effects meta-analysis conducted using risk ratios or mean differences. IPD was reconstructed under Guyot’s protocol. Results 22 articles comprising 364,319 patients were analyzed. EOPC observed in 6.1% of total PC patients. EOPC had a 25% lower hazard of death than non-EOPC (HR = 0.75, p < 0.001). EOPC was higher in males (RR 1.09, p = 0.004), with smoking history (RR 1.22, p < 0.001), but lower diabetes mellitus (RR 0.34, p = 0.001). EOPC were likely to be presented with pain (RR 1.39, p = 0.017), higher metastasis risk (RR = 1.11, p = 0.02), higher T3/T4 stage (RR 1.06, p = 0.002), and higher III/IV stage (RR 1.08, p = 0.008). Using meta regression, metastasis of EOPC was associated with smoking status (ꞵ = 3.06, p < 0.001, residual I² = 11%), but neither with each study country's SDI, tumor location, proportion of obesity, patient’s mean age, nor proportion of alcohol intake. Conclusions EOPC was distinct to non-EOPC with 25% lower hazard of death. Early detection should target younger patients with risk factors such as active smoking to avoid advanced stages of disease.

items.title: TRIM29 may facilitate progression of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma through immune remodeling.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly lethal malignancy characterized by late diagnosis, aggressive progression, and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Biomarkers with both diagnostic value and biological relevance remain urgently needed.
METHODS: Five Gene Expression Omnibus cohorts comprising 548 pancreatic samples were analyzed using differential expression analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and machine learning. Spatial and single-cell transcriptomics, immune infiltration estimates, and survival analyses complemented biomarker screening. Tripartite motif-containing 29 (TRIM29) was evaluated in 80 paired clinical specimens, knockdown and re-expression experiments, and subcutaneous and orthotopic KPC tumor models.
RESULTS: Machine learning identified eight hub genes, including S100P, SFN, TMPRSS4, GJB2, GABRP, TRIM29, SERPINB5, and LAMB3, which showed favorable diagnostic performance across cohorts. Spatial transcriptomics revealed region-specific enrichment of these genes in PDAC tissues. Among them, TRIM29 was preferentially expressed in malignant epithelial cells, markedly upregulated in PDAC tissues, and associated with poor prognosis, reduced CD8+ T-cell infiltration, and activation of PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling. Functionally, TRIM29/Trim29 knockdown suppressed PDAC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, reduced AKT and mTOR phosphorylation, and increased CXCL10 transcript levels and extracellular protein concentrations. TRIM29 re-expression restored AKT and mTOR phosphorylation and reversed the increase in extracellular CXCL10 concentrations. In vivo, Trim29 knockdown suppressed tumor growth and increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration in orthotopic tumors.
CONCLUSION: This study identifies TRIM29 as a machine learning-prioritized diagnostic biomarker and functional regulator of PDAC progression and immune remodeling, suggesting its potential value for biomarker-guided risk assessment and therapeutic exploration in PDAC.

items.title: Restaging the primary tumor in localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma after systemic therapy: a scoping review of the role of CT, FDG-PET, and CA19-9.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: The introduction of improved multi-agent systemic therapies has made restaging and treatment response assessment in patients with localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) increasingly complex. This scoping review aims to assess and compare methods for local disease restaging and treatment response assessment in localized PDAC, with a focus on their association with resectability, overall survival (OS), and R0-resection rates.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This scoping review included studies on restaging in patients with PDAC following systemic therapy using CT and PET/CT from MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL.
RESULTS: Among 4680 identified studies, 20 fulfilled the eligibility criteria. Most (n = 15) studies analyzed CT, and 5 analyzed PET/CT. Groups of restaging methods included new response categories, size-based metrics, volume, vascular contact, tumor attenuation, fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT derived metabolic parameters, and resectability criteria. Dual-energy CT-derived extracellular volume (DECT-ECV) was evaluated as a baseline predictive biomarker. Associations between restaging methods and outcomes were reported inconsistently: some studies found significant associations for specific methods, whereas others did not. No restaging method showed a consistent association with both R0-resection and survival across all studies.
CONCLUSION: Restaging of localized PDAC after systemic treatment remains challenging due to the limited accuracy of RECIST 1.1, particularly for the classifications partial response and stable disease. The current evidence suggests that integrating additional imaging features, alternative imaging modalities, and the biomarker carbohydrate antigen (CA)19-9 may improve the assessment of resectability and prognosis. These findings support a future version of RECIST 1.1 to alert clinicians to this issue.
KEY POINTS: Question How effective are current (PET/)CT-based restaging methods in assessing local disease resectability and prognosis in localized PDAC after modern multi-agent systemic therapy? Findings Current restaging methods show inconsistent association with R0-resection and survival; RECIST 1.1 is particularly limited for the assessment of partial response and stable disease. Clinical relevance Current evidence confirms a need to integrate additional imaging features and the biomarker CA19-9, during restaging in patients with localized pancreatic cancer after modern systemic therapy to improve accuracy and reduce the risk of missed treatment options.

items.title: Chemotherapy After Resection of Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Impact of Different Regimens in a Real-World Population.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The PRODIGE 24/CCTG PA.6- trial has shown an overall survival (OS) up to 55 months in patients treated with (modified) 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, irinotecan and oxaliplatin ((m)FOLFIRINOX) chemotherapy after resection of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). The applicability of these results to a real-world patient population is, however, unknown. This study aimed to assess the efficacy of (m)FOLFIRINOX compared to other adjuvant chemotherapy regimens in a real-world cohort.
METHODS: We performed a post-hoc analysis in a prospectively maintained cohort of patients undergoing PDAC resection in the Regional Academic Cancer Centre Utrecht, the Netherlands, from 2016 to 2020. Median OS was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier curves, primarily stratified by adjuvant chemotherapy regimen and secondarily by eligibility for the PRODIGE 24/CCTG PA.6- trial. Multivariable Cox regression was used to assess the association between chemotherapy regimen and OS, presented as hazard ratio's (HR) with 95% confidence interval (95%CI).
RESULTS: A total of 161 patients with a median follow-up of 51 months (interquartile range (IQR) 43-61) were included. With (m)FOLFIRINOX (n = 30), OS was 29 months (IQR 22-42; [HR 0.26, 95%CI 0.14-0.47, p < 0.01]). Comparing (m)FOLFIRINOX with gemcitabine monotherapy yielded a HR of 0.62 (95%CI 0.33-1.17, p = 0.14), while (m)FOLFIRINOX versus gemcitabine combination therapy had a HR of 0.66 (95% CI 0.35-1.24 p = 0.20). Patients without adjuvant therapy (n = 71) had a median OS of 13 months (IQR 11-23, reference group). In patients receiving gemcitabine monotherapy (n = 31), median OS was 21 months (IQR 15-31; [HR 0.41 95%CI 0.25-0.69, p < 0.01]); for gemcitabine combination therapy (n = 29), OS was 28 months (IQR 23-43; [HR 0.39, 95%CI 0.23-0.66, p < 0.01]) In patients who received (m)FOLFIRINOX and who did or did not meet trial eligibility criteria, OS was 27 months (IQR 12-NR), compared to 30 months (IQR 21-NR) (p = 0.16), respectively.
CONCLUSION: The survival benefit of (m)FOLFIRINOX observed in the clinical trial setting was not observed in our real-world cohort, not even in the selected subset of patients who would have deemed eligible for inclusion in the PRODIGE 24/CCTG PA.6- trial. Survival was not different for patients treated with (m)FOLFIRINOX and gemcitabine combination therapy.
