items.title: EGFR-antibody-decorated cancer-cell-membrane-coated MOF nanoplatform enables targeted delivery of the STING agonist diABZI for pancreatic cancer immunotherapy.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has limited immunotherapeutic effect because of poor drug penetration and tumor immunosuppression. Activation of the stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway may promote antitumor immunity, but systemic administration of STING agonists is constrained by inadequate tumor accumulation. Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is frequently overexpressed in PDAC and is closely associated with tumor growth, invasion, and treatment resistance. Herein, we developed an EGFR-antibody-decorated cancer-cell-membrane-coated metal-organic framework (MOF) nanoplatform loaded with the STING agonist diamidobenzimidazole (diABZI) (EM@MOF/diABZI) for targeted pancreatic cancer immunotherapy. This nanoplatform consists of an acid-responsive diABZI loaded MOF core and an EGFR-antibody-functionalized pancreatic cancer-cell-membrane shell. The nanoplatform displayed preserved membrane-associated proteins and EGFR-binding activity, pH-dependent diABZI release, significantly enhanced cellular uptake and preferential tumor accumulation. In a subcutaneous Pan02 pancreatic cancer mouse model, EM@MOF/diABZI produced greater tumor-growth inhibition and improved survival. Mechanistically, targeted diABZI delivery increased intratumoral p-STING expression and elevated the levels of IFN-β, CXCL10, TNF-α, IL-6, and IFN-γ, accompanied by enhanced infiltration of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. No obvious histopathological abnormalities or substantial systemic toxicity were observed. Therefore, this nanoplatform provides a promising strategy for enhancing the therapeutic effect of STING agonists for pancreatic cancer immunotherapy.

items.title: Preoperative Total Iron-Binding Capacity Is a Potential Surrogate Marker of Long-Term Outcomes After Pancreatectomy for Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study aimed to examine whether preoperative serum total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), which is directly proportional to transferrin level, correlates with long-term outcomes after pancreatectomy.
METHODS: Preoperative TIBC levels, calculated by summing serum iron and unsaturated iron binding capacity, were evaluated in 158 patients who underwent pancreatectomy for pancreatic cancer. We defined TIBC < 258 μg/dL calculated by receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) analysis as low TIBC. We evaluated the relationship between preoperative TIBC levels and long-term outcomes after pancreatectomy.
RESULTS: Low preoperative TIBC levels were correlated with lower body mass index, higher rate of preoperative chemotherapy, lower albumin, and higher amount of intraoperative blood loss compared to those in high TIBC levels (p = 0.041, 0.046, 0.0002, 0.0032, respectively). Patients with low preoperative TIBC levels had significantly poorer overall survival (OS) and recurrence-free survival (RFS) compared to that in high TIBC level in Kaplan-Meier analysis (p < 0.0001, p = 0.0031). Furthermore, these patients were significantly correlated with worse OS and RFS in univariate and multivariate analyses (OS; hazard ratio [HR] 6.22, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.770-21.838, p = 0.0044/RFS; HR 3.24, 95% CI 1.012-13.206, p = 0.048).
CONCLUSION: Preoperative low serum TIBC levels may be a potential surrogate marker of long-term survival after pancreatectomy for pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Difluoromethylornithine modulates mutant K-RAS signaling pathways in pancreatic cancer cells.
items.abstract: Oncogenic mutations in the K-RAS small GTPase occur in more than 90% of human PDACs and cause dysregulation of multiple metabolic pathways, including polyamine metabolism. The goal of this study was to determine whether blocking polyamine synthesis with the irreversible inhibitor α-difluoromethylornithine (DFMO) provides a valid approach to targeting metabolic dependency in mutant K-RAS pancreatic tumors, compared with direct suppression of the oncogenic K-RAS protein. The anti-tumor activity of DFMO was evaluated in vitro and in vivo in the MIA PaCa-2 pancreatic cell line (K-RASG12C) and its isogenic clonally selected line M-27, which does not express a functional GTP-bound RAS protein. MIA PaCa-2 and M-27 cells had comparable intracellular polyamine levels, and DFMO treatment effectively suppressed total polyamine levels in both cell lines (p < 0.01). DFMO reduced the protein levels of phosphorylated extracellular signal-regulated kinases 1 and 2 (ERK1/2) and RAS-like small GTPase A (RalA) but induced the phosphoinositide 3-phosphate kinase (PI3K) signaling pathway. Additionally, the intracellular levels of K-RAS and hypusinated eukaryotic initiation factor 5 A (eIF5AHyp) proteins were suppressed in DFMO-treated MIA PaCa-2 cells. DFMO therapy regimen (500 mg/kg/day by oral gavage) significantly improved survival rates of SCID mice with orthotopically implanted MIA PaCa-2 cell line (MIA PaCa-2 control vs. MIA PaCa-2 DFMO, p = 0.0184), with median survival time comparable to animals implanted with M-27 cell line (MIA PaCa-2 control vs. M-27 control, p = 0.0204). DFMO treatment did not significantly improve survival of mice bearing M-27 tumors (M-27 control vs. M-27 DFMO, p = 0.6055). These data indicate that DFMO treatment suppresses pancreatic tumorigenesis driven by the mutant K-RAS oncogene similarly to the targeted elimination of the active GTP-bound RAS protein.

items.title: Protocol for eVLP-mediated CRISPR-Cas9 and prime editing in pancreatic cancer cell lines.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cell lines resist transfection, limiting gene-editing experiments. Here, we present a protocol for delivering CRISPR-Cas9 or prime editors into PDAC cell lines using retrovirus-derived engineered virus-like particles (eVLPs). We describe steps for generating eVLPs, packaging CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoproteins or prime editors with engineered prime-editing guide RNAs (epegRNAs), and transducing human PDAC cells. We use the HEK3 locus and NQO1 (NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1) exon 6 as example edits and controls, respectively. This protocol adapts readily to other genomic sites.

items.title: RAS Mutations as Prognostic Biomarkers in Digestive Cancers: From Binary Classification to Variant-Specific and Context-Dependent Risk Stratification.
items.abstract: In digestive cancers, activating RAS mutations - primarily KRAS, less frequently NRAS - are among the most prevalent oncogenic drivers. Their clinical significance depends strongly on the tumor type, disease stage, treatment context, and specific RAS variant. In colorectal cancer (CRC), RAS alterations are well-established predictors of resistance to anti-EGFR therapy. However, KRAS G12C-mutant tumors represent a distinct subgroup with demonstrated sensitivity to KRAS G12C inhibitors. However, growing evidence supports the negative prognostic impact of RAS mutations on both primary CRC and colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM) in both post-resection and adjuvant therapies. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), where KRAS alterations are nearly universal, prognostic evaluation has evolved from a binary mutant versus wild-type classification to a more refined approach based on mutation subtype (e.g., G12D/V vs. G12R) and KRAS mutant dosage, both of which influence clinical outcomes. In biliary tract cancers, KRAS mutations occur in a relevant subset and are consistently associated with poor survival. Liquid biopsy approaches increasingly enable noninvasive detection and longitudinal monitoring. In gastric cancer, RAS alterations are less frequent overall but may identify biologically aggressive subsets and may also be associated with inferior outcomes under HER2-targeted therapy in selected populations. This review synthesizes contemporary data supporting RAS alterations as prognostic biomarkers across digestive cancers, highlights practical considerations for integrating variant-level RAS information into risk stratification and trial designs, and discusses how emerging RAS-directed therapies may reshape the prognostic significance of specific molecular subsets.

items.title: Transcription factor-driven metabolic stratification reveals glycolytic and lipogenic subtypes with distinct prognostic and functional features in pancreatic cancer.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits profound molecular and metabolic heterogeneity associated with distinct phenotypic states. However, the contribution of transcription factor (TF)-driven regulatory programs to metabolic subtype stratification remains poorly understood. This study aims to determine whether TF-based classification can identify prognostically relevant glycolytic and lipogenic PDAC subtypes.
METHODS: Bulk transcriptomic data from multiple PDAC cohorts and single-cell RNA sequencing data were integrated to characterize TF-associated metabolic heterogeneity. Metabolic signatures and TFs were quantified using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) and AddModule Score (AMS). Differential expression, enrichment analysis, integrative bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analysis, and deep neural network-based metabolic flux modeling were performed to investigate metabolic programs and functional differences between TF-defined subtypes. Additionally, RNA interference, RT-qPCR, lipid droplets staining, lactate assay, and transwell assays were used to evaluate the roles of TP63 in metabolic regulation.
RESULTS: Glycolytic and lipogenic TF-defined metabolic subtypes were identified across multiple independent PDAC cohorts. These subtypes exhibited distinct metabolic programs, differentiation states, and prognostic outcomes. The glycolytic TF-defined subtype was associated with worse prognosis and differentiation, whereas the lipogenic TF-defined subtype exhibited more favorable clinical features. Integration of public bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses, together with deep neural network-based metabolic flux modeling, revealed consistent metabolic heterogeneity at both cellular and functional levels. Notably, TP63 was identified as a potential regulator of glycolytic-lipogenic metabolic reprogramming in PDAC.
CONCLUSIONS: TF-based classification delineates glycolytic and lipogenic subtypes in PDAC, underscoring the critical role of TF-regulated metabolic programs in patient stratification. These findings highlight the prognostic significance of glycolytic and lipogenic metabolic heterogeneity and support the development of metabolism-targeted therapeutic strategies.

items.title: CGRP remodels the acidic microenvironment and promotes pancreatic carcinoma progression by regulating NHE1 and CA9.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Neurons can regulate cancer cells to modulate their survival and growth, the interplay between calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and the acidic tumor microenvironment (TME) in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains unknown.
METHODS AND RESULTS: Here, we reported that CGRP expression and neuronal activation markers p-ERK/p-CREB were significantly elevated in PDAC tissues. Exogenous CGRP promoted PANC02 cell proliferation and migration, whereas CGRP knockout suppressed orthotopic tumor growth. Mechanistically, CGRP upregulated the proton transporters NHE1 and CA9, facilitating H+ efflux and reducing extracellular pH, thereby exacerbating TME acidification. Clinical analysis revealed that high expression of NHE1 and CA9 correlated with poor prognosis in PDAC patients. Rimegepant, a CGRP receptor antagonist, inhibited orthotopic tumor growth and exhibited synergistic effects with gemcitabine.
CONCLUSION AND DISCUSSION: In conclusion, our findings uncover a functional connection between CGRPergic sensory neurons and the acidic TME, identifying the CGRP signaling pathway as a potential therapeutic target for PDAC. Despite these findings, the mechanistic conclusions remain correlative and require further validation, and the generalizability to human PDAC warrants future investigation.

items.title: PAFAH1B1 stabilization, through PUM2-mediated competitive binding with miRNAs on its' 3'-UTR, takes active actions on ferroptosis to overcome the radioresistance to 125I radioactive particles of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most fatal malignancies with the lowest 5-year survival worldwide. Radioresistance remains the major challenge for pancreatic cancer treatment. The aim of this study is to unravel the mechanism underlying PAFAH1B1-regulated radiosensitivity in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
METHODS: Immunohistochemistry (IHC), western blot or qRT-PCR were employed to detect the expression of PAFAH1B1, PUM2 and other molecules. Two radiation-resistant (RR) PDAC cell lines and a xenograft mouse model were established. CCK-8, colony formation assays and flow cytometry analysis were used to assess cell proliferation and apoptosis in PDAC cells, respectively. Ferroptosis was evaluated using commercial kits and BODIPY 581/591 C11 staining. The association between PUM2 and PAFAH1B1 3'UTR, as well as between miR-421/miR-301a-3p and PAFAH1B1 3'UTR, were detected by luciferase and RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) assays.
RESULTS: PAFAH1B1 was downregulated in PDAC, and it was associated with unfavorable prognosis and radiotherapy response of PDAC patients. PAFAH1B1 overexpression enhanced the radiosensitivity to 125I particle in BxPC-3-RR, PANC-1-RR cells and PANC-1-RR xenograft tumors. Overexpression of PAFAH1B1 potentiated radiation-impaired cell viability and proliferation via triggering ferroptosis in PDAC cells. Mechanistically, PUM2 increased PAFAH1B1 expression via competitively binding to PAFAH1B1 3'UTR with miR-421 and miR-301a-3p. Moreover, PUM2 promoted radiation-induced ferroptosis in a PAFAH1B1-dependent manner.
CONCLUSION: PUM2/PAFAH1B1 axis decreased the radioresistance to 125I radioactive particles in PDAC via triggering ferroptosis.

items.title: Transcriptomic profiling reveals autophagy-associated programs and prognostic biomarkers in anoikis-resistant pancreatic cancer cells.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by aggressive metastatic progression and poor clinical outcomes. During metastatic dissemination, detached tumor cells must overcome anoikis, a form of apoptosis induced by loss of extracellular matrix attachment. Although anoikis resistance is considered a critical prerequisite for metastasis, the adaptive mechanisms supporting detached survival in pancreatic cancer remain incompletely understood. In this study, anoikis-resistant (AR) pancreatic cancer cell models were established through repeated long-term suspension culture using Capan-1 and PSN-1 cells. Transcriptomic profiling was performed to identify conserved molecular programs associated with anoikis resistance in PDAC. Gene set variation analysis (GSVA) demonstrated consistent transcriptomic enrichment of autophagy-associated and suppression of cell cycle-related pathways in both AR models. Differential expression and integrative pathway analyses further identified several core genes associated with autophagy regulation and cytokine signaling. Survival analysis revealed that elevated expression of UBC and ATG14 was associated with poor prognosis in pancreatic cancer patients. Our findings suggest that suspension-selected pancreatic cancer cells undergo coordinated stress-adaptive transcriptional remodeling characterized by enriched autophagy- and ubiquitin-associated transcriptional programs.

items.title: A robust biomarker combining radiomic and CA19.9 information to predict distant relapse-free survival after radiochemotherapy in pancreatic cancer.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The radiomic feature Statistical Percentile 10% (p10%), extracted from [¹⁸F]FDG-PET images, has been previously identified and validated as a robust predictor of distant progression-free survival (DPFS) in unresectable pancreatic cancer (LAPC). This study aimed to maximize its prognostic potential by combining p10% with CA19.9 serum levels and assessing its generalizability across distinct clinical settings.
METHODS: We analyzed 287 LAPC patients treated with chemoradiotherapy (CRT) and a validation cohort of 72 patients enrolled in the CASSANDRA trial (resectable/borderline-resectable PDAC). Cox models combined p10% with CA19.9 levels measured before RT in LAPC patients, and before surgery for CASSANDRA patients.
RESULTS: p10% was independently prognostic in both cohorts and its integration with CA19.9 significantly improved the prediction. In the LAPC cohort, the combined model achieved C-index=0.71, with median DPFS of 4.0-vs-15.0 months (p<0.0001;HR=3.22). In the pre-surgery setting (CASSANDRA trial), the model showed good rank-order discrimination (C-index=0.65), with median survival of 11.6 months vs not-reached (p=0.0018). However, the calibration slope of 0.54 suggests that absolute risk prediction requires recalibration in the surgical cohort.
CONCLUSIONS: Integrating p10% with CA19.9 provides a broader representation of tumor aggressiveness. The combined biomarkers demonstrate consistent performance across different disease stages supporting their use for treatment personalization.

items.title: Omega-3 fatty acids reprogram tumor-associated macrophage cytokine signaling and suppress pancreatic cancer growth.
items.abstract: Dietary polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) shape inflammatory signaling within the pancreatic tumor microenvironment (TME), but the cellular mechanisms underlying their effects on tumor progression remain unclear. Using orthotopic models of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), we show that omega-3 (n-3) and omega-6 (n-6) PUFAs are differentially incorporated into tumor lipid pools, generating spatially heterogeneous lipid microenvironments. While an n-6-enriched diet accelerated PDAC growth, an n-3-enriched diet suppressed tumor growth in a T cell-independent manner. Examining inflammatory effects in PDAC tumors, the n-3 PUFA-enriched diet reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6 family members, and single-cell and spatial analyses identified tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) as the primary diet-responsive population. Indeed, selective conversion of n-6 to n-3 fatty acids within myeloid cells using an inducible fat-1 transgene, which encodes an n-3 desaturase that converts n-6 to n-3 PUFAs in vivo, was sufficient to suppress tumor growth, whereas fibroblast-restricted conversion had no effect. This finding is the first to formally establish that cellular origin of PUFA metabolism within the TME is a key determinant of tumor progression and identifies TAMs as critical mediators of n-3-dependent tumor suppression. Furthermore, the n-3 PUFA-enriched diet reduced Arg1+ immunosuppressive TAMs and promoted C1q+ and MHC-II+ antigen-presenting TAM populations enriched for antigen processing machinery and T cell-recruiting chemokines, alongside reduced IL-6 family cytokine production. Together, these findings establish macrophages as key mediators of n-3-driven tumor control and define a mechanism by which dietary lipids remodel cytokine signaling in the PDAC microenvironment.

items.title: Feasibility of Single-Site Plus One-Port Robotic Distal Pancreatectomy Using the da Vinci SP in Comparison With the Conventional Xi Platforms: A Multicenter Experience.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ongoing efforts in minimally invasive surgery aim to reduce access sites. This study evaluated the feasibility of the da Vinci SP platform for single-site plus one-port robotic distal pancreatectomy (SSRDP) by comparing perioperative outcomes with a previously reported Xi-based approach.
METHODS: Patients who underwent SSRDP using the SP or Xi at two tertiary centres from February 2015 to September 2023 were retrospectively reviewed. Each centre exclusively used one platform.
RESULTS: Thirty-two patients underwent SSRDP (SP, n = 20; Xi, n = 12). The SP group had higher age, body mass index, and ASA scores. Operative time was shorter in the SP group, whereas blood loss, spleen preservation, conversion, postoperative pancreatic fistula, and overall complications were comparable.
CONCLUSIONS: In this early multicenter experience, SSRDP using the SP platform was feasible and achieved acceptable perioperative outcomes comparable to those of Xi-SSRDP.

items.title: Self-Fueling Nanobacteria Harnesses Leaked Pancreatic Fluid to Eradicate Residual Tumors After Surgery.
items.abstract: Postoperative management of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains hindered by two closely linked challenges: the harmful effects of pancreatic fistula and the high risk of local tumor recurrence. Although leaked pancreatic fluid (PF) is generally regarded as a postoperative complication, its abundance of digestive enzymes also suggests an underexplored therapeutic opportunity. Here, we developed a localized therapeutic strategy that converts the enzyme-rich fistula microenvironment from a pathological burden into an antitumor resource. To achieve this, we nano-engineered Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron (B.t.) and integrated it with TRPV1 antagonist-loaded nanomicelles in a GelMA hydrogel, generating the platform TNPs-N@B.t. + Gel. Mechanistically, this system acts in a coordinated manner within the postoperative PDAC microenvironment. B.t. degrades tumor-associated mucins, thereby dismantling the protective barrier that shields PDAC cells from pancreatic enzymes and restoring their vulnerability to enzymatic attack. Meanwhile, PF forms an in situ digestive enzyme corona on the nanoengineered bacterial surface, which promotes deeper tumor penetration by disrupting intercellular adhesion. In parallel, delivery of the TRPV1 antagonist (TRPV1a) suppresses CGRP release, attenuates cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) activation, and facilitates NK-cell-associated antitumor responses. In postoperative PDAC models, TNPs-N@B.t. + Gel showed durable local retention, enhanced tumor accumulation, suppressed recurrence, prolonged survival, and alleviated pain-related behaviors without evident systemic toxicity.

items.title: Optimisation and mechanistic characterization of a selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor in pancreatic cancer cells.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a lethal malignancy with limited targeted therapeutic options. Mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase kinase 4 (MAP4K4) has been implicated in PDAC progression, but the development of effective MAP4K4 inhibitors requires further improvement in potency, selectivity, and mechanistic characterisation. We previously identified F389-0746 as a selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor with anti-cancer activity in pancreatic cancer. Here, we used the F389-0746 scaffold to guide the selection and evaluation of benzoxazine-based analogs, followed by biochemical, structural, selectivity, and cellular characterisation of the most potent analogue. Among the identified analogs, F389-0736 showed the strongest MAP4K4 inhibitory activity, with an IC50 value of 44.0 nM, representing an approximately threefold improvement over F389-0746. Docking and structure-activity relationship analyses identified key binding interactions that support the enhanced potency of F389-0736 within the MAP4K4 binding pocket. Kinase profiling further demonstrated the selectivity of F389-0736 for MAP4K4 across the tested kinase panel. CETSA further demonstrated F389-0736-induced thermal stabilisation of MAP4K4, supporting intracellular target engagement. In pancreatic cancer cells, F389-0736 suppressed TAK1, JNK, and p38 phosphorylation and significantly reduced cell viability and proliferation, with IC50 and GI50 values of 4.41-4.65 μM and 4.03-5.12 μM, respectively. F389-0736 also inhibited clonogenic growth and induced sub-G1 accumulation with activation of apoptotic signalling. RNA sequencing identified 398 differentially expressed genes and revealed enrichment of inflammatory and stress response pathways, programmed cell death programs, oncogenic signalling perturbation, and metabolic reprogramming. These findings identify F389-0736 as a potent and selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor and support its use as a chemical probe and lead scaffold for investigating MAP4K4-dependent signalling and therapeutic vulnerability in pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Ultrasensitive Trace Sample Proteomics for Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Diagnosis Empowered by Dual-Affinity Spherical Ln-MOFs.
items.abstract: Low-abundance exosomal proteins from trace plasma volumes remain challenging to profile by mass spectrometry. Here, we report a lanthanide metal-organic framework (Ln-MOF) functionalized with boronic acid and carboxylate dual ligands, which captures exosomal proteins via synergistic phosphate coordination, boronate-diol complexation, and cation-π interactions. Compared with traditional ultracentrifugation, which identifies 1003 proteins from 200 µL of plasma, the Ln-MOF method identifies 1523 proteins from only 50 µL of plasma. Notably, the method enriches glycoproteins and phosphoproteins by 2.1-fold and 1.8-fold, respectively. Applying this platform to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients and healthy controls, we delineate tumor tissue hypermetabolism vs. systemic immune suppression.

items.title: Gut Microbiota and Nutritional Aspects in Pancreatic Diseases: A Narrative Review.
items.abstract: Pancreatic diseases, including acute pancreatitis (AP) and chronic pancreatitis (CP), pancreatogenic diabetes mellitus (T3cDM), autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP), and pancreatic cancer (PDAC), are associated with metabolic, inflammatory, and nutritional disturbances. Increasing evidence indicates a bidirectional relationship between pancreatic diseases and the gut microbiota. On the one hand, alterations in microbial composition and function, intestinal barrier dysfunction, and bacterial translocation may contribute to their pathogenesis and progression. On the other hand, pancreatic diseases and associated changes in nutrition and treatment may affect the composition and function of the gut microbiota. This narrative review aimed to discuss the role of the gut microbiota and nutritional aspects in selected pancreatic diseases. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched up to May 2026 for English-language publications, with emphasis on studies from the previous 10 years, while earlier relevant studies were also considered. Google Scholar was used as a supplementary source. Human observational, experimental and mechanistic studies, as well as secondary literature, were considered, addressing pancreatic microbiota, intestinal permeability, bacterial translocation, nutrition, and microbiota-targeted interventions. Available evidence indicates that pancreatic diseases are associated with alterations in gut and pancreatic microbial communities, although the reported patterns vary between diseases and studies. These changes may be relevant to intestinal barrier integrity, inflammatory signaling, microbial metabolite production, and, in pancreatic cancer, the tumor microenvironment and treatment response. Nutritional management remains an important component of care, particularly in patients with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and those at risk of malnutrition. However, the causal relationships between pancreatic diseases and microbiota alterations remain incompletely established, and evidence for microbiota-targeted interventions is limited and heterogeneous. Further clinical studies are needed to clarify these interactions and their potential diagnostic and therapeutic relevance.

items.title: Prehabilitation as a Strategy to Modulate the Tumor Microenvironment in Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract: Multimodal prehabilitation aims to enhance resilience to cancer therapy through exercise, nutrition, and psychological optimization. While prehabilitation can improve physical condition and functional status, its biologic influence on the tumor microenvironment (TME) remains poorly characterized. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the TME is dominated by immunosuppressive and desmoplastic features that limit immune cell infiltration and therapeutic efficacy. As an exploratory pilot analysis, this study characterized the cellular composition, spatial relationships, and functional signaling of the pancreatic TME in patients who underwent prehabilitation prior to surgical resection and those who did not. Tumor samples from eight patients (four prehabilitation, four control) were analyzed with a 34-plex protein panel using Imaging Mass Cytometry (IMC), categorizing the tumor-immune landscape and functional status at the single-cell resolution. Prehabilitation tumors demonstrated reduced neutrophil and epithelial/tumor cell density and enrichment of Natural Killer (NK), CD4+, and CD8+ T cells. Spatial analysis revealed an immune-permissive architecture in prehabilitation tumors, in contrast to immune-resistant patterns in controls. Functional marker analysis showed reduced activation and pro-tumor signaling in immunosuppressive populations, including Tregs (HLADR, pAkt, pNFκB) and Collagen+ CAFs (NOS2, pERK, pNFκB, pSTAT3). These preliminary findings raise the possibility that prehabilitation is associated with an immune-permissive TME in PDAC, supporting further investigation of its immunomodulatory potential in larger, prospectively designed cohorts.

items.title: p38α Signaling Is Associated with Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Progression and Represents a Potential Therapeutic Vulnerability.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most lethal malignancies, and approximately 15% of cases arise from intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs). These precursor lesions can progress to invasive cancer through the accumulation of molecular alterations. To identify pathways associated with this transition, we performed comparative transcriptomic analyses of patient-derived IPMN and PDAC samples, followed by protein-level validation in tissue specimens and pancreatic cancer cell lines. Functional studies were conducted using the selective p38α inhibitor ralimetinib in two-dimensional cultures, three-dimensional tumorspheres, and patient-derived tumor organoids (PDTOs). Transcriptomic profiling revealed significant downregulation of the p38 pathway in IPMNs compared with PDAC, suggesting progressive pathway activation during pancreatic tumorigenesis. Immunohistochemical analyses confirmed increased phospho-activated p38α in PDAC tissues, particularly in lesions with advanced malignant features, while PDAC cell lines displayed higher levels of activated p38α than non-tumorigenic pancreatic epithelial cells. Pharmacological inhibition of p38α suppressed downstream MAPKAPK2 phosphorylation, induced apoptotic cell death, and reduced tumorsphere growth and viability. Consistently, PDTOs exhibiting elevated p38α activation showed increased sensitivity to ralimetinib treatment. Collectively, these findings identify p38α signaling as a pathway activated during PDAC progression and support further investigation of p38α-targeted therapies as a potential precision medicine strategy for pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Rewiring Biological Barriers in Pancreatic Diseases with Metal-Organic Frameworks.
items.abstract: Pancreatic diseases, particularly pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), remain among the most challenging disorders to diagnose and treat owing to a series of interconnected biological barriers, including dense stromal desmoplasia, profound immunosuppression, hypoxia, therapeutic resistance, and the lack of effective early-detection strategies. Overcoming these barriers requires multifunctional platforms capable of integrating diagnosis, microenvironment regulation, and precision therapy within a single system. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), a class of highly tunable porous crystalline materials, have emerged as uniquely suited candidates for this purpose because of their programmable composition, structural versatility, catalytic activity, and capacity for multifunctional integration. Notably, MOFs have evolved from passive drug carriers into active regulators of disease-associated biological processes, enabling enhanced drug delivery, extracellular matrix remodeling, ferroptosis- and cuproptosis-based precision therapy, energy-triggered reactive oxygen species generation, immune microenvironment reprogramming, and imaging-guided theranostics. Beyond pancreatic cancer, emerging evidence further supports their potential applications in pancreatitis management and interventional therapeutic enhancement. In this review, we systematically summarize recent advances in the rational engineering of MOFs for pancreatic diseases, focusing on how material design strategies are leveraged to overcome key pathological barriers and improve therapeutic outcomes. We further discuss current challenges associated with biosafety, biodegradation, large-scale manufacturing, and clinical translation, while highlighting future opportunities for the development of next-generation MOF-based precision nanomedicines. By integrating advances across materials science, nanomedicine, and pancreatic disease biology, this review provides a comprehensive framework for the design and translational development of MOF-enabled diagnostic and therapeutic platforms.

items.title: Targeting SERPINB5 and MSLN for Pancreatic Cancer Therapy.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Pancreatic cancer (PC) is a leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States and lacks efficient therapeutic options. Serine peptidase inhibitor, clade B, member 5 (SERPINB5) is non-inhibitory toward serine proteases, yet it has diverse biological functions, including regulating cell migration, cell death, gene expression, and stress responses. Mesothelin (MSLN) is a tumor-associated antigen that is broadly overexpressed on various malignant tumor cells and plays a crucial role in promoting proliferation, invasion, and metastasis. Methods: We integrated public database analyses, cell-line screening, gene knockdown and overexpression, immunoblotting, cell viability and apoptosis assays, flow cytometry, chromatin immunoprecipitation paired with quantitative PCR (ChIP-qPCR), and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy to investigate SERPINB5 and MSLN functions, developing a novel and effective therapeutic strategy for patients with pancreatic cancer. Results: Both SERPINB5 and MSLN are highly expressed and negatively associated with the overall survival of PC patients. Our mechanistic study suggests that SERPINB5 negatively regulates the mitochondrial protein dehydrogenase/reductase 2 (DHRS2) to promote PC cell survival; consequently, SERPINB5 depletion induces PC cell apoptosis. Of note, SERPINB5 depletion increases MSLN transcription by enhancing c-Myc binding to the MSLN promoter region, which in turn suppresses the mitochondrial protein DHRS2 and leads to resistance to apoptosis in PC cells. Our genetic ablation study shows that SERPINB5 and MSLN are critical for PC cell survival, and that depleting both proteins synergistically induces PC cell apoptosis. Gemcitabine (GEM) is a standard chemotherapy drug for PC treatment. Our study shows that SERPINB5-high PC cells display greater sensitivity to GEM than SERPINB5-low PC cells. GEM treatment increases mitochondrial DHRS2 protein expression, similar to the effect of SERPINB5 knockdown, whereas upregulated MSLN confers apoptotic resistance by decreasing DHRS2 levels. Conclusions: Our in vitro study demonstrates that sequential treatment with GEM followed by anti-MSLN chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells is an effective and promising strategy for patients with pancreatic cancer. Future studies using mouse models may validate the efficacy of this sequential treatment strategy in vivo.

items.title: Polygenic Risk Scores for Pancreatic Cancer Risk Prediction and Early Detection: A Systematic Evidence Review of Clinical Utility
items.abstract:
Background:

/Objectives: Pancreatic cancer carries a five-year relative survival of 13%. Polygenic risk scores (PRS) rank inherited susceptibility across common variants. Prior syntheses pooled PRS association and discrimination, but none asked whether a PRS changes a clinical decision. We synthesized evidence on the clinical utility of PRS for pancreatic cancer risk assessment.

Methods:

In this PROSPERO-registered review (CRD42024511326), we searched four databases through May 11, 2026, for studies evaluating a PRS for primary pancreatic cancer risk in adults, alone or with clinical predictors. We recorded discrimination as the prerequisite for utility and organized utility across five prespecified domains: threshold-based accuracy, incremental value, calibrated absolute risk, decision-analytic output, and economic impact. We synthesized narratively and appraised risk of bias with PROBAST.

Results:

Forty-three studies met the inclusion and exclusion criteria, including 25 from the UK Biobank. Ten of 16 standalone discrimination estimates fell between 0.56 and 0.64. Adding PRS to a clinical model increased discrimination by at most 0.05 in general populations. Combined PRS and clinical models exceeded 0.80 only in three diabetes-focused studies. Six studies reported calibration, four reclassification, two decision-curve net benefit, none cost-effectiveness, and 20 had no translational milestone. Thirteen studies were at high risk of bias, with 11 in the analysis domain.

Conclusions:

Pancreatic cancer PRS discriminates modestly alone and adds most where prior risk is highest. Actionable use awaits an externally validated absolute-risk model with a prespecified threshold and a decision analysis.

items.title: Innate immunity-stroma crosstalk in pancreatic cancer: overcoming spatial and metabolic barriers to immunotherapy.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits profound resistance to current immunotherapies, a challenge largely attributed to its uniquely immunosuppressive and desmoplastic tumor microenvironment (TME). At the heart of this therapeutic recalcitrance lies the dynamic, bidirectional crosstalk between innate immune cells-particularly tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs)-and stromal components, notably cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). This review comprehensively delineates how the innate immunity-stroma axis establishes formidable spatial and metabolic barriers that thwart effective antitumor immunity. Spatially, dense collagen matrices, periductal fibroblast organization, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) create physical checkpoints that exclude cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and natural killer (NK) cells from tumor nests. Metabolically, elevated lactate, cholesterol dysregulation, adenosine accumulation, and altered polyamine metabolism synergistically paralyze effector lymphocytes while driving immunosuppressive myeloid polarization. We highlight the key molecular networks orchestrating this pathological crosstalk, including the NF-κB, IL-1β, JAK/STAT3, and TGF-β signaling pathways. Furthermore, we summarize emerging therapeutic strategies designed to dismantle these barriers, encompassing macrophage reprogramming, CAF modulation, and metabolic interventions. Finally, we discuss the multidimensional "3D+R" framework-integrating de-desmoplasia, de-adenosine, de-novo antigen presentation, and rational sequencing-as a conceptual roadmap for rationally designed combination therapies to overcome PDAC immunotherapy resistance.

items.title: Basal Marker ΔNp63α Is Enriched in Pancreatic Cancer Metastases but Not in Primary Tumors Post-Chemotherapy.
items.abstract: Cancer cells within a single pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are most often heterogeneous in their expression of the basal or classical transcriptional program. Predominance of the basal subtype has been associated with poorer patient outcomes and increased resistance to chemotherapy. Based on this, we predicted that basal subtype would be enriched in tumors previously treated with chemotherapy, and in metastases derived from primary PDAC tumors with a mixed basal/classical population. To create matched classical and basal cell lines, we stably transduced two classical PDAC cell lines (AsPC1 and HPAFII) with the basal program transcriptional driver ∆Np63α or an mCherry control and assessed their growth, metastasis, and response to chemotherapy both in vitro and in vivo. Forced expression of ∆Np63α successfully converted both cell lines to basal transcriptomic subtype, yet the basal program failed to drive increased cell growth or chemoresistance in culture and did not affect tumor growth of AsPC1 in the murine pancreas. In mice orthotopically engrafted with ∆Np63α-expressing cells, no statistically significant increase in spontaneous pulmonary metastases was observed for AsPC1 or HPAFII, however, pulmonary metastases were enriched for ∆Np63 expression as compared to established primary tumors, including expression of endogenous ∆Np63 in the mCherry control. Increased resistance to irinotecan chemotherapy was observed in ∆Np63α + HPAFII, yet treatment selected for ∆Np63-negative cells in both HPAFII and ASPC1. In summary, our data show that PDAC metastases are enriched for basal subtype, but chemotherapy treatment does not preferentially select for basal-type cells.

items.title: The type of portal vein reconstruction does not affect the outcomes of pancreatic surgery or the patency of the portal vein.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the safety of the four types of portal vein reconstruction (PVR) as defined by the International Study Group of Pancreatic Surgery (ISGPS) and to analyse long-term survival outcomes in patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
METHODS: A prospectively collected pancreatic surgery registry that was supplemented retrospectively was used. Patients who underwent open pancreatic resection with PVR between 2005 and 2024 were included. Clinicopathological characteristics, outcomes, and computed tomography images were analysed and tested in multivariate and survival analyses. For survival analyses, patients with PDAC who underwent pancreatectomy without PVR served as controls.
RESULTS: Pancreatectomies with PVR (n=386) comprised 63 tangential resections with venorrhaphy (ISGPS type I), 25 patch reconstructions (type II), 147 end-to-end anastomoses (type III), and 151 resections with graft interposition (type IV). Most type IV reconstructions (98.7%) used spiral grafts, predominantly made from the great saphenous vein (GSV). PVR thrombosis rate was 3.1% at 30 days and 5.7% at 90 days following surgery. There were no significant differences between PVR types I-IV in the incidence of PVR thromboses, complications, or mortality. Median survival for PDAC patients with PVR was 22.8 months, with no survival differences between types I-IV, compared with 31.7 months in patients without PVR, p=.003.
CONCLUSIONS: In this setting, where PVR was performed using GSV spiral grafts for interposition, the type of PVR did not associate with pancreatic surgery outcomes or portal vein patency. The rate of PVR thrombosis was low, and other complication rates and long-term survival outcomes were comparable with international standards.

items.title: Limited Survival Benefit of Short-Course Neoadjuvant Gemcitabine Plus Nab-Paclitaxel for Resectable Pancreatic Cancer: A Prospective Phase II Study With a Propensity Score-Matched Analysis.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The optimal duration and clinical benefit of neoadjuvant gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (GnP) for resectable pancreatic cancer (RPC) remain uncertain.
METHODS: We conducted a prospective single-arm phase II study evaluating neoadjuvant GnP in RPC. The primary end point was 2-y relapse-free survival (RFS). Secondary end points included R0 resection rate, safety, overall survival, and the impact of treatment duration on survival outcomes. Survival outcomes were compared with those of a propensity score-matched historical cohort that underwent upfront surgery.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight patients were analyzed. The objective response rate was 17.9%, and curative resection was achieved in 85.7%. Grade ≥3 neutropenia occurred in 64.3% without febrile neutropenia, indicating manageable toxicity. The median RFS was 15.7 mo (95% confidence interval, 12.3-19.2), with a 2-y RFS rate of 29.9%, and the median overall survival was 32.9 mo (95% confidence interval, 30.0-38.8). Propensity score-matched analysis demonstrated survival comparable to historical controls treated with upfront surgery. However, patients who completed four cycles of GnP showed a trend toward longer survival than those receiving two cycles.
CONCLUSIONS: Neoadjuvant GnP provides acceptable safety and tumor control but limited survival benefit in RPC. Prolonged preoperative GnP may improve outcomes, suggesting that treatment duration may be a key determinant of efficacy.

items.title: Bariatric Surgery and Risk of Obesity-Related Cancer by Age and Sex.
items.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Obesity is associated with elevated risks for multiple cancers. How bariatric surgery influences these risks across age and sex is insufficiently understood.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the association between bariatric surgery and obesity-related cancer (breast, endometrial, ovarian, esophageal adenocarcinoma, liver, pancreatic, colon, rectal, kidney, and multiple myeloma) and whether this association varies by age and sex.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This population-based cohort study within the Nordic Obesity Surgery Cohort (NordOSCo) included individuals aged 18 to 59 years with an obesity record in Denmark, Finland, or Sweden from 1992 to 2023. Prospectively collected data on exposure, outcomes, and confounders were obtained from well-maintained national registries. Follow-up continued until cancer diagnosis, death, emigration, or December 31, 2023. These data were analyzed from December 2025 to April 2026.
EXPOSURE: Bariatric surgery vs no surgery among individuals with obesity.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was incidence of obesity-related cancers. Risks were compared using crude and multivariable-adjusted incidence rate ratios (aIRR) with 95% CIs derived from Poisson regression adjusted for age, sex, calendar year, country, and obesity- and lifestyle-related comorbidities. Effect modification by age group (18-39 vs 40-59 years) and sex (female vs male) was evaluated using interaction terms.
RESULTS: Among 784 105 individuals with obesity (569 266 women [73%] and 214 839 men [27%]), 99 614 underwent bariatric surgery. Surgery was associated with a lower risk of obesity-related cancer overall (aIRR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.77-0.85). The magnitude of risk reduction did not differ by age group (individuals aged 18 to 39 years: aIRR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.72-0.88 and individuals aged 40 to 59 years: aIRR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.78-0.86) (P for interaction = .88). Associations for non-sex-specific cancers were similar in men and women (P for interaction = .50). For individual cancers, the strongest inverse associations were observed for liver cancer (aIRR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.34-0.70), endometrial cancer (aIRR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.45-0.59), and ovarian cancer (aIRR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.60-0.87). In contrast, pancreatic cancer risk was increased after surgery, particularly among younger adults (aIRR, 2.21; 95% CI, 1.44-3.39; P = .01).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this study, bariatric surgery was associated with a lower long-term risk of obesity-related cancers, with similar associations across age groups and sexes. These findings suggest that the long-term oncologic benefits of bariatric surgery apply broadly across age groups and sexes, supporting equitable access to bariatric surgery for patients with obesity.

items.title: From Nature to Medicine: Overcoming the Limitations of Herbal Therapeutics for Pancreatic Cancer Treatment Based on Nanotechnology.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies worldwide due to late-stage diagnosis, aggressive progression, and limited therapeutic responsiveness. Although herbal-derived bioactive compounds have demonstrated promising anticancer potential, their clinical application is often restricted by poor aqueous solubility, low bioavailability, rapid metabolic degradation, and insufficient tumor targeting. Nanomedicine has emerged as a promising platform to overcome these limitations through enhanced drug delivery, improved pharmacokinetics, and controlled release capabilities. In recent years, the integration of green nanotechnology with herbal therapeutics has gained increasing attention as a sustainable and biocompatible strategy for PDAC management. Green synthesis approaches utilizing plant extracts, microbial systems, and biopolymers provide environmentally friendly alternatives to conventional physicochemical nanoparticle (NP) fabrication methods while simultaneously enhancing biological functionality. This review aims to explore green nanotechnology-based strategies for improving the therapeutic potential of herbal-derived bioactive compounds in PDAC, with particular emphasis on nanoformulation approaches that enhance solubility, bioavailability, tumor targeting, and anticancer efficacy. In addition, the review discusses the advantages of green synthesis approaches, NP characterization strategies, translational barriers, biosafety considerations, and current clinical challenges. Overall, this review highlights the growing potential of green nanomedicine to improve herbal-based therapeutic strategies against PDAC while emphasizing the key obstacles that must be addressed to facilitate successful clinical translation.

items.title: Multi-modal spatial glycomic analysis of lymphoid aggregates in prostate and pancreatic cancer tissues.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Altered N-glycosylation plays a critical role in immune regulation, yet the spatial distribution of N-glycans within immune niches of immunologically "cold" tumors remain poorly defined. Here, we combine matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry imaging (MALDI-MSI) with highly multiplexed immunohistochemistry using photocleavable mass tags. This integrated workflow enables spatial mapping of N-glycosylation and immune markers within lymphoid aggregates (LAs) in prostate and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma tissues, two malignancies that respond poorly to immunotherapy. Given the role of N-glycosylation in immune regulation, spatially resolved N-glycan profiling may provide insight into molecular heterogeneity within lymphoid aggregates and their surrounding tumor microenvironment.
METHODS: To assess the relationship between N_glycosylation and immune markers, candidate LAs from tissue samples collected from patients with varying stages of prostate cancer, PCa (n=49) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, PDAC (n=26) were identified via histological stains prior to enzymatic release of N-glycans and MALDI-MSI. MALDI-IHC was used to target immune cell markers and extracellular matrix proteins.
RESULTS: In tissues with LAs, three N-glycan structural classes were identified when detectable: oligo-mannose, fucosylated tetra-antennary, and bisecting N-acetylglucosamine in fucosylated bi,- tri- and tetra- antennary structures, with some N-glycans common to both tumor types. LAs showed predominantly central CD20 and CD44 signal surrounded by CD3 signal localized along the tumor periphery.
CONCLUSION: Our analysis revealed unique N-glycan patterns within and surrounding LAs, with variable profiles in distant regions, highlighting heterogeneity in LA-associated N-glycan profiles.

items.title: U2 snRNP inhibition hampers pancreatic cancer cell viability by disrupting DNA repair proficiency and mitotic checkpoint integrity.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive cancer with remarkably poor prognosis. Splicing dysregulation is emerging as a hallmark and possible therapeutic target of PDAC.
METHODS: We performed high-throughput RNA sequencing analyses in PANC-1 cells treated with three drugs targeting the U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (U2 snRNP): Pladienolide B, Thailanstatin A and Indisulam. The efficacy of splicing inhibitors, Talazoparib, Alisertib, AZD7762 and Barisertib, alone or in combination, was assessed in PDAC cells and patient-derived organoids (PDOs) by cell viability assays. RT-PCR, western blot and cell cycle assays were performed to evaluate the expression of DNA repair and mitotic genes and the execution of mitosis. PANC-1 cells were engineered to stably co-express GFP-tagged H2b histone and RFP-tagged β-tubulin by CRISPR/Cas-9 technology and used for time-lapse confocal microscopy and immunofluorescence analyses.
RESULTS: Genes encoding for the U2 snRNP, which recognizes the 3' splice site, are upregulated in advanced PDAC. U2 snRNP-targeting drugs impair the DNA damage response (DDR) pathway in homologous recombination-proficient PDAC cells and PDOs, thus enhancing their sensitivity to PARP inhibitors. Genes whose splicing was disrupted by all three drugs are characterized by higher expression, more exon-intron junctions, weak 5' splice sites and atypical GC content. These features are enriched in mitotic genes (e.g. AURKA, AURKB, CHEK1), whose expression is strongly deregulated by splicing perturbation. Accordingly, splicing inhibition causes severe mitotic defects, leading to the accumulation of cells with misaligned condensed chromosomes on monopolar or bipolar spindles. Notably, high expression of AURKA, AURKB and CHEK1 correlates with poor prognosis in PDAC patients, whereas combined treatments with inhibitors of these mitotic kinases strongly impair the viability of PDAC cells and PDOs.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings uncover gene features associated with sensitivity to splicing inhibitors in PDAC cells and suggest that the DDR and mitosis are biological processes highly sensitive to splicing perturbation.

items.title: MSC-derived exosomes co-delivering anti-miR-221 and gemcitabine for inhibiting the proliferation of pancreatic cancer.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUD: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is among the most aggressive and lethal malignancies, with a dismal 5-year survival rate of approximately 4%. The majority of patients with pancreatic cancer have a poor response to traditional chemotherapy due to its disadvantages, such as drug resistance and biological toxicity. Therefore, a novel therapeutic methods should be developed to improve the efficacy of chemotherapy drugs in pancreatic cancer. In this study, we developed a co-delivery system utilizing exosomes as carriers to simultaneously encapsulate a miR-221-targeting antisense oligonucleotide (anti-miR-221) and gemcitabine(Gem) for treatment of PDAC.
METHODS: A lentiviral plasmid carrying the green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporter gene and anti-miR-221 was constructed and used to transfect the human umbilical cord blood mesenchymal stem cell line (MSCs). Exosomes secreted by the MSCs were purified using the ExoQuick reagent kit. Gemcitabine was loaded into the exosomes via sonication. After DAPI staining, Panc-1 cells were incubated with the exosomes, and uptake of exosomes loaded with anti-miR-221 and Gem by Panc-1 cells was confirmed using fluorescence microscopy. Experimental groups were as follows: blank exosomes (blank-exo group); exosomes loaded with anti-miR-221 (exo-221 group); exosomes loaded with Gem (exo-Gem group); Gemcitabine monotherapy (Gem group); and exosomes co-loaded with anti-miR-221 and Gem (exo-Gem-221 group).The effects of drug delivery system on Panc-1 cell proliferation were assessed using the CCK-8 assay, and miR-221 expression levels in Panc-1 cells were measured via RT-PCR. For the study in vivo, treatments were administered via intratumoral injection into a nude mouse model with subcutaneous Panc-1 xenografts. The tumor volume and weight were measured to calculate the tumor inhibition rate. miR-221 expression in tumor tissues was detected by RT-PCR. Protein expression levels of VEGF and Caspase-3 in tumor tissues were evaluated by immunohistochemistry. Liver and kidney tissues from the mice were collected, subjected to H&E staining, and examined under a light microscope for pathological changes.
RESULTS: In both in vitro and in vivo experiments, miR-221 levels were significantly lower in the exo-221 and exo-Gem-221 groups compared to the blank-exo group (P < 0.01), demonstrating that exosome-delivered anti-miR-221 effectively silenced miR-221 expression in pancreatic cancer cells. The CCK-8 assay showed that cell viability was significantly reduced in the exo-221, exo-Gem, and Gem monotherapy groups compared to the blank-exo group (P < 0.05). Furthermore, the exo-Gem-221 group exhibited a more pronounced decrease in cell viability compared to the exo-Gem, exo-221, and Gem monotherapy groups (P < 0.01). Animal experiments revealed that tumor volume and weight were significantly decreased in the exo-221, exo-Gem, and Gem monotherapy groups compared to the blank-exo group (P < 0.05). The exo-Gem-221 group showed a more significant reduction in tumor volume and weight and a higher tumor inhibition rate compared to the exo-221, exo-Gem, and Gem monotherapy groups (P < 0.01). Immunohistochemistry indicated that protein levels of Caspase-3 were significantly increased, while VEGF levels were significantly decreased, in the exo-221, exo-Gem, and Gem monotherapy groups compared to the blank-exo group (P < 0.05). These changes were even more pronounced in the exo-Gem-221 group compared to the exo-221, exo-Gem, and Gem monotherapy groups (P < 0.01). H&E staining of liver and kidney tissues from nude mice showed hepatic sinusoid atrophy and disordered hepatic plate arrangement in the liver, as well as glomerular shrinkage and peri-glomerular cell necrosis in the kidneys, only in the Gem monotherapy group. No significant pathological changes were observed in the liver or kidney tissues of the other groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Exosomes derived from MSCs and co-loaded with anti-miR-221 and Gemcitabine significantly inhibit the proliferation of pancreatic cancer. This combined antitumor effect is superior to that of exo-221, exo-Gem, or Gemcitabine monotherapy. Furthermore, this approach demonstrates low liver and kidney toxicity, suggesting it may be a safe and effective method for treating pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Clonal heterogeneity in human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and its impact on tumor progression.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive cancer characterized by profound desmoplasia and cellular heterogeneity, which cannot be fully resolved using traditional bulk sequencing approaches. To understand how this heterogeneity contributes to PDAC biology, we analyzed a large cohort of primary tumors (n = 62) profiled using single-cell RNA sequencing (443,451 single cells), including a subset of 11 tumors with matched spatial transcriptomics (53,236 spots), to map clonal, transcriptional and spatial diversity. Moreover, our sample set includes a unique cohort of matched samples from six tumors collected before and after treatment with chemotherapy. Our analysis revealed notable intratumoral heterogeneity, with multiple genetically distinct neoplastic clones coexisting within individual tumors. We observed clone-specific ligand-receptor programs that are modulated by genomic dosage: amplifications of ligands or receptors enriched corresponding interactions, while deletions suppressed them, with genetically encoded differences supported by spatial transcriptomics and multiplex immunofluorescence. Phylogenetic integration identified focal 8q24 (MYC) amplification as recurrently associated with classical-to-basal transitions occurring within tumor lineages at a frequency above chance; these transitions were accompanied by coordinated depletion of immune-response programs. Functional perturbation experiments in murine and primary human models showed that MYC knockdown reactivates classical transcriptional programs and restores immune-response pathways, supporting a role for MYC in maintaining a basal, immune-depleted state. Spatial analyses further revealed dispersed clones enriched for epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition activity and immune suppression, correlating with metastatic potential and colonization of lymph node niches. These dispersed clones shifted toward a basal phenotype, contributing to disease progression. Our findings highlight the critical role of clonal diversity, transcriptional plasticity and tumor microenvironment interactions in shaping human PDAC biology. This work provides a detailed view of the molecular and spatial heterogeneity of PDAC and offers potential avenues for therapeutic intervention targeting clonal evolution and the mechanisms driving metastasis.

items.title: Survival benefit of recurrence-focused treatment after surgery for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: A propensity score matched analysis of patients from a Dutch National and US institutional cohort.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: It is unclear whether recurrence-focused treatment (RFT) improves survival in all patients with recurrent pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). This study aimed (1) to evaluate post-recurrence survival (PRS) in patients treated with RFT versus best supportive care (BSC)-only, and (2) to assess potential effect modification by prognosis at recurrence.
METHODS: This observational cohort study included patients with local or distant recurrence after PDAC resection (2014-2022) at all Dutch pancreatic surgery centers and NYU Langone Health. Patients with unknown RFT or survival status were excluded. Prognosis at recurrence was defined using a previously established PRS risk score, stratifying patients into worse (≥174.5) and better (<174.5) prognostic subgroups. Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed in the overall cohort, and within subgroups. Median PRS in RFT versus BSC-only patients was estimated and compared using Kaplan-Meier curve analysis and the log-rank test. Multivariable Cox regression with robust standard errors clustered by matched pair was used to adjust for residual imbalance after PSM, with results presented as hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (95%CI).
RESULTS: Overall, 1423 patients were included. After PSM, 344 RFT patients were matched to 344 BSC-only patients. The multivariable analysis included ECOG performance score and country as a random effect. PRS was 10 (95%CI 9-12) months for RFT versus 4 (95%CI 3-4) months for BSC-only (adjusted HR0.38, 95%CI: 0.30-0.48, P < 0.001). In the worse prognosis group, PRS was 10 (95%CI 9-11) versus 3 (95%CI 3-4) months (adjusted HR0.38, 95%CI: 0.30-0.50, P < 0.001). In the better prognosis group, PRS was 18 (95%CI 12-27) months versus 8 (95%CI 4-14) months (adjusted HR0.24, 95%CI: 0.10-0.45, P < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Treatment for PDAC recurrence was associated with significantly longer PRS compared with BSC-only, irrespective of prognosis at recurrence. The survival benefit associated with RFT supports its consideration in the management of patients with PDAC recurrence.

items.title: Codon-Specific Divergence of FSP1 and ACSL4 Senescence Co-expression Decoupling in KRAS-Driven Cancers: Convergent Dual Escape in Colorectal Cancer, Enzyme-Selective Escape in Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma
items.abstract: Background. KRAS-mutant cancers upregulate FSP1 (AIFM2) through NRF2 and MAPK activation, conferring ferroptosis resistance parallel to ACSL4. Both enzymes connect to the ferro-aging senescence programme in wild-type tissue. Whether KRAS mutation disrupts their senescence co-regulatory connections, and whether the pattern holds across cancer types and codon variants, has not been examined. Methods. Spearman co-expression correlations between FSP1 or ACSL4 and seven senescence genes were computed in KRAS codon-stratified TCGA-COAD (n = 397; WT n = 337, G12D n = 53, G12V n = 38, G13D n = 30) and TCGA-PAAD (n = 151; WT n = 66, G12D n = 39, G12V n = 26, G12R n = 20). BH-FDR correction was applied within each variant group. The Orphan State Score (OSS) was defined as mean expression / (FDR-significant senescence edges + 0.5). Results. In TCGA-COAD, both FSP1 and ACSL4 lose all FDR-significant senescence co-expression in every KRAS-mutant group (OSS ˜1.1–1.3 in WT vs ˜9.2–9.6 in mutant groups). The decoupling is convergent: both enzymes lose senescence co-regulation simultaneously. In TCGA-PAAD, the pattern diverges by codon. FSP1 decouples in G12D (OSS 8.35, 0 edges) while ACSL4 retains three senescence edges (OSS 1.47). G12V and G12R show the inverse: ACSL4 decouples while FSP1 retains partial or full senescence co-expression. The FSP1–KEAP1 ferroptosis co-expression edge is preserved in WT, G12D and G12V in both cohorts. Conclusions. KRAS mutation disrupts FSP1 and ACSL4 senescence co-expression in both CRC and PAAD, but the enzyme specificity and codon selectivity differ by cancer type. CRC shows convergent dual escape; PAAD shows codon-matched enzyme-selective escape. PAAD G12D may represent a selective FSP1 inhibition opportunity, consistent with published organoid data. All findings are correlational and require functional validation.

items.title: METTL10 trimethylation of eEF1A at K318 enhances protein synthesis and tumorigenesis.
items.abstract: eEF1A is an essential non-ribosomal translation elongation factor that mediates the high-fidelity delivery of aminoacyl-tRNAs to elongating ribosomes. Like histone H3, eEF1A undergoes extensive lysine methylation, with five distinct residues targeted by dedicated lysine methyltransferases (KMTs). However, compared with histone methylation, relatively little is known about the molecular and physiological functions of eEF1A lysine methylation. Here, we focus on METTL10, the KMT that catalyzes trimethylation of eEF1A at lysine 318 (eEF1AK318me3). We show that the METTL10-eEF1AK318me3 axis modestly enhances global protein synthesis and supports pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) tumorigenesis in vivo. We identify the 236 amino-acid isoform as the catalytically active endogenous form of METTL10 and demonstrate that it is required for eEF1AK318me3 generation in multiple human cell lines. Further, we provide evidence that eEF1AK318 is the principal physiologic target of METT10. Loss of eEF1AK318 modestly reduces global protein synthesis across multiple cancer cell lines without substantially impacting polysome formation. METTL10 depletion attenuates proliferation of multiple cancer cell lines, an effect that depends on its catalytic activity. Moreover, elevated eEF1AK318me3 levels in PDAC tumors are associated with poor patient outcomes. Finally, METTL10 ablation attenuates tumor growth and extends survival in a KRASG12D-driven PDAC mouse model. Together, our work identifies the METTL10-eEF1AK318me3 axis as a regulator of protein synthesis and implicates it in PDAC pathogenesis.

items.title: Macrophage-induced ferritin expression protects pancreatic cancer cells from ferroptosis.
items.abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) drive pro-tumorigenic signaling but also promote lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis, making ROS regulation critical during high oxidative stress stages of tumor progression, such as metastasis. Loss of the antioxidant TIGAR in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cells raises ROS and enhances metastatic behavior but also sensitizes cells to ferroptosis. To understand how TIGAR-null cells survive to metastasize, we examine the role of macrophage infiltration, which is increased in TIGAR-null tumors. Co-culturing TIGAR-null PDAC cells with macrophages protects them from ferroptosis. The tumor cells induce macrophage IL-6 secretion, which leads to the activation of STAT3 and upregulation of the iron-sequestering protein ferritin (FTH1) in cancer cells. FTH1 depletion in TIGAR-null cells restores ferroptosis sensitivity and reduces lung metastasis. These results suggest that the outcome of increased ROS in tumors may depend on the activation of mechanisms that selectively prevent ferroptosis while preserving ROS-induced oncogenic signaling and metastasis-promoting pathways.

items.title: Predictive Factors for Occult Metastases in Clinically M0 Pancreatic Cancer: A Prospective Multicenter Analysis of Staging Laparoscopy.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Staging laparoscopy (SL) is a minimally invasive approach for detecting occult metastases in patients with pancreatic cancer (PC) without signs of metastasis on imaging. This study aimed to identify the predictive factors for imaging-negative occult metastases.
METHODS: This prospective study enrolled 199 patients with histologically confirmed PC from three institutions between August 2021 and April 2023. All patients were scheduled for a treatment plan that included SL.
RESULTS: The overall metastasis rate as detected using SL was 25.1%, which varied from 20.6% in patients with resectable PC (R-PC) to 33.8% in those with borderline resectable or locally advanced unresectable PC (BR/URLA-PC). In 152 patients who did not receive neoadjuvant therapy, BR/URLA status (odds ratio 3.261; 95% confidence interval 1.185-9.483, p = 0.022) and pancreatic body/tail lesions (odds ratio 2.653; 95% confidence interval 1.037-7.214, p = 0.042) were independent risk factors for occult metastatic lesions (M1). Among the 107 patients with R-PC, M1 disease was significantly associated with pancreatic body/tail lesions, tumor size, and elevated levels of tumor markers. In particular, elevated carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels were consistent across all patients with M1 pancreatic head cancer. In contrast, no statistical differences were observed for any of these factors in the 45 patients with BR/URLA-PC.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings support the importance of SL in patients with BR/UR PC. For R-PC, patients with pancreatic head lesions and normal tumor marker values may represent a very low-risk subgroup where selective omission of SL can be considered in resource-constrained settings.

items.title: Borderline resectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: a narrative review.
items.abstract: Borderline resectable (BR) pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a well-recognized entity with specific characteristics. Previously considered inoperable, these tumors are now increasingly resectable due to advances in neoadjuvant chemotherapy. This review synthesizes current knowledge on diagnostic, therapeutic, and management approaches for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, especially for BR disease. It covers the definition, criteria, and surgical management, along with various clinical challenges in the diagnosis of borderline disease. Neoadjuvant therapy is the treatment of choice before surgery, but there are still limited data on the selection of optimal therapy and on the early identification of non-responders. Multidetector computed tomography, along with CA19-9 and positron emission tomography, are being used to evaluate resectability after neoadjuvant therapy. Pancreatic resection for PDAC is one of the most complex procedures in abdominal surgery due to the technical and oncological challenges associated with its aggressive growth. Despite these options, management remains challenging.

items.title: First Unscheduled Hospitalization in Pancreatic Cancer: A Point for Palliative Care Integration.
items.abstract:
CONTEXT: Pancreatic cancer is characterized by high symptom burden, rapid deterioration, and poor survival. Despite this complexity, specialist palliative care (SPC) is often integrated late or not at all. The first unscheduled hospitalization may represent a point for SPC assessment.
OBJECTIVES: To characterize frequency, clinical features, and outcomes of the first unscheduled hospitalization in pancreatic adenocarcinoma, explore factors associated with subsequent survival, and describe the timing of SPC assessment.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of consecutive adults with pancreatic adenocarcinoma managed by medical oncology at three tertiary hospitals during 2022-2023, with follow-up through 2025. Overall survival (OS) from hospitalization was estimated with Kaplan-Meier methods; univariable Cox regression assessed associations with survival.
RESULTS: Among 125 patients, 105 (84%) experienced a first unscheduled hospitalization at a median of 4.1 months after diagnosis (IQR, 1.9-8.0). Median OS was 3.8 months (95% CI, 2.1-7.1); 21/104 (20%) died in hospital, and 62/80 (78%) were readmitted after discharge. ECOG performance status 2-4 (HR, 3.30), metastatic disease (HR, 3.05), liver metastases (HR, 2.58), and strong opioid use (HR, 2.10) were associated with shorter survival. Only 11 (10%) underwent SPC assessment before hospitalization; 31 (30%) were first assessed during hospitalization, 40 (38%) afterward, and 23 (22%) remained unassessed.
CONCLUSION: A first unscheduled hospitalization occurred in most patients, marking limited survival, high in-hospital mortality, and frequent readmission. Most lacked prior SPC assessment. This event may serve as a pragmatic safety net for palliative care integration, complementing earlier needs- and prognosis-based referral strategies.

items.title: A Pilot Study of Photon Counting CT Spectral Analysis Following Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma Resection to Differentiate Local Recurrence From Postsurgical Fibrosis.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To assess photon counting CT (PCCT) spectral parameters in the differentiation of locally recurrent pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) from benign postsurgical fibrosis after PDAC surgical resection.
METHODS: Twenty-two patients [12 male, mean±SD: age 71 (8) y] who underwent pancreas protocol PCCT following surgery for PDAC were retrospectively identified. Local recurrence required tissue histopathology or enlarging FDG-avid soft tissue. Nonrecurrence required soft-tissue reduction with stable or decreased CA 19-9. Two blinded radiologists independently drew regions of interest within the surgical bed soft tissue to determine iodine density (I), I normalized to aortic enhancement (I%), fat fraction, and extracellular volume (ECV), which were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. A P<0.05 indicated statistical significance. The intraclass correlation coefficient was used to assess inter-reader reliability. ROC analysis was performed using mean measurements.
RESULTS: On pancreatic parenchymal phase imaging, median [IQR] postcontrast attenuation for patients with nonrecurrence (n=10) and recurrence (n=11) was 32.3 (16.4 to 42.9 HU) and 57.0 (50.2 to 65.5 HU)(P=0.001); enhancement was 23.7 (10.2 to 26.0 HU) and 40.0 (34.4 to 44.5 HU) (P=0.001); I was 0.6 (0.5 to 0.90 mg/mL) and 1.8 (1.5 to 2.0 mg/mL) (P<0.001); I% was 8.3 (6.3% to 11.1%) and 34.3 (29.8% to 40.9%) (P<0.001); and ECV was 5.8 (4.4 to 6.9 mL) and 23.0 (18.0 to 25.8 mL) (P<0.001), respectively. To differentiate nonrecurrent from recurrent soft tissue, a postcontrast 45.7 HU threshold had 100% sensitivity and 80% specificity [AUC=0.92 (0.80-1.00)]; enhancement of 31.9 HU had 81.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity [AUC=0.98 (0.93-1.00)]; 14.0 mL ECV had 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity [AUC=1.00 (1.00-1.00)]; 1.27 mg/mL I had 90.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity [AUC=0.99 (0.98-1.00)]; and 20.3% I% had 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity (AUC=1.00). Inter-reader agreement was near-perfect (ICCs 0.86 to 0.96).
CONCLUSIONS: PCCT spectral parameters demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance in differentiating locally recurrent PDAC from postsurgical fibrosis on pancreatic parenchymal phase imaging.
