items.title: Clinical Efficacy of Tislelizumab Plus Gemcitabine-Nab-Paclitaxel for Borderline Resectable Pancreatic Cancer and Chemoresistance Analysis: A Prospective Pilot Study.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neoadjuvant therapy can improve the survival outcomes of patients with borderline resectable pancreatic cancer (BRPC). However, standard neoadjuvant regimens remain lacking. This study evaluated the clinical feasibility of tislelizumab plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel in the neoadjuvant setting for BRPC.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: In this prospective study, patients with BRPC preoperatively received three cycles of tislelizumab plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, and continued postoperatively. The primary endpoints were R0 resection rate and treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs). Exploratory objectives were resistance to this regimen.
RESULTS: Of 30 enrolled patients, 80.0% (24/30) completed neoadjuvant therapy and underwent surgical resection. R0 resection was achieved in 80.0% (24/30) of the patients and in 100.00% (24/24) of those resected. The 12-month OS and RFS rates were 87.5% (95% CI 64.3-95.8%) and 82.8% (95% CI 60-95.8%), respectively, with median RFS of 28 months (95% CI 16.9-39.1). Most TRAEs were grade I-II, with no serious events. Quantitative proteomics combined with machine learning identified NT5DC2, FAM3D, CXCL5, and TMT1B as candidate biomarkers of resistance to this neoadjuvant regimen. In paired pre- and postoperative tissues from treatment-sensitive patients, CD8+ T-cell infiltration tended to increase and CD163+ M2-like macrophages were significantly upregulated after surgery.
CONCLUSIONS: Neoadjuvant tislelizumab plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel is promising for improving the resection rate in BRPC, with a favorable safety profile. NT5DC2, FAM3D, CXCL5, and TMT1B may serve as candidate biomarkers of preoperative drug resistance, and tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) analysis further reveals immune microenvironment remodeling in postoperative tumors from treatment-sensitive patients. These findings warrant validation in larger-scale studies. Trial Registration Chinese Clinical Trial registry (ChiCTR2200063680).

items.title: SREBF1 expression is associated with lipid metabolism-related signatures, and transient SREBF1 silencing is accompanied by increased apoptosis in pancreatic cancer cells.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a lethal malignancy characterized by extensive metabolic adaptation. Sterol regulatory element-binding transcription factor 1 (SREBF1) encodes sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1), a transcriptional regulator of lipogenic genes. This study investigated the association between SREBF1 expression and lipid metabolism-related transcriptional features in PDAC and assessed cellular responses to transient SREBF1 silencing.
METHODS AND RESULTS: SREBF1 expression was evaluated using RNA-sequencing data from TCGA-PAAD and GTEx and paired microarray data from GSE62452 and GSE183795. The analysis included 179 TCGA-PAAD tumors and 171 TCGA/GTEx non-tumor pancreatic samples, together with 61 matched tumor-adjacent pairs from GSE62452 and 102 matched pairs from GSE183795. TCGA-PAAD tumors were stratified at the median SREBF1 expression level for differential-expression analysis, GSEA, and GSVA. SREBF1 expression was higher in the TCGA/GTEx tumor-versus-normal comparison (P < 0.0001), with concordant increases in GSE62452 (P < 0.05) and GSE183795 (P < 0.01). SREBF1-high tumors exhibited lipid metabolism-related transcriptional features, including higher fatty-acid-metabolism and cholesterol-homeostasis pathway scores. In BxPC-3 and SW1990 cells, transient SREBF1 silencing with one selected siRNA was accompanied by decreased precursor SREBP1 (~ 122 kDa) and FASN protein levels, qualitatively reduced clonogenic outgrowth, and an increased Annexin V-positive apoptotic fraction.
CONCLUSION: SREBF1 expression is associated with lipid metabolism-related transcriptional features in PDAC. Transient SREBF1 silencing was accompanied by reduced FASN protein levels, qualitatively reduced clonogenic outgrowth, and increased apoptosis. These findings identify SREBP1-associated lipid metabolism as a candidate vulnerability that requires further validation but do not establish a direct SREBP1-FASN-cell-survival mechanism or therapeutic efficacy.

items.title: Sialic Acid-Targeting Lectin-Conjugated Oxygen Nanosomes Alleviate Hypoxia and Promote Macrophage Activation in Pancreatic Cancer Cells.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by severe hypoxia and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which contribute to poor therapeutic responses. This study developed sialic acid-targeting Lectin-conjugated oxygen nanosomes (Lectin-ONs) to combine targeted oxygen delivery with hypoxia alleviation and macrophage activation.
METHODS: SNA- and MALII-conjugated oxygen nanosomes (SNA-ONs and MALII-ONs) were prepared and characterized for physicochemical properties, oxygen-loading and release behavior, stability, cytocompatibility, and cellular binding. Their effects on hypoxia and macrophage activation were evaluated in pancreatic cancer cell models and macrophage-pancreatic cancer cell co-culture using hypoxia-sensitive fluorescence and TNF-α secretion, respectively.
RESULTS: Lectin-ONs exhibited stable physicochemical properties, effective oxygen delivery, and cellular binding to pancreatic cancer cells, while reducing hypoxia-associated fluorescence under oxygen-limited conditions. Treatment with Lectin-ONs also increased TNF-α secretion in macrophage-pancreatic cancer cell co-culture, consistent with macrophage activation.
CONCLUSION: Lectin-ONs integrate sialic acid-targeted delivery with oxygen-mediated hypoxia alleviation and were associated with increased macrophage TNF-α secretion in vitro. These findings support Lectin-ONs as a potential platform for modulating the hypoxic and immunosuppressive microenvironment of pancreatic cancer, although further mechanistic and in vivo validation is required.

items.title: Phosphorylated STYK1 Promotes Gemcitabine Resistance via Autophagy-Mediated Cancer Stemness in Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most lethal malignancies, with gemcitabine resistance remaining a major clinical challenge. Although cancer stemness and autophagy have both been implicated in PDAC chemoresistance, the mechanism by which their crosstalk governs gemcitabine resistance remains poorly understood. Here, we identify serine/threonine/tyrosine kinase 1 (STYK1) as a critical mediator of gemcitabine resistance through autophagy- dependent maintenance of pancreatic cancer stemness. Mechanistically, gemcitabine activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which contributes to the enhancement of STYK1-mediated autophagic flux, thereby promoting stemness-associated chemoresistance. Furthermore, AMPK phosphorylates STYK1 at residues Ser91 and Ser304, thereby further potentiating STYK1-mediated autophagy and cancer stemness. Importantly, we developed SAIDP5, a therapeutic peptide disrupting STYK1-AMPK binding, which synergizes with gemcitabine to attenuate chemoresistance. This study reveals that gemcitabine-induced AMPK activation amplifies STYK1-driven autophagy and cancer stemness, thereby contributing to gemcitabine resistance, and highlights SAIDP5 as a promising peptide-based strategy to improve gemcitabine efficacy in PDAC.

items.title: Single-Cell Multiomics Reveals That OTUD7B Is a Central Driver of Epithelial Remodelling and the Immunosuppressive Microenvironment in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PAAD) is characterized by extreme malignancy and profound resistance to therapy, largely driven by a fibrotic and immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment (TME). The deubiquitinase OTU domain-containing protein 7B (OTUD7B) has been implicated in inflammatory and oncogenic signalling, but its role in PAAD and its TME remains unclear. This study integrated single-cell RNA-seq datasets from the GEO and bulk RNA-seq data from the TCGA to delineate the cellular ecosystem of PAAD, and employed cell-cell communication analysis, high-dimensional weighted gene coexpression network analysis (hdWGCNA), and nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) to identify OTUD7B-associated modules and epithelial subpopulations, while assessing the survival and clinicopathologic correlations of OTUD7B in the TCGA-PAAD cohort. Quantitative proteomics of OTUD7B-knockout PAAD cells was performed and combined with GO/KEGG and GSEA to explore downstream pathways, and immune infiltration was inferred by deconvolution algorithms and validated by multiplex immunofluorescence staining of OTUD7B, CD4, and FOXP3. Single-cell RNA-seq revealed the expansion of epithelial cells, fibroblasts, and macrophages with dense ligand-receptor networks, alongside the depletion of effector T and NK cells, indicating a shift toward an immunosuppressive TME. hdWGCNA identified epithelial-ECM modules in which OTUD7B served as a hub gene, and NMF revealed an OTUD7B-high epithelial subset enriched in glycosylation-related metabolic programs and positioned at an early stage of the malignant trajectory. OTUD7B was significantly upregulated in PAAD and was associated with higher grade, lymph node metastasis, and advanced stage, and predicted poorer overall survival. Proteomic profiling of OTUD7B-deficient cells revealed broad remodelling of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, ROS metabolism, and redox homeostasis. OTUD7B expression was positively correlated with M2 macrophage infiltration, immunomodulatory gene expression, and CD4+FOXP3+ regulatory T-cell accumulation, and tissue staining further confirmed the positive association between OTUD7B expression and Treg-rich regions. Collectively, OTUD7B acts as a key integrative node that links epithelial remodelling, mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming, and TME immunosuppression in PAAD, serving as an adverse prognostic biomarker and a potential therapeutic target to remodel tumour metabolism and enhance antitumor immunity.

items.title: Safety and Efficacy of a Multi-Tumor-Associated Antigen-Specific T Cell Therapy in Pancreatic Cancer Patients
items.abstract:
ABSTRACT
Pancreatic cancer (PC) is an orphan disease affecting approximately 67,440 people annually in the US. With a
5-year relative survival of only 13% for all stages combined and 3.2% for metastatic disease, PC represents one
of the most aggressive malignancies. Although surgical resection provides the best curative option, <20% of PC
patients are eligible for surgery at diagnosis. Patients with locally advanced unresectable PC typically have a
median survival of less than 1 year. Standard frontline treatment includes FOLFIRINOX (FFX) or NALIRIFOX
(NLX), yet these result in median overall survival of only 11.1 months and are associated with cumulative
toxicities that limit longer treatment. Patients with locally advanced unresectable PC have an urgent unmet need
for treatments that extend median survival beyond 12 months.
Marker Therapeutics has developed MT-601, a multi-tumor associated antigen (mTAA)-specific autologous T
cell product that recognizes six target antigens expressed by pancreatic tumors: PRAME, NY-ESO-1, survivin,
MAGE-A4, SSX2, and WT1. This non-engineered T cell therapy limits tumor adaptation through negative antigen
selection (immune escape) while reducing on-target, off-tumor effects. MT-601 is manufactured from patient
apheresis material using a simplified process that stimulates and expands polyclonal tumor-specific T cells. The
product consists of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells that recognize target cells via native T cell receptors, interacting with
both class I and II MHC complexes. Preliminary data from the Phase 1 TACTOPS trial of mTAA-specific T cells
in pancreatic cancer demonstrated clinical benefit with 1 complete response, 2 partial responses, and 8 stable
disease among 13 FFX treated patients. To date, mTAA-specific T cells have shown an excellent safety profile
in >200 patients across 7 cancer indications, without cytokine release syndrome, neurotoxicity, or dose-limiting
toxicities. MT-601 represents an improved product with the addition of WT1, higher dosing (400×10⁶ cells vs
20×10⁶), and enhanced manufacturing yielding 4X increased potency.
Therefore, Marker proposes a Phase 1, single-center, open-label clinical trial (PANACEA, NCT# 06549751) to
evaluate the safety and efficacy of MT-601 administered during maintenance capecitabine following FFX or NLX
in patients with locally advanced unresectable PC. The trial includes Dose Escalation using a modified 3+3
design followed by Expansion at the recommend dose. Specific Aim 1 will assess safety and efficacy of MT-601
in combination with maintenance capecitabine, determining the maximum tolerated dose and evaluating
progression-free survival and duration of response. Specific Aim 2 will correlate biological characteristics of MT-
601 with clinical outcomes, including T cell expansion, persistence, clonality, and anti-tumor immune effects.
Successful completion of this trial will provide critical dosing, safety, and efficacy data necessary to advance MT-
601 to a randomized pivotal study comparing MT-601 plus maintenance chemotherapy versus maintenance
chemotherapy alone, ultimately advancing this therapy toward market approval for PC patients.

items.title: Clinicopathologic Characteristics and Prognostic Value of Rhabdoid Features in Pancreatic Undifferentiated Carcinoma.
items.abstract: Undifferentiated carcinoma (UC) is a rare, highly aggressive subtype of pancreatic cancer; UC with rhabdoid features (UCRF) is particularly associated with poor prognosis. This study aimed to compare clinicopathologic characteristics and outcomes of UC between groups of patients defined by presence versus absence of RF. We retrospectively reviewed patients diagnosed with UC by EUS-guided tissue acquisition from 2017 to 2024. Histologically, 11 patients were classified as anaplastic UC and two had UC with osteoclast-like giant cell. Six patients had UCRF. Only 2 patients underwent surgery, while 8 received chemotherapy; 5 of these were treated with gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel. One patient (17%) in the UCRF group was INI-1-negative. CK7 was positive in 3 UCRF patients (50%) and in all 7 UC patients without RF. In the overall cohort, median OS showed no statistically significant difference between UCRF and UC without RF (3.9 vs. 12.9 months; log-rank p = 0.188). However, after excluding two patients with UCOGC, Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated a significantly shorter OS in UCRF (p = 0.009). These findings suggest that RF represents a potential adverse prognostic factor in pancreatic UC. Further studies are warranted to clarify biologic significance and treatment implications of RF in pancreatic UC.

items.title: Endothelial exosomes remodel chromatin accessibility and superenhancer in cancer cells to promote liver metastatic colonization.
items.abstract: Liver-organotropic metastasis occurs in cancers such as uveal melanoma (UM) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and is a leading cause of mortality at the terminal stage. Colonization is a rate-limiting and converging step in the metastatic cascade. The drivers underlying liver colonization have largely remained elusive. In this report, we hypothesized that pioneer transcription factors (TFs) increase chromatin accessibility and superenhancer (SE) remodeling, which subsequently promote colonization-associated cellular features [e.g., proliferation, survival, cancer stem cells (CSCs), motility] by driving the transcription of the respective SE-associated genes. We tested this hypothesis and discovered that the pioneer TF KLF4 promoted chromatin accessibility and SE remodeling by ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq. Chromatin accessibility and SE remodeling significantly increased the transcription of the SE-associated genes MCL1 and RASGRP3, which consequently promoted proliferation, motility, and metastasis. Furthermore, the upregulation of KLF4 expression in UM cells was promoted by RN7SL2-containing exosomes from surrounding endothelial cells. Analysis of clinical datasets revealed that the overexpression of RIG-I, STAT1, KLF4, and RASGRP3 was individually correlated with shorter metastasis-free survival or overall survival in patients with UM and PDAC. In conclusion, the identification of the exoRN7SL2-STAT1-KLF4-SEs-RASGRP3 signaling axis may help elucidate metastatic colonization through interactions between tumor cells and the endothelial niche and may yield novel and viable therapeutic targets.

items.title: Clinical Application of Three-dimensional Laparoscopic Artery-first Pancreaticoduodenectomy in Treating Pancreatic Head Malignant Tumors.
items.abstract: Pancreaticoduodenectomy is a technically demanding procedure associated with substantial surgical risk. Conventional laparoscopic approaches have several limitations, including restricted visualization, which can make exposure of the superior mesenteric artery and identification of vessels and lymph nodes challenging. In patients with vascular adhesion or tumor invasion, surgical dissection is particularly difficult and may increase the risk of intraoperative vascular injury and hemorrhage. In addition, poor delineation of anatomical planes may result in incomplete tumor dissection, inadequate lymphadenectomy, and difficult mobilization of the pancreatic head and duodenum, potentially compromising surgical safety and oncological outcomes. To optimize the surgical workflow, this protocol describes a three-dimensional laparoscopic artery-first pancreaticoduodenectomy with the infracolic artery-first approach as the principal technical modification. By combining early arterial exposure and clear delineation of anatomical planes with the stereoscopic visualization of three-dimensional laparoscopy, this technique facilitates identification of vessel-tissue relationships, vascular control, lymphadenectomy, tumor dissection, and tissue mobilization. These features may help reduce inadvertent vascular injury and intraoperative blood loss while enabling complete tumor resection. The protocol provides a standardized surgical approach, particularly applicable to pancreatic head lesions adjacent to or involving major vessels, and is intended to improve the safety and reproducibility of laparoscopic pancreaticoduodenectomy.

items.title: Microbiome-pancreatic cancer crosstalk: From tumor biology to therapeutic intervention.
items.abstract: Pancreatic cancer (PC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies worldwide, characterized by dense desmoplastic stroma, profound immunosuppression, and poor responsiveness to conventional therapies. Accumulating evidence positions the intratumoral microbiome, encompassing bacteria as well as understudied fungal and viral components, as a critical regulator of PC pathogenesis, tumor microenvironment (TME) remodeling, and therapeutic efficacy. In this review, we synthesize the current understanding of the pancreatic intratumoral microbiome, including its distinct composition relative to normal pancreatic tissue, gut microbiota, and oral microbiota. The PC intratumoral microbiome is characterized by enrichment of validated pro-tumorigenic drivers (e.g., Pseudomonas, Bacteroides species) alongside protective taxa (e.g., Lactobacillus species). These taxonomic profiles vary significantly based on disease stage, patient demographics, and treatment history. We dissected the mechanisms by which microbes and their derivatives drive PC initiation and progression, including immune suppression through modulation of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and regulatory T cells, metabolic reprogramming involving short-chain fatty acids and the tryptophan metabolite 3-indoleacetic acid (3-IAA), and stromal remodeling via activation of cancer-associated fibroblasts. The influence of the microbiome on therapeutic response is examined, with particular emphasis on microbial-mediated mechanisms that undermine treatment efficacy. We further summarize diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers, including salivary microbial signatures with moderate sensitivity and specificity, circulating microbial DNA, and composite microbial risk scores that integrate multiple bacterial species to predict survival. Therapeutic strategies targeting the microbiome are discussed, distinguishing clinically translatable approaches from experimental concepts requiring further validation. Finally, we outline challenges in standardizing profiling methods, validating microbial signatures across diverse populations, and translating preclinical insights to clinical practice, emphasizing the need for multi-omics integration and interdisciplinary collaboration to advance microbiome-driven PC management.

items.title: ESCO1 stabilizes NUFIP2 through acetylation-ubiquitination crosstalk to promote pancreatic cancer progression.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic cancer is a highly aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis, and its molecular pathogenesis remains incompletely understood, with effective therapeutic options still limited. Establishment of sister chromatid cohesion N-acetyltransferase 1 (ESCO1) has been implicated in the development and progression of several malignancies; however, its biological role and underlying mechanisms in pancreatic cancer remain largely unknown. This study aimed to elucidate the clinical significance and molecular mechanisms of the ESCO1/NUFIP2 axis in pancreatic cancer.
METHODS: TCGA, CPTAC, and other publicly available datasets were used to evaluate the expression patterns, diagnostic value, and prognostic significance of ESCO1 and NUFIP2 in pancreatic cancer. In vitro and in vivo experiments were subsequently performed to characterize the biological functions of the ESCO1/NUFIP2 axis and elucidate its underlying molecular mechanisms.
RESULTS: ESCO1 and NUFIP2 were significantly upregulated in pancreatic cancer and were associated with poor prognosis. Functional assays demonstrated that the ESCO1/NUFIP2 axis promoted pancreatic cancer cell proliferation and migration, enhanced tumor growth in vivo, and suppressed apoptosis. Mechanistically, ESCO1 promoted NUFIP2 acetylation and limited its K48-linked ubiquitination and subsequent degradation, thereby maintaining NUFIP2 protein stability. Stabilized NUFIP2 preserved mitochondrial function and suppressed mitochondrial apoptosis, whereas NUFIP2 overexpression or trichostatin A (TSA) treatment partially reversed the effects of ESCO1 depletion. Moreover, the ESCO1/NUFIP2 axis was associated with immune cell infiltration, and depletion of either ESCO1 or NUFIP2 enhanced dendritic cell (DC)-mediated cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) antitumor responses.
CONCLUSION: ESCO1 stabilizes NUFIP2 through acetylation-dependent regulation, thereby preserving mitochondrial function, suppressing mitochondrial apoptosis, and promoting pancreatic cancer progression. The ESCO1/NUFIP2 axis may also contribute to the regulation of antitumor immunity, highlighting its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target in pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Intraoperative Management Strategies for Unresectable Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma: A Propensity-Weighted Cohort Study.
items.abstract: BackgroundWhen pancreatic adenocarcinoma is found unresectable during surgery, the decision to perform palliation must balance symptom relief against recovery and subsequent cancer treatment. We compared clinical outcomes after palliative procedures and nontherapeutic exploration.Patients and MethodsWe retrospectively studied 201 patients with intraoperatively unresectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma treated from 2006 to 2023. Operative findings and procedures were described, and postoperative outcomes, systemic-therapy receipt, and survival were compared using propensity-score overlap weighting.ResultsOf 201 patients, 54 underwent palliation and 147 underwent nontherapeutic exploration. Palliation more often accompanied locally advanced disease and vascular invasion. Observed major complications occurred in 18.5% vs 4.8%, ICU admission in 20.4% vs 3.4%, and 30-day mortality in 11.1% vs 3.4%. Adjusted estimates did not exclude clinically important differences; the ICU-admission odds ratio was 4.40 (95% CI, 0.997-19.43). Systemic-therapy receipt was 46.3% vs 46.9% (weighted odds ratio, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.35-1.71). The weighted survival hazard ratio was 1.43 (95% CI, 0.99-2.07).DiscussionPatients selected for palliation experienced more postoperative complications and ICU use, without clearly greater systemic-therapy receipt. Selection differences and uncertainty in adjusted estimates prevent causal conclusions. Operative decisions should prioritize the patient's symptoms, functional status, expected survival, anatomy, and available less-invasive alternatives.

items.title: Clinical and Genetic Interplay Between Chronic Pancreatitis, Cystic Fibrosis and CFTR-Related Disorders.
items.abstract: Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is a clinically heterogeneous condition that may occur with a broad clinical spectrum, including cases of cystic fibrosis (CF), cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (CFTR)-related disorder (CFTR-RD), acute recurrent pancreatitis (ARP), and CP, including cases of idiopathic CP (iCP) and hereditary pancreatitis (HP). The specific contribution of CFTR variants and pancreatitis-predisposing genes (PPG), i.e., genes responsible for intrapancreatic activation of trypsinogen or pancreatic secretion pathways to CP susceptibility in these different contexts remains incompletely understood. We investigated the occurrence of CP and mutations in PPG genes in: (i) 377 subjects with CF and (ii) 217 subjects with CFTR-RD (including cases expressing with CP alone). Moreover, we studied 136 subjects with iCP. CP occurred in 33/377 subjects (8.8%) with CF carrying CFTR genotypes other than homozygous p.Phe508del and was mainly associated with pancreatic sufficiency (24/33, 72.7%) and at least one residual-function CFTR variant (25/33, 75.8%). Chronic pancreatitis also occurred in 8 CF subjects carrying both CFTR mutations classified as no residual function, and 7 of them also had PPG variants. Subjects with CFTR-RD expressing with ARP/CP alone (n = 92) are genetically indistinguishable from CFTR-RD subjects with diffuse bronchiectasis (n = 45) or congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens (n = 92). In fact, all CFTR-RD subjects had at least one residual-function CFTR variant, all had pancreatic sufficiency, and the sweat chloride was not significantly different between the three subgroups. Finally, 66/136 (48.5%) subjects with iCP harbored pathogenic variants in PPG, with 26/66 cases (i.e., 39.4%) with multiple gene mutations (consistent with a potential role of oligogenic inheritance in CP susceptibility). Idiopathic CP subjects with mutations in PPG (48.5% in our series) are known to be at higher risk to develop pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Our study revealed such mutations also in subjects with CF (with both CFTR mutations classified as no residual function and with pancreatic insufficiency) and in subjects with CFTR-RD, supporting the use of multigene testing and genetic counselling. To conclude: The early diagnosis of CF by NBS enhanced the number of CF subjects who develop ARP and/or CP, independently by the pancreatic status and by the CFTR genotype. Mutations in PGP genes further increase such risk. Thus, we suggest: (i) to test for PGP genes and counseling all cases of CF with pancreatitis; (ii) large multicenter studies to investigate why a subset of CFTR-RD appear with ARP/CP alone; and (iii) a careful investigation of familiarity and the analysis of a large panel of PPG genes to better define the profile of risk for HP in all cases of idiopathic ARP/CP.

items.title: Negotiating Mortality: A Qualitative Systematic Review and Thematic Synthesis of the Psychosocial Experiences of Pancreatic Cancer Across the Illness Trajectory.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Pancreatic cancer is associated with poor survival and substantial psychosocial burden, yet little is known about the psychological, emotional, and social dimensions of patients' experiences across the illness trajectory. This review aimed to identify, analyse, and synthesise empirical qualitative literature on the psychosocial aspects of receiving, living with, dying with, or surviving pancreatic cancer. Methods: Seven bibliographic databases were searched from inception to 4 September 2025, with reference list screening and forward citation tracking undertaken. Records were managed in Covidence. Following screening of 4357 titles and abstracts and 412 full texts, 30 papers representing 28 studies were included. Methodological quality was appraised using the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research. Data were extracted into a shared Excel workbook and synthesised using Thomas and Harden's thematic synthesis approach. Results: Four overarching themes were developed: (1) from ambiguous symptoms to the shock and threat of diagnosis; (2) navigating care, information, and support; (3) embodied disruption, relational change, and reworking everyday life; and (4) living on borrowed time and coping with uncertainty and mortality. Across the included studies, pancreatic cancer was experienced as a profound disruption to participants' lives, futures, and sense of selves; involved complex informational and care-navigation work; altered everyday lives; and provoked ongoing uncertainty around progression, recurrence, and survival. Conclusions: Pancreatic cancer exerts a profound psychosocial impact across early and advanced disease, with psychological, social, and emotional challenges intertwined with complex symptomatology, functional decline, uncertainty, and mortality awareness. Thus, substantial unmet psycho-oncology and supportive care needs exist for patients and their families.

items.title: Pancreatic Cancer-Associated Pain Management Beyond Opioids: Integrating Oncological Treatment, Palliative Care, and Interventional Pain Medicine.
items.abstract: Pain is one of the most frequent and burdensome symptoms of pancreatic cancer and may substantially impair quality of life throughout the disease trajectory. Its complex and evolving etiology, involving visceral, neuropathic, somatic, and treatment-related mechanisms, frequently makes adequate pain control challenging. This critical narrative review provides a multidisciplinary overview of pancreatic cancer-associated pain management, integrating oncological treatment, palliative and pharmacological care, and interventional pain management into a practical clinical framework. Anticancer therapies, including chemotherapy and radiotherapy, may provide clinically meaningful analgesia in addition to their disease-controlling effect. Early integration of palliative care enables repeated symptom assessment, individualized pharmacological treatment, and management of the psychological, social, and spiritual dimensions of total pain. When conventional analgesic strategies provide insufficient relief or cause intolerable adverse effects, interventional techniques such as coeliac plexus neurolysis, splanchnic neurolysis, or intrathecal drug delivery can complement ongoing oncological and palliative treatment. Rather than following a rigid stepwise analgesic approach, pancreatic cancer-associated pain management should be individualized according to pain mechanism, disease stage and anatomy, previous treatments, functional status, expected survival, and patient preferences. Based on the available evidence and multidisciplinary clinical considerations, we propose a practical patient-centered pathway that dynamically integrates disease-directed, pharmacological, supportive, and interventional strategies throughout the disease course. Early multidisciplinary collaboration and continuous reassessment may facilitate timely treatment escalation and improve pain control while minimizing treatment burden.

items.title: Aldehyde Dehydrogenase 2 Activity Assessed Using the Acetaldehyde Breath Test Is Associated with Benign Pancreatic Disease and Pancreatic Cancer: A Case-Control Study.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) detoxifies acetaldehyde, and impaired ALDH2 activity has been implicated in carcinogenesis. The acetaldehyde breath test (ABT) enables noninvasive functional assessment of ALDH2 activity, but its association with pancreatic disease remains unclear. We examined associations between ABT-assessed ALDH2 activity and pancreatic disease outcomes. Methods: This case-control study included 287 health checkup participants, 131 patients with benign pancreatic disease, and 65 patients with pancreatic cancer. Participants underwent ABT, and the acetaldehyde-to-ethanol (A/E) ratio was calculated. The ALDH2 inactive phenotype was defined as an A/E ratio ≥ 23.3. Multinomial logistic regression used health checkup participants as the reference. Results: The median A/E ratio was higher in patients with benign pancreatic disease and pancreatic cancer than in health checkup participants (21.7 and 24.2 vs. 13.6; p < 0.001). The ALDH2 inactive phenotype was associated with benign pancreatic disease (relative risk ratio [RRR], 3.55; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.85-6.83) and pancreatic cancer (RRR, 4.82; 95% CI, 2.13-10.88). The highest A/E ratio category was also associated with benign pancreatic disease (RRR, 8.77; 95% CI, 3.59-21.39) and pancreatic cancer (RRR, 12.79; 95% CI, 4.41-37.09). Exploratory spline analyses showed associations between higher A/E ratios and pancreatic disease outcomes without clear evidence of nonlinearity. Conclusions: A higher ABT-derived A/E ratio was associated with benign pancreatic disease and pancreatic cancer in this selected case-control study. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether functional assessment of aldehyde metabolism provides clinically useful information for pancreatic disease risk assessment. Trial registration number: UMIN Clinical Trials Registry (UMIN-CTR), UMIN000052609; registered 1 November 2023.

items.title: Sequential Dual Nanoparticle Approach for Extracellular Matrix Remodeling and Targeted Chemotherapy through Liposome-Exosome Hybridization in Pancreatic Cancer.
items.abstract: Pancreatic cancer remains one of the most aggressive and treatment-resistant malignancies, with a poor prognosis and limited response to conventional therapies. Although liposomal doxorubicin (DOX) formulations reduce systemic toxicity, their clinical use is constrained by insufficient tumor targeting and poor intratumoral penetration. Here, we report a sequential dual-nanoparticle approach that integrates extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling with tumor-targeted chemotherapy to overcome these barriers. Hyaluronidase-loaded liposomes (LH) were first employed to degrade hyaluronic acid-rich ECM, followed by the administration of DOX-loaded liposome-exosome hybrid nanoparticles (HLD) engineered using pancreatic cancer cell-derived exosomes to confer intrinsic tumor-homing capability. The DOX-loaded hybrid nanoparticles demonstrated enhanced cellular uptake, potent cytotoxicity, and strong immunogenic cell death (ICD) responses in pancreatic cancer cells. ECM degradation by LH significantly improved intratumoral accumulation and penetration of subsequently administered HLD in vivo. In a pancreatic cancer xenograft model, sequential LH and HLD treatment resulted in superior tumor growth suppression compared with monotherapies, without inducing systemic toxicity. Collectively, this work demonstrates a modular, sequential nanotherapeutic platform that synergistically combines ECM remodeling and exosome-mediated targeting, offering a promising strategy to improve drug delivery and therapeutic efficacy in stromal-dense solid tumors, such as pancreatic cancer.

items.title: SERPINB5 promotes pancreatic adenocarcinoma progression through FBXO32-mediated regulation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAAD) is a highly aggressive malignancy. This study aimed to investigate the clinical significance and biological functions of SERPINB5 in PAAD.
METHODS: Differentially expressed genes were screened from the TCGA-PAAD, GSE32676, and GSE101448 datasets. The candidate gene SERPINB5 was identified using LASSO Cox regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. SERPINB5 expression in PAAD cell lines was validated via in vitro experiments. The effects of silencing SERPINB5 on cellular phenotypes and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) were assessed using CCK-8, colony formation, and Transwell assays, as well as immunofluorescence and Western blotting. Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) and rescue experiments were conducted to explore the relationship between SERPINB5 and FBXO32.
RESULTS: A risk model identified seven candidate prognostic genes, including SERPINB5. Independent single-gene ROC analysis assessed its ability to discriminate PAAD tumors from normal pancreatic tissues across three transcriptomic datasets, with areas under the curve (AUC) values of 0.851, 0.966, and 0.965. Expression analysis revealed consistently high SERPINB5 levels in both PAAD tissues and cell lines. Functional studies showed that silencing SERPINB5 inhibited PAAD cell proliferation, colony formation, migration, and invasion. Mechanistic studies indicated that SERPINB5 knockdown upregulated E-cadherin expression while downregulating Vimentin and N-cadherin levels. Co-IP experiments confirmed a physical interaction between SERPINB5 and FBXO32, and SERPINB5 knockdown resulted in reduced FBXO32 expression. Furthermore, FBXO32 overexpression reversed the malignant phenotypes and EMT-related changes caused by SERPINB5 silencing.
CONCLUSION: Our findings indicate that SERPINB5 may be a candidate diagnostic and prognostic marker for PAAD. Functionally, the SERPINB5/FBXO32 axis appears to promote PAAD progression, at least partly, through epithelial-mesenchymal transition regulation.

items.title: Emphysematous Gastritis Precipitated by Malignant Gastric Outlet Obstruction from Advanced Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Emphysematous gastritis is a rare, frequently fatal infection of the gastric wall caused by gas-forming organisms. Gastric outlet obstruction is well recognised as a cause of benign gastric emphysema but is seldom reported as a precipitant of emphysematous gastritis. This report adds a rare presentation of emphysematous gastritis with malignant gastric outlet obstruction as a risk factor.
CASE DESCRIPTION: An 86-year-old man with locally advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma presented after a fall preceded by generalised weakness, abdominal bloating, diarrhoea, nausea and fever. He was hypotensive and tachycardic, with acute kidney injury and severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Computed tomography scan demonstrated a markedly distended stomach with intramural gas and distal obstruction from progressive pancreatic malignancy; blood cultures were negative. He was managed non-operatively with aggressive resuscitation, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and gastric decompression, with subsequent clinical, biochemical and radiological improvement.
CONCLUSION: Malignant gastric outlet obstruction, compounded by chemotherapy-related immunosuppression, can precipitate emphysematous gastritis. In selected patients without perforation or ischaemia, even those who are frail and immunocompromised, conservative management can achieve resolution.
LEARNING POINTS: Malignant gastric outlet obstruction from advanced pancreatic cancer can precipitate emphysematous gastritis, a rare and often fatal infection, particularly when compounded by chemotherapy-related immunosuppression.This case adds to the growing evidence that carefully selected patients without perforation or ischaemia can be managed conservatively with antibiotics and gastric decompression rather than surgery.

items.title: Cellular proximity and conditional coordination in the colorectal and pancreatic tumor microenvironment: a patient-level analysis of multiplexed imaging
items.abstract: Immune cells in the tumor microenvironment are organized, and in colorectal and pancreatic cancer their arrangement around the tumor epithelium carries prognostic information. Multiplexed tissue imaging records the position and phenotype of every cell in a section, and studies of such images now routinely report that two cell types are spatially associated. However, the summaries behind these reports answer different questions. A proximity statistic asks whether two cell types lie close together more often than expected by chance. A conditional network asks whether their local densities rise and fall together once the other cell types are held fixed. The two can disagree, because every cell type is abundant where tissue is cell-dense and because the images of one patient are repeated measurements of that patient. We asked how epithelial and immune cells are organized in two settings: colorectal cancer with a Crohn's-like reaction (CLR) or diffuse inflammatory infiltration (DII), in 140 CODEX images from 35 patients, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) against its precursor, intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN), in 207 multiplex immunofluorescence images from 141 patients. We developed a patient-level analysis that keeps proximity, recurrent local composition and conditional coordination as separate quantities, tests conditional organization as a function of local epithelial density within each section, checks before every conditional estimate that the two cell types are disjoint sets of cells observed together in enough images, and calibrates each conclusion by patient-label permutation, cellularity adjustment under two definitions, spatial-scale perturbation and fully nested leave-one-patient-out prediction. In colorectal cancer, the conditional association between epithelial and myeloid density turned negative with local epithelial density about four times faster in DII than in CLR (difference $-0.0553$ per quartile; 95% CI, $-0.0833$ to $-0.0273$; patient-label familywise $P=0.006$), with no accompanying difference in proximity. In the pancreas, cytotoxic and helper T cells were closer together in PDAC than in IPMN at every scale examined ($q\leq0.023$), whereas their conditional association differed between the two diseases under only one of the two cellularity definitions. Recurrent neighborhoods carried the most patient-level information in colorectal cancer (AUC 0.794) and combined spatial features in the pancreas (AUC 0.771). Pancreatic epithelial--immune and regulatory T-cell quantities could not be estimated from these cores and are reported as such. The analysis is implemented in the R package spatialMIFtools, available at https://github.com/sagnikbhadury/spatialMIFtools.

items.title: When to Operate After Neoadjuvant Therapy for Borderline Resectable Pancreatic Cancer: A Critical Review and Multidimensional Decision Framework.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Surgical timing after neoadjuvant therapy for borderline resectable pancreatic cancer remains difficult because post-treatment imaging may not reliably distinguish residual tumor from fibrosis, whereas tumor biology and patient fitness strongly influence surgical benefit.
METHODS: We performed a critical narrative review of studies and guidelines addressing surgical timing, radiological response, tumor-marker dynamics, pathological response, and physiological readiness after neoadjuvant therapy for borderline resectable pancreatic cancer.
RESULTS: Current evidence supports a multidimensional approach rather than reliance on anatomical imaging alone. Informative tumor-marker trajectories, especially carbohydrate antigen 19-9 when reliable and alternative markers such as Duke pancreatic monoclonal antigen type 2 when carbohydrate antigen 19-9 is non-informative, are central to assessing systemic disease control. Selective use of liver magnetic resonance imaging, diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging, and positron emission tomography-based modalities may help clarify discordant scenarios or detect occult metastatic disease. Patient fitness, including performance status, nutritional reserve, organ function, and recovery from treatment-related toxicity, remains essential before exploration.
CONCLUSION: Surgical timing after neoadjuvant therapy for borderline resectable pancreatic cancer should integrate biology, anatomy, and patient condition. A biology-first multidisciplinary framework may help avoid futile pancreatectomy while preserving timely surgical opportunities for appropriate candidates.

items.title: Actinomycetota-Derived Metabolites in Pancreatic Cancer: Chemical Diversity, Metabolic Vulnerability, and Translational Barriers.
items.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma remains among the deadliest malignancies worldwide, and effective therapies are still lacking. Actinomycetota are among the richest microbial sources of bioactive secondary metabolites, and three agents in clinical use against pancreatic malignancy derive from them - streptozotocin, everolimus and doxorubicin - though all three are indicated for neuroendocrine rather than ductal tumors. This review provides a critical narrative synthesis of Actinomycetota-derived metabolites evaluated in pancreatic cancer models, with every potency value re-derived from the primary literature and interpreted alongside assay conditions and available mechanistic and in vivo evidence.
RECENT FINDINGS: Fifty-two compounds from 25 primary reports encompass polyketides, nonribosomal peptides, depsipeptides, RiPPs, alkaloids, ionophores and hybrid scaffolds. Rather than a simple ranking of increasingly potent cytotoxins, the literature poses a sharper question about selectivity. Two compounds are conditionally active: kigamicin D only under nutrient deprivation and BE-43547A2 only under hypoxia, exploiting the metabolic state that defines the disease rather than any intrinsic difference between malignant and normal cells. Both were recovered by screens built to detect that behavior, and neither has been shown to hold a therapeutic window in vivo. Separately, thiogochangamide B retains activity in gemcitabine-resistant models, while trienomycin A binds STAT3 directly, suppresses proliferation across eight pancreatic lines, achieves 84-98% tumor growth inhibition in xenografts at doses producing no detectable toxicity, and distributes preferentially to pancreatic tissue. Conditional activity is best read as a hypothesis about how such compounds should be sought rather than as an established route to selectivity. Despite remarkable chemical diversity, translation remains constrained by the limited use of normal-cell controls, predictive biomarkers and clinically relevant preclinical models. Screens conducted in nutrient-replete, normoxic monolayer culture will systematically miss compounds of this kind. Future efforts should prioritize compounds that exploit the metabolic liabilities of pancreatic cancer rather than pursuing greater cytotoxic potency.

items.title: Laparoscopic Duodenum-Preserving Pancreatic Head and Neck Resection.
items.abstract: The selection of surgical approaches for benign and low-grade malignant tumors of the pancreatic head and neck, such as serous cystadenomas, neuroendocrine tumors, and intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs), has long been controversial. Traditional pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) is associated with substantial trauma and requires gastrointestinal reconstruction, which alters normal physiological structures. With a deeper understanding of pancreatic function and the advancement of minimally invasive techniques, duodenum-preserving pancreatic head resection (DPPHR) has gained increasing attention because it preserves the integrity of the duodenum and bile duct, better maintaining physiological conditions. However, this procedure imposes extremely high technical demands on surgeons, particularly when performed laparoscopically. Laparoscopic duodenum-preserving pancreatic head resection (LDPPHR) is frequently confronted with high risks of intraoperative bleeding and postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF). With proficiency in LDPPHR attained by the present authors and its indications extended to lesions of the pancreatic head and neck, the surgical workflow was optimized to reduce the incidence of complications. Under precise preoperative three-dimensional visualization planning and meticulous dissection guided by intraoperative ICG fluorescence and AR navigation, the anterior and posterior pancreaticoduodenal arterial arcades were preserved, and the pancreatic cut surface was reconstructed using a modified Blumgart pancreaticojejunostomy, so that curative tumor resection is accomplished while organ function is maximally preserved and patient outcomes are improved. This report is presented as a demonstration of the technical feasibility of completing each step of the protocol; its safety and effectiveness require evaluation in larger series.

items.title: Identification of Novel Tubulin Dimer Inhibitors for Pancreatic Cancer Using an Integrated Computational Approach.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Despite advances in medical science, pancreatic cancer is still among the deadliest forms of cancer, and only 10% of patients survive because they are usually diagnosed late and do not respond to standard treatments. Inhibition of microtubule behaviour by disrupting their dimeric structures is a potential treatment for pancreatic cancer. This study aims to identify new inhibitors that will bind to the tubulin dimer using an integrative computational drug discovery approach.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: An advanced series of in silico experiments was conducted using molecular docking, Density Functional Theory (DFT), Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations, and Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Compounds from DrugBank were selected based on their strong interactions with the tubulin dimer. Moreover, DFT was utilized to investigate electronic interactions, whereas MD simulations (1 μs) were used to understand the stability and behaviour of the studied complex.
RESULTS: The molecules Bisphosphonate-8 and Fenoldopam were selected as inhibitors, whereas Paclitaxel was chosen as a reference compound. Analysis of docking and binding free energy showed that Bisphosphonate-8 has approximately twice the binding affinity for the α-β tubulin dimer compared to Paclitaxel. The DFT calculations indicated a high interaction capacity. MD simulation showed that Bisphosphonate-8 forms a stable complex during the simulation, whereas Paclitaxel demonstrated notable instability. Principal component analysis corroborated that Bisphosphonate-8 is highly adaptable and stable.
DISCUSSION: This computational approach successfully identified Bisphosphonate-8 as an inhibitor of the α-β tubulin dimer, with better binding affinity and stability than well-known compounds and desirable pharmacokinetic properties.
CONCLUSION: Based on the results presented above, Bisphosphonate-8 is a promising candidate for targeting the α-β tubulin dimer in pancreatic cancer, with stronger interactions and greater conformational adaptability. The computational data provide an excellent starting point for further experiments aimed at developing novel therapeutic approaches to target the α-β tubulin heterodimer in pancreatic cancer.

items.title: CD11b agonist GB1275 potentiates oncolytic bacterial therapy against pancreatic cancer in mouse tumor models.
items.abstract: Oncolytic bacteria are microorganisms with cytotoxic activity capable of lysing cancer cells while simultaneously activating both innate and adaptive immune responses to exert anti-tumor effects. However, the innate immune activation targeting oncolytic bacteria within the tumor microenvironment (TME) is a limiting factor. Here we find that the CD11b-targeting agonist GB1275 can modulate bacteria-immune interaction and inhibit the infiltration of CD11b⁺ innate immune cells such as neutrophils and macrophages, thereby suppressing the antimicrobial immune defenses in the TME in mice. This then avoids the clearance of oncolytic bacteria and increases the efficacy of bacteria-mediated tumor immunotherapy. Furthermore, the gemcitabine-loaded bacteria combined with GB1275 treatment activate innate immune responses in tumor, as mediated by Toll-like receptors (TLR), NOD-like receptors (NLR) and cGAS-STING pathways, while simultaneously enhancing dendritic cell (DC)-dependent antigen cross-presentation; this then upregulates the adaptive anti-tumor immune response and inhibits the growth of both subcutaneous and in situ pancreatic cancers in mouse tumor models. Our results therefore demonstrate that modulating innate immune responses while subsequently strengthening adaptive immune activation can significantly improve the efficacy of bacteria-mediated tumor immunotherapy.

items.title: First-year functional recovery after pancreaticoduodenectomy with pancreaticogastrostomy: prospective PGAQoL study of quality of life, exocrine function and nutritional status
items.abstract:
Background/Objectives: Recovery after pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) is described through survival and complications, whereas patient-reported, exocrine and nutritional trajectories after pancreaticogastrostomy (PG) remain insufficiently defined. This study evaluated first-year functional recovery after PD with PG for malignancy. Methods: Adults undergoing PD with PG between January 2022 and June 2024 were assessed at baseline and 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. The primary endpoint was EORTC QLQ-C30 Global Health Status/quality of life. Secondary outcomes included exocrine insufficiency, PERT, nutritional indices, sarcopenia, morbidity and survival. Results: Of 133 eligible patients, 109 underwent PD with PG; 59 (54.1%) had pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Severe morbidity was 18.3% and 90-day mortality 2.8%. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency was 84.4% at 1 month and 81.9% at 12 months; 71 of 83 12-month survivors (85.5%) required PERT. Global quality of life declined from 60 at baseline to 43 at 1 month and recovered to 68 at 12 months. Among 82 paired patients, 39 (47.6%) improved, 22 (26.8%) remained stable and 21 (25.6%) deteriorated. QoL trajectories did not differ between PDAC and other malignancies (interaction P=0.453). In PDAC, 25/59 initiated adjuvant therapy; each 10-point higher 1-month QoL score was associated with greater odds of initiation (adjusted OR 1.32, 95% CI 1.00-1.75; P=0.048).

Conclusions:

After PD with PG, quality of life recovered among 12-month survivors, whereas exocrine and nutritional sequelae remained highly prevalent. Follow-up should include symptom control, PERT optimisation and nutritional surveillance.

items.title: MRI for restaging pancreatic cancer.
items.abstract: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is a tumor with a dismal prognosis, as the majority of patients are diagnosed when the tumor is not resectable. Neoadjuvant treatment has significantly improved prognosis, but assessing treatment response can be challenging for radiologists. Given the fibrotic nature of the primary tumor, differentiating between residual viable tumor and fibrotic response can be difficult. MRI can have a role in reassessing the primary tumor and disease spread. In this review, we discuss MR techniques that can be used for this assessment, including routinely used sequences (e.g., DWI) and sequences that are not yet routinely included in pancreatic protocols (e.g., T1 mapping, ECV imaging, and USPIO contrast for nodal staging). KEY POINTS: Question Imaging assessment of the response of pancreatic adenocarcinoma to neoadjuvant treatment is difficult and still has limited accuracy. Findings Different MRI sequences and techniques have been suggested as possibly improving this assessment, reflecting on better patient management. Critical relevance statement We summarize the available evidence on MRI for restaging pancreatic carcinoma after neoadjuvant treatment.

items.title: Cumulative obesity exposure and hepato-pancreato-biliary cancer risk following different weight-loss interventions: retrospective cohort study.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Obesity is a time-dependent carcinogenic exposure associated with an increased risk of hepatopancreatobiliary (HPB) cancers. Although weight-loss interventions improve metabolic status, the comparative oncologic impact and the role of cumulative obesity duration remain unclear.
OBJECTIVES: To compare HPB cancer incidence across lifestyle-based, pharmacologic, and surgical weight-loss strategies and to assess whether differences in cumulative obesity exposure before and after weight reduction may influence cancer risk.
SETTING: A retrospective cohort study at a tertiary university hospital in Israel.
METHODS: We analyzed 1131 adults who achieved weight loss between 2010 and 2024 through lifestyle modification, weight-loss medications, or bariatric surgery. For each patient, the duration of obesity before and after weight loss, the magnitude of BMI reduction, and follow-up intervals were recorded. HPB cancers - including hepatocellular carcinoma, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, and gallbladder carcinoma - were identified through national registry linkage. Group differences were evaluated using analysis of variance, Kruskal-Wallis, χ2 tests, and unadjusted risk ratios and odds ratios.
RESULTS: Twenty-seven HPB cancers were identified. Incidence did not differ significantly among lifestyle (2.05%), medication-induced (3.24%), and surgery-induced (1.05%) groups (P = 0.334). Bariatric surgery had the lowest numerical incidence, whereas pharmacologic therapy had higher numerical rates; however, these differences were not statistically significant and should be interpreted cautiously. Obesity duration before weight loss differed significantly across groups (P < 0.001), and post-weight-loss duration showed a borderline difference (P = 0.050). BMI reduction was similar across interventions.
CONCLUSIONS: Although no statistically significant differences in HPB cancer incidence were observed among weight-loss strategies, exploratory numerical differences were noted, with the lowest crude incidence in the bariatric surgery group. Given the limited number of events, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and viewed as hypothesis-generating only. Further adequately powered prospective studies are required before any clinical inference can be made.

items.title: CT Radiomics and Deep Learning-Based Non-Invasive Model for Tracing Primary Sites of Adenocarcinoma Liver Metastases: Automatic Differentiation of Multiple Primary Digestive Tumors
items.abstract: This is a retrospective observational study. Liver metastasis occurs frequently in digestive-system cancers. Identification of the primary tumor source of liver metastasis may pose clinical challenges. Biopsy is an invasive procedure associated with potential sampling errors. This study aims to develop and validate a non-invasive artificial-intelligence model based on contrast-enhanced CT images. The model integrates CT radiomics and deep learning to automatically determine the primary origin of adenocarcinoma liver metastases, including gastric adenocarcinoma, colorectal adenocarcinoma, biliary/gallbladder adenocarcinoma, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. The investigators will retrieve historical medical records and de-identified abdominal contrast-enhanced CT images from patients diagnosed at West China Hospital, Sichuan University between January 2015 and August 2026. No new intervention or treatment will be administered to participants in this study.

items.title: ZnO-Pd nanobolts-based immunoanalytical detection of a pancreatic cancer biomarker and its software-assisted digital quantification.
items.abstract: Early and reliable detection of pancreatic cancer (PC) remains a formidable clinical challenge, largely owing to the limited sensitivity, operational unreliability, and enzyme dependence of existing carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) immunoassays. In this work, we determine for the first time that ZnO-Pd nanobolts show intrinsic oxidase-like activity. Furthermore, this attribute was used to fabricate a colorimetric immunoanalytical sensor based on nanozymes for the sensitive and specific detection of CA19-9, a biomarker for PC. In this research, immunoreagent optimization, smartphone-assisted signal analysis, and kinetic analysis of nanozyme catalytic activity were employed to enable highly sensitive detection of CA19-9. Enzyme-kinetic studies showed low Michaelis-Menten constants (KM) of 0.99 mM, as well as high turnover numbers (kcat) and catalytic efficiencies (kcat/KM) of 4.48 × 10-4 s-1 and 0.453 M-1 s-1, respectively, indicating high substrate affinity. The optimized nanozyme was functionalized with Goat anti-mouse IgG (GAM IgG), thereby facilitating antigen recognition and signal transduction. The proposed immunoassay demonstrated high analytical sensitivity (LOD of 0.000159 U mL-1 and LOQ of 0.000482 U mL-1) and exceptional selectivity even in complex biological matrices. Software-assisted signal processing enabled precise assessment of the limit of detection (LOD) of 0.000359 U mL-1 and the limit of quantification (LOQ) of 0.00108 U mL-1. The practical utility of the fabricated immunoassay was further examined using human serum, with recovery rates ranging from 100.6% to 102%, indicating high accuracy and reproducibility. Furthermore, the successful digitalization of assay results into software-based readable data demonstrates the sensing approach's potential for portable, cost-effective, and point-of-care PC diagnostics.

Nuclear Receptors In Cancer Cachexia
items.abstract:
PROJECT SUMMARY
 Cancer cachexia is a devastating muscle-wasting condition leading to poor quality of life and heightened
mortality in cancer patients. While cachexia is responsible for nearly 30% of cancer deaths, there are currently
no effective clinical interventions, highlighting a critical need for therapeutic target discovery for managing
cachexia. We previously showed that estrogen-related receptors α and γ (ERRα/γ) are indispensable muscle
fitness factors needed for skeletal muscle homeostasis, driving muscle mitochondrial biogenesis, vascularization
and regeneration. However, their role in muscle wasting and atrophy is unknown. We postulated that ERRα/γ
could play an anti-atrophy role in cachectic muscle wasting by virtue of its effects on mitochondrial and vascular
homeostasis, and other potentially uncovered muscle size regulatory pathways. We have found that ERRα/γ
protein and transcripts, as well as their mitochondrial and angiogenic gene targets are repressed in atrophic
muscles isolated from murine models of cancer cachexia (pancreatic). Muscle C2C12 cells treated with
conditioned media from KPC (KrasG12D/+; Trp53R712H/+; Pdx1-Cre) pancreatic cancer cells resulted in myofiber
atrophy. Overexpression of ERRα/γ alone or in combination via adeno-associated virus (Ad-Esrra, Ad-Esrrg)
prevented cancer cell-conditioned media induced atrophy and repressed cachexia-associated wasting genes.
Conversely, an ERRα inverse agonist (XCT 790) in conjunction with cancer cell conditioned media worsened
atrophy and expression of cachectic wasting markers. In KPC orthotopic murine pancreatic cancer model, which
exhibits severe wasting, we found a deficit in ERRs and their metabolic-angiogenic gene signaling in cachectic
muscles. Intramuscular injection of an adeno-associated virus (AAV9) carrying Esrra (ERRα) or Esrrg (ERR γ)
gene neutralized the elevated expression of cachexia-related muscle wasting genes. Therefore, we will test the
hypothesis that ERRs, along with their target metabolic and angiogenic genes, are repressed in cachectic
muscles, and rescuing ERRα/γ pathways mitigates cachexia-associated muscle dysfunction. The hypothesis will
be tested in two specific aims. In Aim 1, we will investigate whether ERRα/γ activation in skeletal muscle mitigates
cancer-induced muscle wasting. In Aim 2, we will explore potential mechanism through which ERRα/γ protects
against cancer-induced muscle atrophy. We will use pre-clinical pancreatic cancer cachexia model, as well as
in vitro cachexia model, along with transgenic, gene therapy and pharmacological approaches to activate ERRs.
We expect to identify a critical role for ERRs in muscle mass regulation, which could lead to advanced studies
on these receptors as therapeutic target for cancer cachexia.

items.title: Global Landscape of Clinical Studies Open to Enrollment in Carbon Ion Radiotherapy: A PTCOG Review.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Radiotherapy with high linear energy transfer (LET) has shown promise for improving cancer outcomes. Carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) combines charged-particle dose conformality with enhanced biological effectiveness. However, clinical development remains constrained by limited center availability, modest trial accrual, and few randomized studies. We reviewed the global landscape of CIRT studies open to enrollment to identify current priorities and gaps.
METHODS: This Particle Therapy Cooperative Group (PTCOG)-sanctioned project, conducted within the CIRT Guidelines Subcommittee, identified studies through registry review and institutional verification. ClinicalTrials.gov and the Japan Registry of Clinical Trials were searched from December 2025 through February 2026. We included interventional CIRT trials and prospective registries open to new enrollment and excluded studies not open to enrollment, retrospective cohorts, proton-only studies, and preclinical studies.
RESULTS: Thirty-six studies were identified: 35 interventional trials in 6 countries and 1 North American registry-based comparative-effectiveness study. Japan had the largest share, followed by Germany, China, Italy, Austria, and France. Three centers (SPHIC, QST, and HIT) accounted for 21 of 36 studies. The portfolio included 7 phase I, 23 phase II, 5 phase III, and 1 registry study. Pancreatic cancer and sarcoma-related tumors each accounted for 7 studies; head and neck cancers, 5; prostate and breast cancers, 3 each; glioblastoma, lung cancer, and gynecologic malignancies, 2 each; and mucosal melanoma, mixed solid tumors, kidney cancer, esophageal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma, 1 each. Most studies were conducted at a single institution and emphasized feasibility, toxicity, local control, progression-free survival, or overall survival.
CONCLUSIONS: This expert-verified inventory shows that CIRT studies open to enrollment remain concentrated by center, disease site, and phase. Future progress may depend more on shared outcome definitions, transparent biological dose reporting, and registry-enabled or multicenter comparative designs than on additional isolated single-institution studies.

items.title: Raman Spectroscopy, Machine Learning and Pancreatic Tumors
items.abstract: Pancreatic cancer remains difficult to diagnose at an early stage, motivating the development of label-free methods capable of detecting biochemical changes in tissue, cells, and biofluids. Raman spectroscopy provides molecularly specific measurements, but their diagnostic interpretation increasingly relies on chemometric, machine-learning, and deep-learning methods. This review critically examines Raman-based studies related to pancreatic cancer, with particular attention to acquisition modalities, preprocessing, feature extraction, classification, and validation design. Across the reviewed literature, high internal classification performance is frequently accompanied by small numbers of independent biological units, spectral pseudoreplication, unclear patient- or specimenlevel partitioning, data-dependent processing outside training folds, and limited external validation. Differences among instruments and preprocessing pipelines further restrict direct comparison across studies. We therefore distinguish evidence of spectral separability within a dataset from evidence of diagnostic generalization to independent patients. Priorities for the field include transparent reporting, patient-grouped evaluation, training-only preprocessing and model selection, harmonized acquisition and processing procedures, and shared benchmark datasets with sequestered test sets. Raman spectroscopy remains a promising source of biochemical information for pancreatic cancer research, but clinical translation requires reproducible performance across independent patients, laboratories, and acquisition conditions.

items.title: Comparison of Endoscopic Ultrasound, Computed Tomography and Magnetic Resonance Imaging for Preoperative Tumor-Size Assessment in Resected Pancreatic Neoplasms
items.abstract: Background and Aims Current imaging‑based T staging of pancreatic cancer relies primarily on computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). However, discrepancies are frequently observed between tumor size reported on CT or MRI and the actual size measured after surgery. This study aimed to compare the absolute deviation of EUS with that of CT and MRI in evaluating pancreatic tumor size. Methods This retrospective single-center study included 60 patients with confirmed pancreatic malignancy who underwent surgical intervention, endoscopic ultrasound (EUS), computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging. Tumor size measured by en bloc resection was regarded as the reference standard. Measurements obtained from EUS were compared with those from CT and MRI to evaluate relative precision. The primary outcome was absolute deviation of evaluating tumor size by different imaging techniques. Results In tumor smaller than 40 mm, EUS demonstrated the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) in tumor size measurement compared with surgical specimen (0.41), followed by MRI (0.47) and CT (0.68). Paired analysis showed EUS was more accurate than CT (n = 48, p = 0.03; 95% CI: -0.52 to -0.03). Conclusions In this retrospective surgical cohort, EUS showed lower absolute tumor-size deviation than CT for tumors < 40 mm, whereas its accuracy was comparable to MRI. These findings support further evaluation of EUS as a complementary modality for preoperative tumor-size assessment.

items.title: Myoclonus as a neurologic manifestation of hypoglycemia in dogs.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Myoclonus consists of brief, shock-like jerks and is not reported in dogs as a neurological manifestation of hypoglycemia.
HYPOTHESIS/OBJECTIVES: To describe hypoglycemia-associated myoclonus in dogs and report diagnostic findings, treatment, and outcome.
ANIMALS: Ten dogs presenting myoclonus and concurrent hypoglycemia.
METHODS: Multicenter, retrospective study of dogs presenting hypoglycemia-related myoclonus.
RESULTS: All dogs presented with myoclonus. Neurological examination was abnormal in 5/10 (50%). Myoclonus was generalized in 8/10 (80%) dogs and focal (head) in 2/10 (20%), with progression to generalized tonic-clonic epileptic seizures in 5/10 (50%). Hypoglycemia (<3.3 mmol/L) was observed in all dogs (median, 2.07 mmol/L) during the myoclonic episodes. Insulinoma was a suspected (n = 1), presumptive (n = 5), or definitive (n = 3) diagnosis in 9/10 (90%) dogs. One dog (10%) developed iatrogenic hypoglycemia after IV administration of fast-acting human insulin and myoclonic episodes resolved after dose reduction. Among dogs with suspected, presumptive or confirmed insulinoma, 5/9 (56%) received medical treatment alone, 3/9 (33%) combined medical and surgical treatment, and 1/9 (11%) was not treated. Medical treatment included, prednisolone (n = 6), diazoxide (n = 3) and therapeutic diet (n = 6). Surgical treatment consisted of pancreatic mass resection. Medical or surgical treatment resulted in short-term improvement in myoclonus frequency in all dogs, however, four were later euthanized due to recurrence of hypoglycemia and myoclonus.
CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPORTANCE: Myoclonus might represent an underrecognized neurological manifestation of hypoglycemia in dogs. Measurement of blood glucose concentrations is a fundamental diagnostic approach for identifying hypoglycemia-related myoclonus. Treatment can lead to clinical improvement, but prognosis is dependent on the underlying cause.

Review on carbon ion minibeam radiotherapy: Dosimetry, dynamic phantoms and radiobiology.
items.abstract: Carbon ion minibeam radiotherapy (CIMRT) is an emerging technique that intends to combine the biological and physical advantages of carbon ions with the normal-tissue sparing potential of spatially fractionated dose delivery. The increased linear energy transfer (LET) and higher relative biological effectiveness (RBE) of carbon ions compared with photons and protons, together with the immunomodulatory effects reported for carbon ion therapy and the biological responses observed after minibeam irradiation for photons and protons, suggest the potential for enhanced tumor control while preserving normal tissue during CIMRT. Given the poor prognosis associated with tumors such as pancreatic cancer, CIMRT may offer an option to increase therapeutic efficacy for these kinds of tumors. However, the clinical translation of CIMRT remains challenging due to unresolved questions in beam physics, dosimetry, radiation biology, and treatment robustness. A comprehensive understanding of carbon-ion-specific biological effects in spatially fractionated fields is required, and accurate dosimetric methods must be developed to characterize steep peak-to-valley dose gradients in high-LET environments. Furthermore, geometric and anthropomorphic phantoms are needed for treatment validation, and the influence of organ motion on the minibeam pattern should be systematically investigated. This review summarizes the current progress in CIMRT from four key perspectives: (i) physical and biological aspects, including the particularities of carbon-ion RBE and the biological responses to minibeam irradiation; (ii) dosimetric approaches for high-LET spatially fractionated fields; (iii) development of anthropomorphic and motion-capable phantoms; and (iv) the impact of organ motion and motion mitigation strategies. By highlighting recent advances and remaining challenges, this review provides a framework for future CIMRT development. It evaluates the requirements for its long-term transition from an experimental technique toward a clinical treatment modality.

items.title: Targeting host ferroptosis in cancer cachexia: Tumor-immune triggers, tissue wasting, and the therapeutic paradox.
items.abstract: Cancer cachexia is a systemic wasting syndrome driven by tumor burden, chronic inflammation, disrupted nutrient handling, and neuroendocrine stress. Supportive nutrition, exercise, and symptom management rarely restore lean mass, function, or treatment tolerance once wasting is established. Ferroptosis, iron-dependent cell death caused by phospholipid peroxidation, may connect inflammatory iron redistribution, lipid remodeling, mitochondrial stress, and impaired antioxidant defenses. This review critically evaluates ferroptosis in cachexia from a tumor-host pharmacology perspective, distinguishing causal evidence from associated oxidative signatures. We highlight two experimentally supported mechanisms: neutrophil-derived lipocalin-2 in lung cancer cachexia and tumor exosomal miR-203a-3p in pancreatic cancer-associated muscle wasting. We also examine the paradox that tumor ferroptosis induction may weaken host-tissue resistance and worsen muscle and adipose loss. We propose a "split-ferroptosis" strategy combining tumor sensitization with host-protective iron modulation, lipid peroxide scavenging, endogenous defense reinforcement, and biomarker-guided patient selection to expand the tumor-host therapeutic index.
