Modified Appleby with laparoscopic aorto-hepatic bypass for pancreatic adenocarcinoma: expanding the limits.
items.abstract: Celiac axis involvement has long defined unresectability in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) due to its association with adverse tumor biology and the risk of hepatic ischemia after arterial sacrifice. Contemporary neoadjuvant regimens and refined vascular techniques have challenged this paradigm. We report a 65-year-old woman with locally advanced PDAC of the pancreatic body encasing the celiac trunk, splenic artery, and proximal common hepatic artery. Following FOLFIRINOXbased neoadjuvant therapy, restaging demonstrated a marked biochemical and radiologic response, with no evidence of systemic disease. Given this favorable tumor biology, the patient underwent distal pancreatectomy with en bloc celiac axis resection (modified Appleby procedure) combined with a totally laparoscopic aortohepatic bypass to ensure reliable antegrade hepatic inflow. R0 resection was achieved without intraoperative morbidity. Final pathology revealed a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma (ypT2N0) with perineural invasion. Postoperative recovery was uneventful, with preserved hepatic function and no ischemic or vascular complications. At 11 months, the patient remains recurrence-free, with sustained graft patency. This report demonstrates that, in highly selected responders to neoadjuvant therapy, radical arterial resection supplemented by minimally invasive vascular reconstruction is feasible, oncologically sound, and may extend the boundaries of curative-intent surgery in locally advanced PDAC within experienced multidisciplinary programs.

items.title: Expression of Annexin A4 in Cancer: A Tissue Microarray Study Involving More than 17,600 Cancers from 148 Tumor Entities.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Annexin A4 (ANXA4) is one of twelve members of the annexin superfamily that bind membrane phospholipids in a calcium-dependent manner, and which are involved in several processes related to the membrane. Methods: To learn more about the role of ANXA4 in cancer, the ANXA4 expression was analyzed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) on tissue microarrays (TMAs) containing 17,654 tumors and precursor lesions from 148 tumor types. Results: ANXA4 immunostaining was found in 10,858 (83.4%) of 13,017 analyzable tumors, and was considered weak in 10.1%, moderate in 16.6%, and strong in 61.8% of cases. Of 148 tumor categories, 144 showed ANXA4 staining in at least one case and 133 included at least one case with strong staining. Among tumor entities with at least 10 evaluable samples, strong ANXA4 staining in >50.0% of cases was seen in 56 of 120 entities, while absence of staining in >50.0% of cases was seen in 13. Clinically important tumor entities where ANXA4 staining was always positive (>99.5%) included gallbladder adenocarcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, pancreatic/ampullary, various subtypes of salivary gland tumors, papillary renal cell carcinoma, urothelial carcinoma, squamous and basal cell carcinoma of the skin, and epithelioid mesothelioma. A reduced ANXA4 expression was linked to features of cancer aggressiveness in breast cancer, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, urothelial carcinoma, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, colorectal adenocarcinoma, and follicular thyroid carcinoma. Conclusions: It is concluded that ANXA4 is abundantly expressed in human malignancies and that a reduced expression may be linked to unfavorable disease characteristics in many important tumor entities.

items.title: BHLHE40 as a transcriptional rheostat: decoding microenvironmental signals in context-dependent tumor plasticity.
items.abstract: The basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor BHLHE40 (also known as BHLHB2, DEC1, STRA13) functions as a critical molecular rheostat in cancer biology, exhibiting context-dependent roles that contribute to tumor plasticity. This review synthesizes current knowledge of BHLHE40, with emphasis on its structural features, including DNA binding, dimerization, and regulatory domains, as well as its integration of key physiological signals, such as circadian rhythm regulation, hypoxic adaptation, cellular senescence, and immune modulation. Pancancer analyses indicate that BHLHE40 expression is dysregulated across multiple tumor types. Elevated expression is associated with poor prognosis in cancers such as glioblastoma, acute myeloid leukemia, and ovarian cancer, whereas it correlates with favorable outcomes in breast and kidney cancers. Notably, the functional role of BHLHE40 is highly tissue-dependent. It promotes tumor progression in hepatocellular carcinoma, gastric cancer, colorectal cancer, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma by enhancing proliferation, invasion, migration, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and therapeutic resistance. In contrast, BHLHE40 exhibits tumor-suppressive effects in prostate cancer by inducing cellular senescence, and in endometrial cancer by inhibiting EMT. The tumor microenvironment plays a pivotal role in modulating BHLHE40 activity, with factors such as hypoxia, cytokine signaling, and immune cell interactions shaping its oncogenic or tumor-suppressive functions. Importantly, its role in maintaining CD8+ T-cell effector function during immune checkpoint blockade highlights its therapeutic potential. However, the context-dependent duality of BHLHE40 presents significant challenges for clinical targeting. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including targeted protein degradation approaches and advanced tumor models such as patient-derived organoids, offer promising avenues for intervention. Future studies integrating multi-omics data and spatial transcriptomics will be essential to fully elucidate the role of BHLHE40 and to harness its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target for overcoming tumor progression, therapeutic resistance, and immune evasion.

items.title: End-to-end automated radiotherapy planning using transfer learning to overcome data scarcity.
items.abstract:
PURPOSE: To develop and benchmark 3D dose prediction algorithms for volumetric modulated arc therapy for head-and-neck (HN) and pancreatic cancer treatments, and to demonstrate the clinical feasibility of converting the predicted doses into deliverable plans.
METHODS AND MATERIALS: Three deep learning models were pretrained on 3232 public plans and fine-tuned on institutional cohorts (256 HN and 72 pancreas patients). The accuracy of the fine-tuning strategy was compared with the baseline trained from scratch using only institutional data. In a prospective setting, the predicted dose was used as the planning goal for fully automated plan generation. Automated plans were benchmarked against clinical plans using Plan Quality Metrics. The deliverability of the fully automated plans was verified by Mobius ion-chamber patient-specific quality assurance (PSQA).
RESULTS: Relative to training from scratch, transfer learning significantly accelerated convergence and minimized prediction error in scenarios with limited site-specific data. For HN cases, fine-tuning yielded a prediction error of 1.76 Gy. Notably, models fine-tuned on just 5% (n = 12) of the dataset achieved accuracy comparable to models trained from scratch using 50% (n = 116) of the training data. In the pancreas cohort, fine-tuning resulted in a mean absolute error of 1.35 Gy, representing a 14.6% reduction compared to the baseline trained solely on institutional data. When used for automated planning, these predicted 3D doses improved planning target volume homogeneity and organs at risk sparing (esophagus and trachea) in HN plans, while pancreas plans aimed to meet clinical goals with reduced dose to the spinal cord and right kidney. All automated plans were confirmed as clinically deliverable via PSQA.
CONCLUSION: Compared with models trained from scratch on institutional data, transfer learning significantly reduced prediction error and improved robustness. The feasibility of converting predicted doses into clinical plans while maintaining plan quality through a fully automated process was demonstrated.

items.title: Cancer risks associated with BRCA1 and BRCA2: Overview and management.
items.abstract: The BRCA1 and BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes are integral to the repair of DNA double-strand breaks. Therefore, germline pathogenic variants (PVs) in either of these genes are associated with an increased risk of developing hereditary cancers. For over 30 years, studies have demonstrated a well established and markedly increased lifetime risk of female breast cancer and ovarian cancer for individuals with a PV in BRCA1 or BRCA2. Additional canonical cancers include prostate cancer, pancreatic cancer for males and females, and male breast cancer. Several noncanonical cancers have also been reported in association with BRCA1 or BRCA2, including stomach cancer and endometrial cancer. This review summarizes the established and evolving cancer risks associated with germline PVs in BRCA1 or BRCA2 as well as current clinical management recommendations. With increased uptake and diversified utility of germline genetic testing, this summary provides a current overview for clinical management of both male and female individuals with a PV in BRCA1 or BRCA2.

items.title: Exploring Patients' Care Needs in Digital Free-Text Messages During Cancer Treatment: Qualitative Analysis Guided by the Fundamentals of Care Framework.
items.abstract:
AIM: To describe the content of patients' free-text messages submitted within a digital symptom-monitoring system during cancer treatment, and to explore how these messages reflect relational, integrated, and contextual care needs as conceptualised in the Fundamentals of Care Framework, and to generate implications for the future development of digitally mediated cancer care.
DESIGN: Exploratory qualitative study using inductive and deductive content analysis.
METHOD: Free-text messages (n = 2097) from 180 patients receiving treatment for breast, prostate, or pancreatic cancer were analysed. These messages were collected between 2013 and 2017 within three clinical trials, in which intervention-group participants used a symptom-reporting app and could submit free-text messages alongside their reports. Summative counts and inductive qualitative content analysis were conducted first, followed by a deductive interpretation using the Fundamentals of Care Framework to examine how communication reflected relational, integrated, and contextual care needs.
RESULTS: Three interconnected categories were identified: navigating uncertainty and taking an active role, reassurance and confirmation, and going beyond predefined symptom ratings. These formed the overarching theme of expressing experiences and negotiating shared care. Patients used free-text messages to seek clarification, describe symptoms and contextual factors, articulate self-care efforts, set boundaries for communication, and maintain relational continuity with nurses. Deductive interpretation suggested that patients actively contributed to sustaining therapeutic relationships, integrating symptoms with everyday life experiences, and managing substantial self-care responsibilities.
CONCLUSION: Free-text communication enabled patients to articulate needs not captured in structured symptom questionnaires, supporting more person-centred and contextually informed assessment. Implications for the profession and patient care: Future digitally mediated cancer care should not only monitor symptoms but also support relational continuity, preserve integrated patient narratives, and facilitate collaborative sense-making around self-care and symptom management. WHAT PROBLEM DID THE STUDY ADDRESS?: Structured questionnaires do not fully capture patients' experiences or care needs or the relational and contextual dimensions of care during cancer treatment. WHAT WERE THE MAIN FINDINGS?: Patients used free-text messages to negotiate shared care, contextualise symptoms, maintain relational contact with nurses, and support self-care decision-making during cancer treatment.
IMPACT: Findings inform the future development of digitally mediated cancer care by highlighting the importance of supporting patients' relational work, preserving integrated patient narratives, and enabling collaborative sense-making around self-care.
NO PATIENT OR PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT: This study did not include patient or public involvement in its design, conduct, or reporting.
REPORTING METHOD: The Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (SRQR).
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02479607; NCT02477137.

SOMATIC EVOLUTION AND PRE-CANCER OF TP53 MUTANT CLONES
items.abstract:
PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT
Somatic mutations are continuously acquired in all cells in all tissues and accumulate with age to number
hundreds or thousands per cell (depending on the tissue). These mutations are considered to be founding events
in cancer, even though it may take decades from first mutation to malignancy development. Remarkably, even
though many clone-driving mutations can be cancer-causing, and virtually all tissues harbor some of these
clones, not everyone gets cancer. Furthermore, even though all genes have acquired mutations across all
tissues, the constellation of mutations that causes positive selection of clones is unique to each tissue. Even
TP53, which encodes a broadly important tumor-suppressor, is most often mutated in association with certain
cancer types, such as breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and hematologic. Importantly, TP53 mutations are not
exclusive to cancers, and are commonly found in histologically normal tissues, including breast, lung, blood,
endometrium, skin, esophagus, colon, and bladder. We hypothesize that a key role of pre-cancer mutations is
to promote expansion of a nascent clone in competition with other cells in a tissue-specific manner. Here, we
will establish a strategy to test this concept in a novel mouse model, in the context of Trp53 mutations. We
hypothesize that p53-mutant cells are positively selected for in only some tissues and mostly with age, leading
to increased p53-mutant clonal expansion and tumor incidence. We have established a novel mosaic mouse
model bearing the Trp53R245W mutation (equivalent of the human TP53R248W hotspot) in just a few cells in a sea
of normal cells. TP53R248W is a commonly occurring mutation that leads to poor cancer prognosis in humans and
in mice. Preliminary data indicate our ability to generate mosaic mice with unbiased contribution of control cells
across tissues and to measure the overall degree of mosaicism in young mice. Therefore, in aim 1, we will
examine the relationship between tissue-specific expansion of p53mut clones and oncogenesis. Preliminary data
also indicate that expression of Trp53R245W in blood or breast tissue of young adult mice leads to clonal
expansion. In aim 2, we will determine the role of aging on p53mut-driven clonal expansion and cancer initiation.
Understanding how age exacerbates tissue-specific clonal expansion will aid in the identification of the trigger(s)
that tip p53-mutant cells into expansion and those that push it further into a malignant state. Given that TP53 is
the most commonly mutated tumor suppressor across cancers, fundamental insights into how it impacts clonal
expansion as a function of age has the potential to identify factors that inhibit nascent clonal outgrowth. Despite
a great deal of work on p53, the role of p53 mutations in clonal evolution as a pre-requisite to cancer has been
little studied. If the concept is established in this developmental/exploratory R21 proposal, the work will offer a
new perspective on cancer initiation that may have significant therapeutic implications. Mice develop cancer in
ways very similar to humans, and thus they are an ideal setting in which to look at the very first stages of cancer.
Mice allow us to examine many tissues at different stages of life with a deep level of analysis, which would not
be possible to do with cell-culture strategies or humans.

items.title: Pancreaticoduodenectomy after Laparoscopic Sleeve Gastrectomy with Preservation of Gastric Arterial Inflow: A Case Report.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Obesity is an established risk factor for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. As laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) has become increasingly prevalent, pancreatic surgeons may encounter malignancies in patients with a surgically altered gastric anatomy. Pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) after an LSG is rare and requires meticulous preoperative planning to prevent ischemic and anastomotic complications.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 47-year-old man with morbid obesity (BMI 59.1 kg/m2) underwent LSG. Twenty-three days later, obstructive jaundice led to the diagnosis of pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. After neoadjuvant chemotherapy and substantial weight reduction (BMI 34.9 kg/m2), subtotal stomach-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy with wedge resection of the superior mesenteric vein was performed. Preoperative CT confirmed the preservation and patency of both the left and right gastric arteries. The left gastric artery was preserved intraoperatively. Gastrojejunostomy was performed using a hand-sewn anastomosis between the greater curvature side of the sleeve stomach and the jejunum. The patient developed a grade B postoperative pancreatic fistula but was discharged with no ischemic complications.
CONCLUSIONS: PD after an LSG is feasible, but careful vascular assessment, a preplanned reconstruction strategy, consideration of the patient's metabolic and nutritional status, and careful intraoperative assessment of the remnant stomach may enhance surgical safety.

items.title: NAD+ limitation and α-ketoglutarate depletion define cancer induced muscle atrophy
items.abstract: Tumour-host crosstalk is an emerging hallmark of malignancy. It is increasingly recognised that cancer alters non-tumour bearing distant organs, with important consequences for disease progression and survival. Skeletal muscle loss, a defining feature of cancer-associated cachexia, contributes to morbidity and reduced quality of life, yet its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study we analysed the secretome of pancreatic cancer cells and identified a metabolite-driven signal that induces myotube atrophy. Our data suggests that atrophy, which seems to involve cytoskeletal stress and increased myosin contractility, arises from cancer cell-dependent reductive metabolic rewiring. Pancreatic cancer cells conditioned their environment with elevated levels of lactate, generating a lactate-rich extracellular milieu that decrease the NAD+/NADH ratio in myotubes. This redox imbalance impaired oxidative metabolism, decreasing α-ketoglutarate (αKG) levels and disrupted αKG-dependent processes. Restoration of NAD+ or αKG levels rescued myotube atrophy. Skeletal muscle from cancer-associated cachexia mouse models exhibited reduced αKG levels. Collectively, these findings identify a targetable metabolite-mediated mechanism of tumour-muscle crosstalk.

items.title: MYC targeted de novo binders impair tumor growth
items.abstract: MYC is one of the most frequently dysregulated oncogenic drivers across many cancers, yet direct therapeutic targeting has remained difficult because its function is mediated by disordered regions and transient protein-protein interactions. Here we design proteins that bind epitopes within regions of MYC whose sequence is conserved between human and mouse, including intrinsically disordered motifs required for oncogenic activity. In vitro, the designs bind MYC with nanomolar affinity and in cells they engage MYC, disrupt interactions with MAX, and remodel MYC-associated protein complexes. Expression of the binders decreases cell proliferation across diverse MYC-dependent hematopoietic, liver, pancreatic, and patient-derived tumor models, and in an orthotopic pancreatic cancer model, binder-expressing tumor cells were selectively depleted. This work establishes de novo protein design as a generalizable strategy to therapeutically target intrinsically disordered transcription factors.

items.title: Pancreatic Ascites Complicated by Salmonella Enteritidis Peritonitis: A Diagnostic Challenge and the Role of Surgical Source Control.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ascites is an uncommon complication of pancreatic disorders resulting from persistent leakage of pancreatic juice into the peritoneal cavity, most commonly due to disruption of the main pancreatic duct or rupture of a pancreatic fluid collection. Bacterial peritonitis complicating pancreatic ascites is rarely reported. We report the case of a 40-year-old man who presented with massive pancreatic ascites associated with a marked elevation of serum lipase. Analysis of the ascitic fluid strongly supported its pancreatic origin, and conservative management with enteral nutrition and a somatostatin analogue was initiated. One week after biliopancreatic magnetic resonance imaging, the patient developed sudden deterioration with septic shock, tense ascites, acute kidney injury, and purulent ascitic fluid. Emergency laparoscopy was performed because of concern for secondary peritonitis from an occult gastrointestinal perforation. Approximately 9 L of purulent ascites were evacuated, followed by extensive peritoneal lavage and drainage. No gastrointestinal perforation or other intra-abdominal source of contamination was identified. Peritoneal fluid cultures isolated a fully susceptible Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis, while blood cultures remained negative. Antibiotic therapy was subsequently de-escalated to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid based on antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and a full seven-day course was completed. The postoperative course was favorable. Six weeks later, MRI showed complete resolution of the ascites and a 5-cm organized pancreatic collection communicating with the distal main pancreatic duct. This case highlights an unusual occurrence of Salmonella Enteritidis peritonitis complicating pancreatic ascites in the absence of gastrointestinal perforation or documented bacteremia. Sudden clinical deterioration in patients with pancreatic ascites should prompt immediate reassessment for infectious complications and, when indicated, urgent surgical exploration for source control. Definitive management of the pancreatic ductal leak may be deferred in selected patients when the infectious complication has been controlled and clinical evolution is favorable.

items.title: Transmural migration of an internal pancreaticojejunostomy stent causing delayed intra-abdominal sepsis: a case report.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Internal pancreatic duct stents are commonly used during pancreaticojejunostomy (PJ) reconstruction following pancreaticoduodenectomy to facilitate drainage and potentially reduce postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF). These stents are typically expected to migrate distally and pass without consequence. However, rare complications related to stent migration may occur and can present with atypical clinical and biochemical findings, creating diagnostic challenges.
CASE DESCRIPTION: A 63-year-old woman underwent pancreaticoduodenectomy for pancreatic adenocarcinoma with placement of an internal PJ stent. Her initial postoperative course was uneventful, with normal drain amylase levels. On postoperative day (POD) eight, she presented with fever, leukocytosis, and abdominal pain. Computed tomography (CT) demonstrated peripancreatic fluid and gas collections suspicious for POPF; however, drain amylase levels remained low, creating diagnostic uncertainty. Despite initial nonoperative management, the patient's clinical status deteriorated, prompting exploratory laparotomy. Intraoperatively, the PJ anastomosis was intact, but diffuse enteric contamination was present. Intraoperative ultrasound revealed transmural migration of the pancreatic duct stent through the jejunal wall into the mesentery, resulting in a concealed perforation with extraluminal leakage of enteric contents. The stent was retrieved via controlled enterotomy, the defect was repaired, and the abdomen was irrigated. The patient subsequently improved with resolution of sepsis and was discharged in stable condition.
CONCLUSIONS: Transmural migration of an internal PJ stent is a rare but serious complication that may present with intra-abdominal sepsis in the absence of elevated drain amylase levels. This case highlights an important diagnostic pitfall, as enteric contamination rather than pancreatic leakage may predominate. In patients with unexplained postoperative deterioration following pancreaticoduodenectomy, particularly when imaging is equivocal and biochemical markers are discordant, stent-related complications should be considered. Early recognition and prompt surgical intervention are critical for optimal outcomes.

items.title: Pancreatic Tuberculosis Mimicking Pancreatic Cancer in a Young Immunocompetent Man: A Case Report and Literature Review.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic TB is extremely rare, even in endemic areas. Clinically and radiographically, it may resemble a malignant process. Herein, we present a case of pancreatic TB who underwent surgery with a preoperative diagnosis of pancreatic malignancy.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 34-year-old Afghan man presented with a one-year history of intermittent epigastric pain, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Physical examination showed stable vital signs with mild epigastric tenderness. Laboratory examinations revealed mild anemia with mildly increased liver enzymes and lipase. The CA19-9 level in serum was mildly elevated, and the serologic test for HIV antibody was negative. An abdominal CT scan revealed a 57×30 mm multiloculated hypoattenuating mass-like lesion in the head of the pancreas with no evidence of biliary system dilation. As EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration/biopsy (EUS-FNA/FNB) was not available at our institution and the lesion was highly suspicious for pancreatic malignancy, the patient underwent Whipple resection. On macroscopic examination, a well-defined creamy soft mass with necrotic consistency was found in the head of the pancreas. Microscopic examination showed significant caseating granulomatous inflammation containing Langhans giant cells, and the Ziehl-Neelsen staining revealed a large number of acid-fast positive bacilli in favor of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Anti-TB medicine was administered. No clinical or radiologic deficits were discovered during the 10-month follow-up visits.
CONCLUSION: Pancreatic TB should be considered a differential diagnosis in pancreatic lesions, particularly in young patients from tuberculosis-endemic areas. Whenever feasible, preoperative EUS-guided FNA/FNB combined with microbiologic study may help avoid unnecessary invasive surgeries.

items.title: Exceptionally Durable Response to First-Line S-1 Monotherapy in Metastatic Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma: A Case Report.
items.abstract: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma with distant metastases is associated with a poor prognosis, and exceptionally durable responses to systemic chemotherapy are uncommon. We report a rare case of pancreatic adenocarcinoma with radiologically suspected multiple liver metastases that achieved a prolonged response to first-line tegafur/gimeracil/oteracil (S-1) monotherapy. A 76-year-old man with a history of cerebral infarction and diabetes mellitus was referred to our department because of rapidly worsening diabetes. Imaging revealed an approximately 3-cm pancreatic head tumor and multiple hepatic lesions highly suspicious for metastases. Serum carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) was markedly elevated. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) of the pancreatic head tumor demonstrated adenocarcinoma on both cytological and histopathological examinations. Gemcitabine plus nanoparticle albumin-bound paclitaxel (nab-paclitaxel) was proposed; however, the patient preferred oral treatment. Considering his age, quality of life, and treatment preference, S-1 monotherapy was initiated at 100 mg/day on a 2-week-on/2-week-off schedule. Following initiation of S-1, the pancreatic and hepatic lesions progressively regressed, accompanied by rapid normalization of CA19-9. By approximately 14 months after treatment initiation, the previously identifiable pancreatic primary tumor and hepatic lesions were no longer clearly visualized on computed tomography (CT). S-1 monotherapy was continued with few interruptions, and no apparent radiological progression was documented for approximately 47 months. Approximately two and a half months after the last CT showing no apparent progression, the patient developed fever and dyspnea. CT demonstrated newly developed bilateral ground-glass and interstitial pulmonary opacities, along with new-onset ascites, without evidence of regrowth of the pancreatic or hepatic lesions. S-1-induced interstitial lung disease (ILD) was clinically suspected; however, occult malignant progression could not be definitively excluded. His respiratory condition deteriorated despite treatment, and he subsequently died. This case demonstrates that an exceptionally durable response may rarely occur with first-line S-1 monotherapy even in pancreatic adenocarcinoma with radiologically suspected metastatic disease.

items.title: An Atypical Abdominal Presentation of Pancreatic Panniculitis in a Patient With Suspected Pancreatic Cancer: A Case Report.
items.abstract: Pancreatic panniculitis (PP) is an uncommon manifestation of pancreatic disorders and usually presents as painful erythematous subcutaneous nodules involving the lower extremities. We describe a 79-year-old man with a pancreatic head tumor clinically suspected to represent pancreatic cancer who developed a painful, erythematous, approximately 10-cm abdominal wall lesion. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed inflammatory changes involving the subcutaneous and abdominal wall adipose tissue. Despite the extensive lesion, pancreatic enzyme elevation was modest, with a lipase level of 157 IU/L and pancreatic amylase level of 86 IU/L. Malignant involvement and soft-tissue infection were initially considered because of the lesion's location and appearance. Histopathological examination demonstrated lobular panniculitis, fat necrosis, and anucleated adipocytes with thickened borders and eosinophilic material, consistent with ghost-like adipocytes of PP. Klebsiella pneumoniae was isolated from the aspirated material, raising the possibility of secondary bacterial infection. Cefmetazole was administered at 1 g twice daily for five days; subsequent susceptibility testing showed cefmetazole resistance. After the histopathological diagnosis of PP was established, symptomatic treatment with oral loxoprofen was initiated. The pain, erythema, and swelling gradually improved, and the lesion had markedly resolved by day 60, with corresponding improvement of the abdominal wall inflammatory changes on follow-up computed tomography. This case illustrates that PP may occur at an atypical abdominal site despite only modest pancreatic enzyme elevation and may mimic infection or malignant involvement. Histopathological evaluation of a subcutaneous lesion can be particularly valuable when clinical and biochemical findings are atypical, and a definitive pathological diagnosis of the underlying pancreatic lesion is not obtained.

items.title: Post-engagement CAR release, rather than equilibrium affinity, governs repetitive stromal targeting by CAR-NK cells
items.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) cell therapies have transformed haematological cancer treatment but remain largely ineffective against desmoplastic solid tumours, where a fibroblast-rich matrix restricts effector cell infiltration. Depleting that stroma requires repeated clearance of abundant fibroblasts, yet CAR binders are still commonly selected and optimized around equilibrium affinity. Here we show that how quickly a CAR releases antigen after killing, rather than how tightly it binds, governs repetitive stromal targeting. We identified endoglin (CD105) on the abundant fibroblasts organizing this barrier in pancreatic cancer, then screened CD105 binders in matched CARs. The lead binder bound 40-fold more weakly than the reference antibody yet killed fibroblasts far more effectively, dissociating 11-fold faster. The difference lay after cytolysis: killing was equally fast, release was not, and faster release reset the synapse, reduced antigen trogocytosis and sustained serial killing. In fibroblast-rich tumours, a humanized variant opened a window for mesothelin-directed CAR-T and CAR-NK cells. Release kinetics therefore determine whether a CAR cell works as a reusable stromal-remodelling effector, and tuning them may improve any CAR that must clear abundant targets.

Pemphigus herpetiformis: association with malignancies and therapeutic challenges.
items.abstract: This case series examines the histopathological, immunological, and therapeutic characteristics of 7 patients diagnosed with pemphigus herpetiformis (PH) at a tertiary hospital between 1989 and 2025. The most common clinical manifestation was pruritic annular lesions. Direct immunofluorescence was positive in all cases, whereas serological testing (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, indirect immunofluorescence, and immunoblotting) performed at 2 independent referral centers detected anti-desmoglein 1 antibodies in only 2 patients, with negative antigen-specific results in the remaining patients. An association between PH and malignancy was observed in 43% of cases, particularly with lung cancer, including the first reported case of PH associated with pancreatic cancer. These findings underscore the importance of recognizing this potential association to optimize patient management. Regarding treatment, conventional therapies such as corticosteroids and dapsone showed variable efficacy, whereas rituximab appeared less effective than in other pemphigus variants.
